articles.title: Metaplanet to Issue $329M Convertible Bonds to Pay Debt, Fund Share Buybacks
articles.text:
Metaplanet to issue $329M convertible bonds to pay debt, fund share buybacks
Metaplanet plans to issue zero-interest bonds with a five-year maturity to improve its debt structure and cut its reliance on Bitcoin-collateralized loans without selling holdings.
Metaplanet will issue 52 billion yen ($329 million) in zero-coupon, euro-yen convertible bonds due in 2031.
Japanese investment and Bitcoin treasury company plans to use about 23.6 billion yen ($149 million) of the net proceeds to repay Bitcoin-collateralized loans and about 28.3 billion yen ($179 million) for share buybacks, according to a Tuesday announcement.
The buybacks are part of Metaplanet’s new share repurchasing program, which targets up to 60 billion yen ($380 million) in total buybacks.
The proceeds seek to improve the treasury company’s debt structure by reducing its reliance on Bitcoin-collateralized loans without selling any Bitcoin (BTC) holdings. Metaplanet ranks as the second-largest Bitcoin treasury firm, with 44,000 BTC in total holdings, worth $3.6 billion, according to BitcoinTreasuries.
Metaplanet’s share price closed 1.5% lower in Tokyo on Tuesday, adding to its 52.6% 12-month slide, according to Yahoo Finance.
Earlier this month, Metaplanet revealed a revised capital allocation framework proposing to allocate up to 15% of total assets to strategic investments to fund its Bitcoin accumulation and dividend payments.
In September, management drew shareholder criticism for expanding Metaplanet’s Series 10 executive stock option pool almost sevenfold. On Sept. 11, the Tokyo-based company shared plans to cut the stock pool by 41% by reducing the number of potential shares underlying the rights by 131.3 million, from 319.464 million to 188.19 million, the level before its September 2025 international share offering.
Related: Metaplanet buys 2,823 BTC, surpasses 43,000 in Bitcoin holdings

articles.title: MediaMarkt Parent Pulls Ledger Wallets Amid Tampering Reports
articles.text:
MediaMarktSaturn pulls Ledger products amid tampering reports
European retailer MediaMarkt pulled Ledger products as the wallet maker probes tampering reports beyond CryptoBilis in Southeast Asia.
[Update Oct. 13, 1:10 PM UTC: This article has been updated with new statements from MediaMarktSaturn and Ledger.]
MediaMarktSaturn, the parent company of European electronics retailer MediaMarkt, has removed Ledger products from its physical stores and online platforms amid reports of tampered hardware wallets.
“The products have been removed from our product lineup internationally in all of our countries. We did this as a precautionary measure,” a MediaMarktSaturn spokesperson told Cointelegraph.
Ledger said Tuesday that MediaMarktSaturn suspended sales in coordination with the wallet maker following a report of a hardware implant from a customer in Germany. Ledger said no fund losses had been reported in connection with that case and that it had no indication its infrastructure, systems or services were compromised.
An X user known as Johannes claimed Monday that he purchased two Ledger wallets from separate MediaMarkt stores. He said both contained unauthorized cables and cellular modules.
The security concerns emerged Friday after Ledger said it is investigating reports of losses involving devices sold through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis. Ledger said Tuesday that implants transmitted users’ recovery phrases over cellular networks and that it was investigating reports beyond CryptoBilis.
Separately, former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès said Tuesday that a Ledger Flex purchased at Singapore’s airport contained a spy implant. Ledger responded by referring users to its latest CryptoBilis investigation update, without directly addressing the Singapore case.
Felix Ng contributed reporting.
Related: Ledger implant tests Bitcoin ETFs as safer custodial solutions than hardware wallets

articles.title: Trezor Cuts Its Resellers After Ledger Finds Spy Implant in Crypto Wallets - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Trezor told partners their reseller authorization ends January 1, 2027, and that it will ship them no new stock, saying there is no evidence its devices were compromised.
- Ledger's Donjon team says wallets sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis held an implant that captures recovery phrases from the screen and sends them over LTE.
- Onchain investigator Specter traced more than $86 million in suspected thefts, a figure Ledger says it has not verified.
Trezor is cutting its network of authorized resellers, telling partners their authorization ends on January 1, 2027, days after rival hardware wallet manufacturer Ledger started an investigation that eventually confirmed a hidden spy implant in crypto wallets sold through a third-party store.
The company announced the move on X on Tuesday, saying “there is not a single piece of evidence” that Trezor devices have been compromised. It described the cut as a preventive step taken out of caution.
“Following recent supply-chain incidents, we decided to reduce the number of resellers so we can more effectively check those we work with,” Trezor wrote.
A hardware wallet is a small device that keeps the secret keys to your crypto offline, away from hackers. Setting one up produces a 24-word recovery phrase that works as a master password: whoever has those words can empty the wallet from anywhere in the world.
Ledger's Donjon security team says wallets sold by CryptoBilis, a reseller in Southeast Asia, contained an unauthorized component that reads the screen and decodes the recovery phrase when it appears. The spy implant then sends the words out over LTE, the same mobile data network your phone uses, through an eSIM, a SIM card built into the hardware. Ledger says the implant does not alter the chip that stores the keys or the device's operating system, so a tampered wallet looks and works normally.
Trezor CCO Danny Sanders shared the letter that the company sent to those providers that Trezor is ditching. “If you are receiving this letter, your authorization ends on 1 January 2027. On that date we will remove you from our list of authorized Trezor resellers,” the letter reads. “I am sorry. This decision says nothing about your effort or the way you represented us.”
This is a precautionary measure to protect our supply chain and our customers,” he wrote. “If things change in the future we will review it.”
Affected resellers will get no new stock, but they can keep selling what they have through Black Friday and the holiday season. Sanders said the decision just reflects how many partners Trezor can vet closely itself.
Neither the post nor the letter says how many resellers are affected. Trezor says it reviewed each country on its own, weighing revenue and distribution against its own presence there, and that resellers who stay will face an updated legal framework and tighter rules on how devices are sourced, stored, and handled.
Trezor said on X earlier this week that CryptoBilis was already off its seller list and that it had received no reports of tampered Trezors from the retailer.
Hi, don’t open it. Forcing the casing open can damage the device, and if it’s a Safe 7, the built-in battery makes that genuinely risky. If something about your device worries you, reach out via https://t.co/wzwW038oLv, and we’ll take a look.
We are actively investigating the…
— Trezor (@Trezor) October 12, 2026
In May 2022, Trezor warned that counterfeit Model T wallets were being sold on a Russian marketplace by a seller that was not an authorized reseller. The devices had been opened, resealed, and fitted with replaced internal components, and Trezor said the recovery phrases they generated were predictable or predefined, meaning someone else could already know the words.
Trezor's advice then was to buy only from its official shop or an authorized reseller. The second option is the network it is now shrinking.
In August, shipping partner ShipMonk exposed Trezor customer data after unauthorized access, and Trezor's September update put the total at 80,689 customers. Trezor says its systems, devices, private keys, and wallet backups were not affected.
Ledger told anyone who bought from CryptoBilis in the past 90 days not to set up their device, and told those who already did to move their funds to a new seed phrase on a device bought from Ledger. Ledger and Trezor have each warned buyers against unauthorized sellers.

articles.title: Metaplanet unveils $380 million share buyback after stock crashes nearly 90% from peak
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Metaplanet unveiled a $380 million buyback program alongside a $329 million convertible bond offering to restructure its finances.
- The financing would reduce Bitcoin-backed loans without selling BTC, while repurchases could improve investors' Bitcoin exposure per share.
- CEO Simon Gerovich's 55 million-share lending arrangement could enable selling pressure that offsets demand from the buyback.
Metaplanet plans to raise $329 million to refinance Bitcoin-backed loans and fund share buybacks after its stock has declined 90% from its peak.
On Oct. 13, the Japanese Bitcoin treasury company announced plans to issue ¥52 billion ($329 million) in unsecured, zero-coupon Euro-yen convertible bonds due in 2031.
Expected to close on Oct. 29, the offering will target investors primarily in Europe and Asia, with the bonds slated for listing on the Singapore Exchange.
The financing would let Metaplanet replace part of its interest-bearing, Bitcoin-collateralized debt with borrowing that requires no regular interest payments. The company expects the restructuring to free up pledged Bitcoin, reduce financing costs and improve financial flexibility without selling its cryptocurrency holdings.
Bitcoin-backed debt pressures Metaplanet's capital strategy
Metaplanet's refinancing comes as its reliance on Bitcoin-backed borrowing has exceeded the company's internal risk limits.
As of Sept. 30, the company had approximately $649.5 million outstanding under an $800 million credit facility secured by its Bitcoin holdings.
That represented 17.7% of the net asset value of its Bitcoin reserves, well above management's guideline to keep the ratio below 10%.
Metaplanet, which held 44,000 BTC at the end of September, acknowledged that further declines in Bitcoin prices could increase the borrowing ratio by reducing the value of its cryptocurrency holdings.
To address this exposure, the company plans to allocate about ¥23.6 billion ($149 million) of the new bond proceeds to repay part of its outstanding loans in November.
The repayment would reduce borrowing under the facility to approximately $500.5 million. Based on September's reported asset values, that would lower the borrowing ratio to roughly 13.6%, assuming Bitcoin's value and other conditions remained unchanged.
However, that would still leave Metaplanet above its preferred leverage threshold, suggesting that the company remains exposed to further declines in Bitcoin prices.
Metaplanet acknowledged that replacing its existing Bitcoin-backed loans with convertible bonds would not immediately reduce its total liabilities, even as it lowers interest expenses and reliance on pledged collateral.
Although the new bonds mature in 2031, investors can demand repayment after three years, potentially forcing the company to refinance earlier than the stated maturity.
Metaplanet targets share buybacks as stock struggles
Beyond restructuring its debt, Metaplanet also plans to allocate up to ¥28.3 billion ($179 million) of the proceeds to share repurchases as part of a newly authorized ¥60 billion ($380 million) buyback program.
The company simultaneously terminated its previous ¥75 billion ($475 million) repurchase authorization, established in October 2025, under which it had not acquired any shares.
The new program allows Metaplanet to repurchase up to 200 million common shares, representing approximately 14.7% of its outstanding stock, between Oct. 14, 2026, and Oct. 13, 2027.
It plans to begin the program on Oct. 14 through the Tokyo Stock Exchange's ToSTNeT-3 off-auction trading system, targeting up to 96.9 million shares for approximately ¥25.3 billion ($160 million).
If fully executed, the planned transaction could reduce the company's outstanding share count by about 7.1%, though the final volume will depend on the number of shares offered for sale.
The renewed buyback effort comes amid a prolonged decline in Metaplanet's stock, as Bitcoin's struggles have weighed on investor sentiment toward cryptocurrency treasury companies.
Metaplanet shares have declined approximately 36% this year, closing at ¥261 on Oct. 13. The stock has also lost nearly 90% of its value from its June 2025 peak of ¥1,930.
By comparison, Strategy, the world's largest publicly traded corporate Bitcoin holder, has gained about 1% this year despite cryptocurrency market volatility.
The contrasting performances highlight the challenges Metaplanet faces in maintaining investor demand for its shares while pursuing a Bitcoin accumulation strategy.
Its declining valuation has also complicated its ability to raise capital through common equity without diluting existing shareholders.
Under its revised capital allocation policy, Metaplanet generally avoids issuing common shares when its market-to-net-asset-value ratio (mNAV) falls below 1.
The measure compares the company's enterprise value with the net asset value of its Bitcoin holdings. Issuing shares below that threshold could reduce existing shareholders' per-share exposure to Bitcoin.
Repurchases could improve that metric by reducing outstanding shares, although the benefits will depend on execution prices and any subsequent equity issuance.
However, the buyback program comes with a potential counterweight. Metaplanet CEO Simon Gerovich has agreed to lend up to 55 million personally held shares through his wholly owned Gerovich Family Holdings Limited to support hedging activities associated with the convertible bonds.
The arrangement, which carries an annual lending fee of 0.75%, would allow investors to borrow and potentially sell Metaplanet shares to hedge their exposure.
Such transactions could create selling pressure even as the company repurchases its own stock, although the number of shares ultimately borrowed or sold remains uncertain.
The bonds could also dilute existing shareholders if investors convert them into equity. Metaplanet intends to set the conversion price above the share price corresponding to an mNAV of 1 at issuance, but it has not yet determined the final conversion terms.

articles.title: AI Powered PlayStation Crack Could Let You Play GTA 6 on PC at Launch - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- AnyPS5 is an open-source, AI-powered project on GitHub that converts PS5 game executables into programs that run natively on PC.
- Speculators believe that the tool will allow users to get higher performance out of PS5 games by using high-powered PCs.
- Some gamers hope that the project will be able to run GTA VI on PC at launch, although Discord members warn there's likely to be roadblocks.
Vibe coders are porting PlayStation 5 applications to Windows and Linux, leaving some users optimistic that the project will unlock better performance for PS5 games, and could even work for GTA 6 at launch.
AnyPS5 is an open-source, AI-powered project on GitHub that converts PS5 game executables into programs that run natively on PC, swapping Sony’s system libraries for its own version rather than emulating the console. A community-run tracker lists more than 180 PS5 titles that have been tried with the tool, but only a handful have been verified as playable.
An important distinction to make is that this is not an emulator and that games will be running natively on PC. As a result, some speculators believe that users will be able to get better performance from PS5 games by playing them on a high-powered PC.
"GTA 6 most likely will be able to run on your PC at launch, and [with] significantly higher frames than it would on your PS5," pseudonymous gaming content creator Schlayerr said on TikTok. "We live in a crazy time."
"Technically, this is feasible given the similarities between console and PC architectures, and AI can dramatically accelerate the reverse engineering work," Theodore Agranat, Director of Web3 at Gunzilla Games, the game studio behind battle royale Off the Grid, told Decrypt. However, he remained skeptical over whether they "can deliver the quality, performance, and fidelity players expect from AAA games at scale."
🚨 ANYPS5 SYSTEM LIBRARY SUPPORT JUST HIT 86%! 🤯🔥
Development has been FAST since Friday, and the library side is becoming the next phase to watch.
• 3,005 / 3,475 declared system functions implemented
• Overall system library support is now 86.47%
• libc: 99%
•… pic.twitter.com/S1AekKNtOf
— Chris Mizo (@MizoChris) October 12, 2026
The latest project update claims that 100% of the PS5 GPU shaders have been ported while 88% of the system libraries have been ported. Discord community members believe the final 12% for system libraries is likely to take a long time, especially as new system libraries are continuously being discovered.
In the Discord showcase channel, some users have shown off rudimentary demos of PS5 games on PC. One community developer reported running GTA 5 at 27 frames per second, or FPS, in the performance graphics mode. Others have reported getting 4 FPS on Epic Mickey, 25 FPS on Phasmophobia, and 60 FPS on Vampire Survivors. It's still a work in progress.
Still, in all of these examples, the games aren't fully playable due to the incomplete system library port as well as game-specific bugs being encountered.
A potential roadblock in playing GTA 6 on PC at launch is a mandatory firmware update, Discord members say. This is because the AnyPS5 project would need to overhaul its converted files to the latest update in order to get GTA 6 running. As such, there is likely to be a delay before the game is available on PC via AnyPS5.
"Firmware updates could create hurdles, particularly around DRM, but likely wouldn’t invalidate the entire approach," Agranat said.
A response to Sony's disc ban?
AnyPS5 bans any form of piracy in its Discord server, meaning using the tool requires purchasing the game on the PlayStation Store. That said, there is nothing stopping an individual using AnyPS5 with a pirated copy of a video game.
Some PlayStation users have speculated that the movement is a response to Sony's plan to discontinue physical game discs.
"The reason this all happened is because Sony discontinued discs," pseudonymous gaming content creator The 1st Gamer said on TikTok. "They wanted to go digital, and they did, but just not on PS5."
Sony announced in July that it plans to stop producing physical discs at the start of 2028. The decision was met with major community backlash, including a petition called "Don't Kill the Disc" gaining over 385,000 signatures. Shawn Layden, a former PlayStation executive, called the move a "heavily spreadsheeted decision" and said it has damaged the company's reputation.
In August, Sony argued in a California court that purchasing a digital game in the PlayStation Store does not equate to ownership of it. Sony claimed its Terms of Service and the Software Product License Agreement explain this and that users should understand it as a fact.
"Even without Sony stopping physical discs, this was bound to happen with AI accelerating dev," Agrant said. "My hope is that projects like this push platform holders to offer the same flexibility themselves, but at a much higher standard," he told Decrypt, hoping for a future where Sony rolls out games on PC as well as console. "That would be a genuine win-win."

articles.title: Bitcoin Battles $84,000 Sellers Amid South Korea’s Tech Sell-Off
articles.text:
Bitcoin hits $84K resistance as Korean tech rout deepens KOSPI losses
Bitcoin’s liquidity kept BTC price below $84,000 amid a mounting South Korean tech and semiconductor stock sell-off.
Bitcoin (BTC) rebounded toward $84,000 on Tuesday as crypto markets skirted fresh losses for South Korean stock markets.
Key points:
- Bitcoin diverged from plummeting Asian tech stocks on Tuesday, rebounding from a low near $81,000.
- Semiconductors led an exodus from South Korea’s KOSPI amid ongoing investors’ nerves over AI and Chinese competition.
- BTC price upside was capped at $84,000 by a wall of resistance on exchange order books.
South Korea’s KOSPI loses 200-day trend line as panic returns
Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD up more than 2.5% on Tuesday, reaching $83,944 on Bitstamp to retrace Monday’s drop.
BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
The gains came as a fresh tech sell-off gathered pace on South Korea’s KOSPI Composite Index, which extended its losses for the week to 7.4%. The index fell below its 200-day moving average for the first time since late July.
KOSPI Composite Index one-day chart with 200-day moving average. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Semiconductor stocks came under particular pressure, with SK Hynix closing more than 10% lower, while the rout compounded existing problems for Samsung after it reported lower-than-expected Q3 earnings last week. Foreign investors sold around 173 trillion won ($129 billion) worth of SK Hynix and Samsung shares since the start of 2026, accounting for the vast majority of year-to-date KOSPI sales.
The weakness echoes August’s sell-off, when concerns over the AI boom and associated corporate debt obligations sparked sharp losses that soon spread to global markets.
“Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks,” UBP senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling told CNBC on Monday.
Ling was among those who flagged competition from China as increasingly problematic for Korean investors, while acknowledging that the Chinese sector still faced “technology hurdles.”
Bitcoin price rebounds despite waning ETF demand
In contrast to the August sell-off, Bitcoin avoided a copycat move and moved toward the upper end of its local trading range between $80,000 and $87,000.
Related: South Korea moves to block 27 crypto websites, including KuCoin, MEXC
At the time, analysis attributed Bitcoin’s relative strength to potential monetary policy easing by central banks. Major US inflation data is due out this week ahead of the Federal Reserve’s Oct. 28 rate decision, with markets expecting rates to stay at their current levels of 2.75-4%.
Bitcoin’s relative strength also comes despite declining investor appetite for BTC exposure in October, with outflows from the US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recording $451 million in net outflows so far this month, including $69 million on Monday.

articles.title: UK Court Rules Chinese Law Applies to 61K Bitcoin Claims
articles.text:
Chinese fraud victims lose key court battle over 61,000 Bitcoin
Chinese fraud victims seeking to recover 61,000 seized Bitcoin face a legal setback after a UK court ruled that Chinese law governs their claims.
Chinese fraud victims seeking to recover 61,000 Bitcoin seized by the British government have lost a key legal battle after London’s High Court ruled that Chinese law, rather than English law, should govern claims to the assets.
On Monday, Justice Mark Turner rejected arguments for applying English law or a combination of English and Chinese law to the victims’ ownership claims. The judge ruled that Chinese law must determine whether the claimants have property rights in the seized Bitcoin, leaving the validity of claims for subsequent proceedings.
“The relevant damage occurred in China. The Applicants parted with their money in China,” Turner wrote. “The contractual relationships thereby induced were entered into in China.”
The dispute stems from an investment fraud scheme orchestrated by Zhimin Qian between 2014 and 2017, with British authorities seizing the assets during a money-laundering investigation. In March, victims challenged a proposed compensation arrangement involving a Chinese redress scheme, arguing that it could leave British authorities with much of the gains from Bitcoin’s appreciation.
The victims had sought to apply English law because it could have allowed them to claim direct ownership of the Bitcoin, rather than merely seek compensation as creditors. However, the UK ruling does not determine who ultimately owns the seized assets, with the victims’ property rights under Chinese law still to be assessed.
Fraud victims plan to appeal Bitcoin ruling
According to a Financial Times report, Law firm Fieldfisher, which represents claimants in the dispute, is pursuing an appeal against Turner’s ruling.
Despite the ruling, the case will remain before the High Court in London rather than being transferred to a Chinese court. FT reported that the next stage will involve expert evidence on Chinese law to determine whether the victims can establish ownership interests in the Bitcoin.
The Crown Prosecution Service told the FT that a further hearing would examine how Chinese law applies and whether any victims can establish an interest in the seized assets.
Related: UK sanctions three crypto exchanges tied to Russian illicit funds
The dispute involves more than 128,000 investors reportedly affected by the fraud, according to earlier Cointelegraph coverage. In March, Cointelegraph reported that law firm Candey represented about 5,700 victims.
Prosecutors previously argued that certain claims could allow a smaller group of victims and litigation funders to recover more than their actual losses.
The seized Bitcoin is currently worth more than $5 billion, according to CoinGecko.

articles.title: Ledger Finds LTE Implant That Stole Recovery Phrases in Suspected $86M Drain - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Ledger said its Donjon security team found an unauthorized hardware implant in a wallet sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis.
- The implant reads the 24-word recovery phrase from the device's screen during setup and transmits it over LTE using a provisioned eSIM.
- Ledger has not confirmed how many users were affected or how much was lost, and is reviewing reports of implants in other devices and locations.
Ledger said its security research team has found an unauthorized hardware implant that captured recovery phrases inside wallets sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis, in a tweet on Tuesday.
The Paris-based hardware wallet manufacturer said it confirmed the implant on Saturday in one affected user's device. All confirmed losses from the incident, which Ledger disclosed on Friday, involve devices sold through CryptoBilis, and the company said it has not verified a drain linked to a device bought elsewhere.
Update from Ledger Donjon on the CryptoBilis investigation 🔽@DonjonLedger is investigating Ledger signers sold by CryptoBilis, a reseller in Southeast Asia, that contained an unauthorized hardware implant. Ledger confirmed this on October 10th for one affected user's signer.…
— Ledger (@Ledger) October 13, 2026
A Ledger device, which the company calls a signer, shows a 24-word recovery phrase during setup. Anyone holding that phrase can restore the wallet and control its funds.
According to the analysis by Ledger Donjon, the company's security team, the implant sits inside the device's enclosure and reads what is shown on the screen. When it detects the recovery phrase screens, its microcontroller decodes the words and transmits them over LTE using a provisioned eSIM.
The implant is a separate component, Ledger said, adding that it does not modify the device's Secure Element or the Ledger operating system, nor does it alter transactions or signatures.
CryptoBilis has confirmed it stopped selling Ledger devices while the investigation continues, according to Ledger.
Ledger said it has not confirmed the total number of affected users or the value lost, and that figures circulating online come from third parties it has not fully verified. Onchain investigator Specter traced more than $86 million in suspected thefts across Ethereum, Tron and Bitcoin, Decrypt reported on Friday.
Ledger reviewing reports beyond CryptoBilis
Ledger said it is also reviewing reports of implants in other signers and locations. An X user has claimed to have found two tampered Ledger devices bought from retail stores in Europe, a claim that has not been independently verified.
The company told CryptoBilis buyers who have not set up their device not to do so and to contact Ledger Support. Those who have should move their assets promptly to a new device with a new recovery phrase, and should not enter or restore any recovery phrase on a device bought from CryptoBilis.
Users who lost funds or hold a tampered device should also file a report with local law enforcement, Ledger said, and should not send the device to anyone, or open it, before speaking to Ledger Support or the police.
Buyers who did not purchase from CryptoBilis can inspect the inside of their device using a Ledger guide, though the company warned that opening a signer can damage it and urged users to back up their recovery phrase first.
Ledger reiterated that it will never call users, message them directly or ask for their recovery phrase. The Donjon will analyze the devices it receives and share more as the investigation continues, the company said.

articles.title: US deposit rates choke USDC adoption, and a BIS model reveals why
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Historical BIS estimates link deposit repricing to a larger slowdown in USDC growth than USDT growth.
- Coinbase funds variable USDC rewards, making platform eligibility and rates part of the adoption comparison.
- Substitution evidence measures demand for balances and does not establish losses of aggregate bank deposits or lending.
A study released by the Bank for International Settlements on Oct. 13 links bank deposit repricing to a larger estimated slowdown in USDC growth than in USDT growth, so banks' offers can shape stablecoin adoption differently for each issuer.
Higher deposit rates give holders a stronger financial reason to keep balances at a bank. In the study, a one-basis-point deposit-rate increase was associated with about 4.8% less cumulative USDC growth over ten weeks, compared with 1.9% less growth for USDT.
Researchers Rashad Ahmed and Iñaki Aldasoro used weekly data from January 2019 through June 2025. The BIS published the October edition after a first version appeared on March 24, and the earlier abstract already reported the stronger USDC response.
Exchanges can offer variable rewards to eligible customers, adding another price to the competition for balances. That makes the historical issuer split useful for adoption forecasts while leaving today's bank-versus-platform comparison to be established.
How the issuer estimates compare
The paper's deposit-rate measure averages six national savings and money-market deposit-account series. It is distinct from the Federal Reserve's policy rate and from the rate on any particular high-paying account.
The ten-week OLS point estimates separate the two issuers:
| Stablecoin | Estimated change in cumulative log market-cap growth per 1 basis point of deposit repricing | 
|---|---|
| USDC | −4.8 percentage points | 
| USDT | −1.9 percentage points | 
Ordinary least squares (OLS) is the baseline statistical model, while the negative estimates describe slower growth relative to the model's comparison path.
The authors interpret USDC's larger response as consistent with its closer connections to US institutional and decentralized finance users. Those holders may have more reason to compare bank deposits with stablecoin balances, and they associate USDT's weaker response with its offshore and developing-economy uses.
The data cannot identify which individual holders switched or which bank accounts were involved, so the issuer explanation is an interpretation of the pattern.
For adoption forecasts, the implication is that a deposit-rate assumption applied to all stablecoins can conceal different competitive pressures. The point estimates suggest a stronger US deposit-pricing relationship for USDC in this sample, without establishing a fixed response for either token in every market environment.
For stablecoins in aggregate, the baseline ten-week estimate is about 2.8% less cumulative growth per basis point of deposit repricing. A second model, using an instrumental-variable approach intended to isolate deposit repricing, produces a larger estimate of about 9.1% less growth.
That approach exploits banks' stronger pass-through of policy-rate changes when the federal-funds target midpoint four weeks earlier was at least 3.125%. It depends on the resulting variation affecting stablecoin demand through deposit repricing after the other controls.
The controls cover policy and Treasury rates, Bitcoin prices, the dollar index, and market volatility, helping distinguish deposit-price competition from broader investment conditions, without proving the identification assumption.
The authors flag instrument weakness: the first-stage F-statistic is 9.78, below the conventional threshold of 10 they cite. With only one high-rate episode in the sample, the larger estimate has limited evidence to support its application to a different rate cycle.
In the paper's instrumental-variable charts, USDC's ten-week 95% confidence band remains below zero, while USDT's includes zero.
A separate deposit-tier comparison also supports the direction of the relationship, using differences in how banks reprice preferred money-market and savings accounts.
Checks for the Silicon Valley Bank episode, crypto events, trading volume, and DeFi yields retain negative relationships. Responses among balances supplied to lending protocols remain imprecise. The evidence supports competition, but its magnitude depends on the model and sample.
Rewards change what holders compare
The return on a stablecoin balance is also shaped by the platform on which it sits. In research published June 19, the BIS distinguished two economic models for exchange payments to stablecoin holders.
Under reserve-based remuneration, an exchange transmits part of the income generated by the issuer's reserve assets to holders. Under activity-based remuneration, payments are tied to lending, trading, and other market activity.
The bulletin uses Coinbase and Binance as respective examples, while acknowledging that the boundaries are imperfect.
In its historical exchange-yield evidence, Coinbase's USDC holding yield followed policy and reserve yields more closely, while Binance's yields were more exposed to crypto activity. These are different ways to fund returns on balances, with different reasons those returns change.
Coinbase's current rewards terms describe USDC Rewards as a loyalty program funded by the exchange without using or lending a customer's USDC without instruction.
Coinbase also requires customers to be in an eligible region, be eligible to trade, and hold at least $1 of USDC. Its FAQ also requires Coinbase One membership in several regions, including the US and UK.
Rates vary by country, account type, and ongoing experimentation, and Coinbase can change them or discontinue the program. The public FAQ directs users to account-specific rates and does not establish one current annual percentage yield (APY) available to every USDC holder.
These conditions complicate a bank-account comparison. The relevant return depends on the actual customer and offer, alongside any membership costs and differences in risk. Coinbase says USDC balances in its accounts are not deposit accounts and lack FDIC or SIPC insurance.
Exchange rewards already existed during part of the study's sample, and the working paper acknowledges third-party yields and includes a DeFi-yield control in its robustness analysis.
That control does not estimate today's Coinbase membership requirements or every exchange's account-specific reward spread. Native issuer interest, exchange-funded rewards and yields from lending tokens remain distinct mechanisms.
Demand competition leaves the lending question open
The working paper's authors explain that stablecoin funds are ultimately reinvested, potentially redistributing deposits across institutions and depositor types depending on the issuer's counterparties.
Reserve routing and depositor composition could affect bank funding costs. The current demand estimates address a different part of that chain: how stablecoin balances respond to what banks offer depositors.
A larger response for USDC cannot be converted directly into a figure for lost bank lending. That would also require evidence on where reserves go, how banks replace funding and how they adjust credit provision.
The study estimates responses to changes in deposit rates, but its coefficients cannot be applied directly to a Federal Reserve rate move, because bank repricing and the return available on each platform are separate inputs.
A useful forecast would distinguish issuers, the location and preferences of their holders, banks' repricing, and access to exchange rewards. Updated evidence connecting issuer growth with the actual bank-versus-platform returns available to comparable users would help establish how far the historical relationship extends into the next phase of adoption.
USDC is +0.02% over the past 24 hours and currently sits at rank #6 by market cap.

articles.title: Ledger Says LTE Implants Copied CryptoBilis Wallet Recovery Phrases
articles.text:
Ledger details LTE-enabled spy implants in wallets sold by CryptoBilis
Ledger detailed how LTE-enabled implants exposed wallet recovery phrases as CryptoBilis halted sales and Trezor and OneKey cut ties with the reseller.
Malicious implants in Ledger wallets sold by CryptoBilis captured users’ recovery phrases from device screens and transmitted them over cellular networks, the French hardware wallet maker said.
Ledger Donjon, the company’s security research team, found that the implants used a microcontroller to decode the 24-word phrases displayed during setup and transmitted the data over LTE networks using an embedded SIM (eSIM), according to a Tuesday X post by Ledger.
The implants did not compromise the devices’ security chips or alter transactions, Ledger said.
The incident surfaced Friday after crypto losses were reported involving Ledger devices sold through CryptoBilis, a reseller listed as authorized in Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines.
Ledger confirmed Saturday that one affected device contained an unauthorized implant. Blockchain investigator Specter said losses could exceed $86 million, while cybersecurity outlet Yfarmx raised its own estimate to $103 million. Ledger hasn’t confirmed the total.
Ledger says it has sold more than 8 million hardware wallets, devices that keep users’ private keys offline and let them approve transactions on-device.
Ledger probes implants beyond CryptoBilis
Ledger urged users who suspect tampering to contact its support team and file a police report.
Ledger directed concerned customers who bought devices elsewhere to an inspection guide, which warns that opening a device could damage it and advises users to back up their recovery phrases first.
Although confirmed losses have so far involved devices sold by CryptoBilis, Ledger said it is examining reports beyond the reseller.
Separately, X user Johannes posted photos of two Ledger devices he said he bought from separate stores of MediaMarkt, a European consumer electronics chain. He said he found implants in both devices. Ledger has not confirmed whether the European reports are linked to the CryptoBilis incident.
CryptoBilis halts all wallet sales as Trezor, OneKey cut ties
CryptoBilis said in an X post on Saturday that it had suspended sales and shipments of all hardware wallet brands across Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia, expanding an earlier halt limited to Ledger devices.
The reseller also temporarily closed its physical stores and said it was reviewing its processes with independent specialists.
Related: Ledger implant tests Bitcoin ETFs as safer custodial solutions than hardware wallets
Trezor said Monday that it had received no reports of tampered Trezor devices sold through CryptoBilis and found no indication that its products were affected. It nevertheless removed CryptoBilis from its authorized reseller network.
OneKey reported no related user losses as well, but terminated CryptoBilis’ reseller authorization. It also suspended onboarding new resellers and began reviewing its existing distribution network. The company offered free replacements for OneKey devices purchased from CryptoBilis between March 1 and Oct. 12, 2026, with customers able to apply through Dec. 31.

articles.title: Lido DAO exposes token flaw and forces a budget review
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Lido contributors are discussing a budget-linked buyback threshold for the 2027 grant request.
- NEST’s counter measures spending capacity, and its allocator had funded no purchases when checked Oct. 13.
- Annual resets lift modeled purchases about 8% without improving underlying profit.
Lido’s DAO is debating whether its 2027 grant budget should guide automated purchases of the LDO governance token.
The Oct. 7 discussion puts two choices on the table: link NEST’s revenue threshold to approved spending, or periodically clear the buyback engine’s negative spending counter.
NEST had made no purchases funded by its allocator when checked on Oct. 13. Genuine cost cuts could leave more income available for buying, while a reset would only remove past constraints.
Governance contributor Kuzmich proposed the budget link on Oct. 7. In an Oct. 9 response, Jenya_K supported considering it in the 2027 grant request, but said the amount must come from bottom-up planning.
Kuzmich’s Oct. 11 follow-up corrected the treatment of staking rebates and tested profits without assumed treasury income.
What the counter measures
Under Lido’s implemented specification, NEST compares measured staking revenue with a daily baseline of $109,589, approximately $40 million a year. Half the difference feeds a running spending counter.
Revenue below the baseline subtracts from that counter, and stronger revenue must repair the shortfall before purchases can start. A treasury can hold assets while the counter remains negative, and a positive counter would not by itself establish accounting profit.
The latest captured checkpoint on Oct. 13 recorded a counter of minus $564,230.96 and a skipped allocation.
Separately, the allocator held about 41.12 stETH when checked on Oct. 13. Its complete indexed transfer history showed one 41-stETH top-up on Aug. 28 and no outgoing trans
Any future spending must satisfy sufficient counter capacity and funded stETH. It also faces a $50,000 daily cap, a $10 million cap over fixed 365-day windows, and a $1,000 allocation minimum.
Lido’s separate discretionary stETH-to-LDO acquisitions are a different program, and the community reconstruction identifies an August trade as a route test.
NEST does not currently capture monthly Community Staking Module rebates or Earn income. Jenya_K said CSM rebates are already included in financial reporting, so adding them again to reported net revenue would double-count them.
Lido’s unaudited accounts for the first half show $15.7 million in net staking revenue plus $230,000 from Earn, producing $15.9 million in net DAO revenue. Foundations expenses of $14.3 million left an operating surplus of $1.6 million, and a $6 million Kelp-related one-off turned the total result into a $4.4 million loss.
The report separately places $1.4 million of treasury income and a $60.9 million asset-price effect in its treasury bridge, outside the profit-and-loss statement. Jenya_K also warned that treasury operations can include losses.
The 2026 grant request presents a $43.8 million baseline, and the first-half report references $41 million and projects full-year expenses of $37.7 million. The cited materials do not explicitly reconcile the two baseline labels, and none is interchangeable with NEST’s $40 million revenue threshold.
The budget model needs an expense correction
Kuzmich’s Oct. 11 model uses 1,000 ETH price paths over 12 months from Oct. 1, beginning at $2,679.84 with 61% annual volatility and no expected arithmetic price drift. Its purchase frequencies are not measured probabilities of what will happen next.
In the published Oct. 1 simulations under the current rule, mean purchases were about $2.3 million, but the median was zero. Stronger ETH paths lift the average even when more than half the simulations produce no purchases.
Lower budget-linked thresholds produce larger purchases in that model. However, its profit comparison contains a consequential mismatch: the forum says actual expenses match the approved budget, while the code scales a forecast expense curve by each budget divided by $43.8 million.
That curve implies about $39.8 million of expenses across the modeled year before scaling, and only $27.3 million in the row labeled $30 million.
The table below holds the published revenue paths and purchase rules constant, but sets actual expenses equal to each threshold. Profit excludes treasury income and is measured before purchases.
| Annual threshold and actual expenses | Mean modeled purchases | Median modeled purchases | Mean modeled profit before purchases | 
|---|---|---|---|
| $40 million | $2.32 million | $0 | −$1.92 million | 
| $35 million | $3.35 million | $1.26 million | $3.08 million | 
| $30 million | $4.71 million | $3.18 million | $8.08 million | 
The expense correction leaves the purchase amounts unchanged because this version of NEST buys against the revenue threshold, without checking actual expenses.
At $30 million in actual expenses, mean modeled profit excluding treasury income falls from the published $10.7 million to $8 million. Among paths with purchases, the fraction ending in a loss rises from 12.6% to 22.2%.
A separate CryptoSlate sensitivity starting Oct. 13, assuming continued funding and using the refreshed counter and explorer ETH quote but unchanged September fee volumes and first-half deduction and Earn assumptions, produced a $2.1 million median for the $30 million case.
The economic direction remains clear within these assumptions: real spending cuts improve the modeled profit balance. Lowering the contract’s threshold alone permits additional buying even when the DAO’s broader operations finish at a loss.
A reset loosens the spending brake
An annual reset would discard a negative counter at a calendar-year boundary while retaining positive capacity.
CryptoSlate’s reset comparison corrects a period overlap in the published script: whole-month purchase totals count September 2028 in two adjacent 365-day profit periods.
That recalculation gives average spending of about $2.6 million per modeled 365-day period with carry-forward and $2.8 million with annual resets, resulting in a roughly 8% gain. Quarterly resets produce about $2.9 million.
With treasury income excluded, periods ending in a loss account for about 19.5% of purchase-making periods under carry-forward, compared with 30.0% under annual resets. Their shares of purchase dollars are much smaller, about 3.5% and 4.4%, respectively.
The result supports a limited conclusion: a reset cannot make the DAO more profitable, and its modeled spending effect is smaller than the budget changes.
The existing allocator has no direct reset function. Its Voting-controlled threshold setters preserve the accumulated counter and apply changes prospectively, so a recurring reset needs a different implementation or governance arrangement.
The 2027 grant process would need to set a feasible spending budget and its corresponding threshold, account for additional revenue without double-counting, and fund any permitted purchases.
The treasury-only design returns purchased LDO tokens to the DAO, with no automatic burn or holder payout. Jenya_K reported no specific plans for the acquired LDO, burns remain a discussion proposal, and liquidity mode requires a separate DAO decision.
Lido’s report treats token acquisitions as asset swaps or purchases without an immediate profit-and-loss effect, with LDO excluded from headline treasury value. More buying can change the treasury’s asset mix without establishing stronger earnings, guaranteed price support, or better ETH staking returns.
That leaves the grant request with a concrete economic test: whether net income improves after actual costs, and whether the acquisition policy preserves those gains.

articles.title: UK Moves Closer to Keeping $5B Bitcoin Haul After High Court Ruling - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- The High Court in London ruled that Chinese law applies to victims' claims on 61,000 BTC seized in the case of fraudster Zhimin Qian.
- English law had been seen as more favorable to the victims, who must show they own a share of the Bitcoin to succeed.
- Lawyers for the victims plan to appeal, while the content of Chinese law and how it applies to the claims will be decided later.
The UK government's chances of keeping a 61,000 BTC haul seized from convicted fraudster Zhimin Qian have improved after the High Court in London ruled on Monday that Chinese law should govern victims' claims to the coins.
The Bitcoin is worth about $5 billion at its current price of around $83,200, per CoinGecko data.
Qian was jailed for more than 11 years last year after pleading guilty to fraud and money laundering charges over a Ponzi scheme that defrauded investors in China between 2014 and 2017. According to the ruling, at least 128,409 investment contracts were entered into, and victims paid in about RMB 40.2 billion, roughly £4.1 billion. About RMB 34.1 billion of that was paid back out to some victims.
Thousands of victims have applied under the Proceeds of Crime Act to have parts of the Bitcoin declared theirs. To succeed, each must show a proprietary interest in the coins, Justice Mark Turner wrote, because the law creates no broader compensation scheme for people who lost out to crime.
English law had been seen as substantially more favorable to the victims, the Financial Times reported, because it could have let them argue the Bitcoin belonged to them.
Chinese law applies
Turner sided with the Director of Public Prosecutions, who heads the Crown Prosecution Service and brought the case, finding that the fraud, the victims' payments and the contracts all took place in China. "The relevant damage occurred in China. The Applicants parted with their money in China," he wrote.
The judge reached the same answer under each of the legal routes he considered, concluding that the governing law "is Chinese law." Because the Bitcoin was bought in China, he added, tracing the coins in England cannot revive any property rights the victims lost under Chinese law when that purchase took place.
The decision does not settle who keeps the Bitcoin. Questions about the content and proof of Chinese law are matters for a later stage, Turner wrote. Prosecutors have previously said victims could be compensated through a redress scheme run from China.
Unnamed Treasury officials have privately raised whether the seized Bitcoin, worth around $7 billion at the time of Qian's trial, could help fill a shortfall in the UK's public finances, the FT reported last year.
Law firm Fieldfisher, which represents the claimants, said it is pursuing an appeal, according to the FT. "There will be a further hearing to determine the application of the law and if any of the victims are able to establish an interest in the bitcoin," the CPS said.

articles.title: Why NFT Collectors Are Cheering Blur’s Website Shutdown
articles.text:
Blur is shutting down its website, so why are NFT collectors cheering?
Blur’s planned website closure revived criticism of the royalty policies and token rewards that helped it overtake OpenSea during the NFT boom, but hurt creators.
Nonfungible token marketplace Blur, which once overtook OpenSea as the largest NFT marketplace by trading volume, says it is shutting down its website next month — and some NFT collectors couldn’t be happier.
Blur made the announcement on X on Monday, its first post on the platform in more than a year. It said the frontend will shut down on Nov. 12, while its onchain marketplace will remain operational.
Blend, a peer-to-peer perpetual NFT lending protocol, will also stop matching new loans. Blur said borrowers have until Nov. 12 to repay outstanding loans or allow them to default. It also promised a withdrawal interface after the shutdown.
“Good riddance. You destroyed NFTs. Please shut down and never come back,” said NFT collector Cryptobscure in a reply to the post on X.
“You may not have been able to complete your mission to destroy NFTs. But you acted with extreme determination and tried everything. Congratulations to us for surviving you,” NFT collector starfruit said in another post.
The post renewed criticism of the strategy that helped Blur reach the top of the NFT charts in 2023: optional creator royalties and token rewards that encouraged traders to bid and flip NFTs. Its rise accelerated a shift toward lower creator royalties, with rival OpenSea later moving to optional creator fees for new collections.
Blur launched on Oct. 19, 2022, allowing sellers to customize royalty payments while offering larger prospective token rewards to those who paid higher creator royalties.
But it entered a market where royalty protections were already weakening: competing marketplace Magic Eden had moved to optional royalties the previous week.
By July of the following year, blockchain analytics platform Nansen reported that effective creator royalty fees fell to 0.6% in July 2023 from an average of 2.5% in 2022, attributing much of that gap to Blur’s growth, its minimum royalty policy and OpenSea lowering its own royalty requirements to compete.
NFT sales slump from boom-era highs
Blur didn’t disclose why it made the decision to shutter its frontend and wind down new lending activity on Blend.
Related: Magic Eden scare puts 3,832 NFTs in whitehat protective custody
However, the decision comes as NFT trading remains far below its boom-era levels. Data from CryptoSlam shows total NFT sales in September were $167 million over 2.9 million total transactions. The peak was in January 2022, when there was $6 billion in sales over 13.7 million transactions.
Gemini-owned Nifty Gateway and social collecting platform Rodeo announced plans to wind down in January, while Foundation announced its closure in April after a sale intended to keep it operating fell through. Binance also ended NFT support on its exchange, shifting asset management to Binance Wallet.
Cointelegraph reached out to Blur founder Tieshun “Pacman” Roquerre for comment.
