articles.title: Ngoại hình khác lạ của cậu bé sống cách đây 8.300 năm
articles.text:
Dựa vào hài cốt và dấu tích trong hang động thời Đồ Đá, các chuyên gia phục dựng chân dung cậu bé 15 tuổi mắc dị tật về sọ.
Bản phục dựng toàn bộ cơ thể một thiếu niên thời kỳ Đồ Đá mang tên Vistegutten đang được trưng bày tại bảo tàng Hå Gamle Prestegard, miền nam Na Uy, Live Science hôm 15/2 đưa tin. Dự án phục dựng kỳ công được thực hiện trong suốt nhiều tháng.
Cậu bé Vistegutten có thể từng sống gần bờ biển Na Uy. (Ảnh: Oscar Nilsson).
Các nhà khảo cổ phát hiện hài cốt Vistegutten trong một hang động ở Randaberg, dọc theo bờ biển phía tây Na Uy năm 1907. Cậu bé 15 tuổi cao 1m25, khá thấp so với lứa tuổi, kể cả theo tiêu chuẩn của thời kỳ Đồ Đá giữa. Có thể Vistegutten đã chết một cách cô độc vì hài cốt của cậu bé trông như đang ngồi dựa vào vách hang.
"Có thể cậu bé được đặt ở tư thế này sau khi mất, nhưng cũng có khả năng cậu bé thực sự chết trong tư thế này", Oscar Nilsson, nghệ nhân pháp y Thụy Điển, người tái tạo chân dung Vistegutten, cho biết.
Vistegutten mắc chứng đầu hình thuyền (scaphocephaly), xảy ra khi đường nối dọc trên đỉnh hộp sọ đóng lại quá sớm khiến đầu dài ra theo hướng trước sau mà không mở rộng sang hai bên, dẫn đến phần trán nhô ra.
"Tuy nhiên, dị tật này không đi kèm với các vấn đề về khả năng phát triển hay thiểu năng trí tuệ", Sean Dexter Denham, chuyên gia về xương tại Bảo tàng Khảo cổ thuộc Đại học Stavanger (Na Uy), nói. Hộp sọ bất thường và vóc dáng thấp bé có thể khiến Vistegutten sở hữu ngoại hình khác lạ, nhưng những dấu vết để lại cho thấy cậu bé vẫn được ăn uống đầy đủ và khỏe mạnh.
Nghệ nhân pháp y Oscar Nilsson mất nhiều tháng để tái tạo hộp sọ cậu bé. (Ảnh: Oscar Nilsson)
Để phục dựng, nhóm chuyên gia tiến hành chụp cắt lớp vi tính (CT) hộp sọ hai lần. Từ đó, Nilsson tạo ra một bản sao bằng nhựa in 3D. Vì không rõ độ dày mô trên khuôn mặt cậu bé, Nilsson đã dựa vào số đo của những thiếu niên 15 tuổi ở Bắc Âu hiện đại.
Nilsson nhận thấy cậu bé có trán tròn và hơi nhô, sống mũi mảnh nhưng phần dưới mũi khá rộng. Phân tích ADN cũng cho thấy màu da, tóc và mắt của cậu gần giống với những người Na Uy khác trong thời kỳ đó, chủ yếu là mắt nâu, tóc sẫm màu và màu da trung bình.
Trang phục của Vistegutten do nhà khảo cổ Thụy Điển Helena Gjaerum thiết kế với những kỹ thuật thuộc da thời tiền sử. Trang phục gồm áo tunic dài từ da nai sừng tấm cạo lông, hai tấm da cá hồi quấn quanh eo, túi treo ở thắt lưng làm từ da hươu. Xương của những con vật này đều được tìm thấy tại địa điểm khảo cổ. "Bộ đồ được khâu bằng cả sợi gân và dây da, sau đó bôi thêm tro và mỡ để trông chân thực hơn", Gjaerum chia sẻ. Ngoài ra, cậu bé còn đeo vòng cổ từ xương sống của cá hồi và vỏ sò vỡ.

articles.title: 'It gives us a glimpse of a different kind of Viking life': Archaeologist Neil Price on the sea-kings, sorcerers and Sámi who lived during the Viking Age
articles.text:
'It gives us a glimpse of a different kind of Viking life': Archaeologist Neil Price on the sea-kings, sorcerers and Sámi who lived during the Viking Age
Archaeologist Neil Price delves into the lives and deaths of Viking Age people, including warriors, traders, thralls, sorcerers and children.
In the early medieval period, the Vikings were just one part of a vast tapestry of Scandinavians who ruled, sailed, traded and fought around the world, from North America to Asia. In his new book, "The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age" (Basic Books, 2026), author Neil Price, professor and chair of archaeology at Uppsala University in Sweden, reveals the true diversity and complexity of people who lived during the Viking Age (often dating from A.D. 793 to 1066).
Price investigates more than 20 burials from the Viking Age, lingering on details that can tell us about these individuals and their world. He also shines a light on frequently overlooked groups, including the enslaved people known as thralls that the Norse ruled over and even sacrificed in some of their burials. Price also delves into the realms of powerful women, including a "shield-maiden" buried with war-grade weapons in Sweden, a "sorceress" in Denmark, and an elderly matriarch whose children carved out a local empire in Sweden.
In an interview with Live Science, Price talks about his new book, and the evidence we have for the familiar yet foreign lives they lived centuries ago.
Laura Geggel: The Vikings are popularly known for being brutish and bloodthirsty pillagers, but the individuals in your book show the rich diversity of people from this time. Why did you decide to write this book and feature their stories?
Neil Price: I think quite simply because of the cliche that you've just mentioned, the idea that the Vikings are all barbarian raiders who go about burning down churches and frightening the English and things. Those raiders were certainly real, but they were only ever a tiny minority of the Scandinavian population, and I wanted to bring out all the different kinds of Viking lives, and that's why this book really came together.
It's divided into chapters, each one of which looks at a different kind of person, you know, a farmer, or an ambassador, or someone who uses magic, or a hunter. And I'm quite pleased that the Viking — the sort of raiding and pillaging Viking — it takes a while to get to him.
LG: How would you define the epitome of a Viking from that age?
The actual Viking, it comes from an old Norse word from their own language: víkingr. And really it's a job description, it means something like pirate — not necessarily negatively. It just describes maritime robbery with violence. So it is the classic image of the Viking stereotype.
But it was never a name for a people. If we could go back in time and just meet some people in Scandinavia and say, "Did you know that you're all Vikings?" — they'd be astonished.
It's a name, a collective name that we've given them. It started in the 19th century, really. So, they wouldn't have called themselves that.
LG: Your book starts with the sea-king, a commander and his crew who were buried in boats with swords and shields in Estonia. Usually, the Viking Age is said to have begun in 793 with the raid on the island of Lindisfarne in the U.K., but you say this burial suggests that the Viking Age started earlier and in another part of Europe. Can you tell us more about this?
NP: When I started studying Vikings at college — so this is back in the early 1980s, a long, long time ago — the Viking Age did start not just in 793; It started on the eighth of June 793 with the Lindisfarne raid.
Obviously it's absurd that an entire period of time starts on an afternoon, you know, not the day before or the day after. So it's obvious that we're talking about something that is really a matter of social processes, things that go on over a long period of time. But the thing that makes the finds that are in the sea-king chapter — they're from this place called Salme in Estonia — really interesting is that they seem to be the remains of, or the traces of a raid.
It's decades before Lindisfarne, it's about 750. And obviously on an island on the Estonian coast, it's going east, not west. So it really pushes that [raiding] behavior a lot earlier and it reorientates it. Even then, we shouldn't see the Vikings in that find as being the first Vikings. Actually the Scandinavians had been raiding all over the place for generations.
LG: I really enjoyed your focus on women, since stereotypically the Viking Age is associated with burly male warriors. What are some roles that women held in the Viking Age that you don't think most people know about?
NP: Something that particularly interests me, which is something I've worked on for a very long time now, is that when we think about Norse religion, everyone thinks about the gods. You know, they're still around in Marvel movies and things — we think of Thor and Odin and Freya and so on.
But actually, the [thing that was] far more present than the gods in people's lives were lots of kinds of local spirits and creatures and the elves that live in the stone behind your house. Getting in contact with that world of supernatural creatures and forces and powers — or whatever we call them — was something that was very much in the domain of women.
And it's a really important thing. So we shouldn't just say, "Oh, and some of them did magic." They're like negotiators, because you want to get on well with all these little creatures. If you don't, they could mess up your life, you know — your cattle could die, your crops could fail, that kind of thing. You could get sick.
So the practice of, it's hard to know what to call it in English. Sorcery or magic — they're not very good words, but there's lots of Norse words for it. To be able to do that is a very powerful thing and it's a very prominent role in society. And this was very much in the domain of women.
I think actually women could take on many of the roles that we conventionally assign to men. In terms of capability, of course they could. There are some, rather few I think, but there are some female Vikings, like actual Vikings, there are women conducting trade, owning property, investing in business ventures, things like that. So they have a very prominent role in Norse society.
We talked about Lindisfarne just now. When I started studying the Vikings, Viking women were one display case in the museum exhibition, next to the display case on pottery or something. Not half the population, and that has really changed. I think we look at Viking Age people now, not just assuming they're male by default.
LG: Actually, to linger, you described a number of women and their professions. Could you tell me more about these two amazing women in your book from Birka: the merchant and the warrior?
NP: Birka is this huge town. It's Sweden's first urban center, and it's absolutely surrounded by burial mounds. So you have the area of the town and then all the people who lived in it. You can wander through their cemetery, which is a pretty spectacular place — there's 5,000 burial mounds.
The merchant woman that you mentioned, she's one of the earlier graves [circa 840s], so she's one of the first people who would have identified as being someone who lives in a town. Today we talk about "I'm a city person" or a "country person," and that's an identity that was only just beginning to be created in the Viking Age, because everybody was country people. With the first towns, people start to live in a different way, and this woman was one of them.
If we look in her grave, she has things that have come from all over the western Viking world, things that I think probably came as loot from the raids, so she knew somebody who was involved in those things.
But you look at the stuff that's there, it seems pretty likely that she is a merchant in her own right, perhaps someone dealing in textiles. This idea of a businesswoman setting up a shop in Birka and maybe importing textiles or making them, having them made, because she's probably not working the loom, you know. It gives us a glimpse of a different kind of Viking life, one that I don't think we're accustomed to seeing and we should.
And then the warrior is about 100 years later than the merchant woman, when Birka has grown; it's quite a big settlement by then that's a really powerful place.
It's become quite militarized, so it has a fortification wall and it has a fortress, and there's a garrison building, which is a really amazing structure actually. It's partly made of weapons. There are weapons in the walls and on the floors. Around the building are a number of burials with lots of weapons in them. It's quite easy to say that a burial with lots of weapons is a warrior, but that's an interpretation. We can't be sure that the things buried with the dead were their possessions. We kind of assume that that's the case, but clearly not always. So there's a bit of a question mark there.
This burial was excavated like most of the ones in Birka in the 1870s, so a long time ago. And this grave is absolutely full of weapons. It's got all the weapons. And out of all the about 1,100 burials that were excavated on Birka, only two have a complete set of weapons, so this is rare. It's a very spectacular grave.
This burial has been reprinted again and again. [Iit's] in like every book on the Vikings. So it's been put forward as a kind of ultimate Viking: This is what proper Vikings looked like, you know, all the gear. And because it was excavated in the 1870s, it's always been assumed that this person was male. It's not hard to see where that assumption comes from, but it's actually been consistent ever since.
Then, between 2011 and 2017, first a series of osteological studies looking at the bones, and then DNA, confirmed that this person was female. And actually the team that worked on it, which included me, none of us were particularly surprised.
It was kind of exciting and interesting, but it's like, "Oh wow, you know, they really did have female warriors." So all the previous interpretations, it seemed to us, were pretty valid, it's just that this is a female, the ultimate Viking.
[Editor's note: Following the 2017 study, there was an intense reaction to the interpretation that the woman in the grave was a Viking Age warrior.]
LG: So you weren't expecting the backlash that occurred afterward?
No, we weren't, it was extreme. I'm not going to go into that in any detail, but some people were very, very happy, and some people were really not, and there we are.
It also highlights that all of these things are interpretations. You very rarely find something that is beyond any doubt what it is. Then there's also things with all of the burials in the book and all the burials that we excavate — people have quite long lives, hopefully. And if you were a warrior when you're 18 and you live to be 70, are you buried with all the weapons? Maybe not. Who knows?
That applies to any other kind of profession. So we don't know [if the different events and professions] in somebody's life course [are] represented in the burial. Is it when they die, or is it somebody who did something famous when they were young, and that is in the grave. We don't know. So there's lots of question marks, but the one thing it does show is the diversity of life in the Viking Age. There's so many different kinds of people, which is not a surprise, really, but it's something I just wanted to bring out in the book.
LG: You don't just talk about Vikings, but about those who lived alongside them. In one chapter, you describe a Sámi burial of a bear that they had killed and feasted on. What do we know about bear burials and why the Sámi did them? [Editor's note: The Sámi are an Indigenous people who currently live in the northern Nordic countries and part of Russia.]
NP: Well, the bear is a holy animal to the Sámi, and it's obviously a massive source of protein and food and pelts, you know, all kinds of useful things. But what I really wanted to get at was the idea of personhood. If you think about all the different kinds of prejudice, some people are sort of "more people" than others. Think about racism, for example.
In the Viking Age, not every human was [seen as] a person, but not every person was human. There are animal persons as well, sentient animals. Everything is sentient actually, and the idea that you converse with animals, that you talk to them, you respect them, they have their personalities.
I wanted to bring out in that chapter a different kind of way of looking at "persons." So the fact that the Sámi bury the bears they hunt with tremendous respect, it's partly to ensure that the bear will come back in the future from the spirit world as another bear, so that the cycle of hunting and life can go on.
LG: You also talk about "thralls," people who were enslaved by the Norse. Can you share some of the archaeological evidence we have for thralls and what their burials look like?
NP: We don't really know whether they have burials at all, actually. The institution of slavery, or thralldom, is absolutely central to the Norse economy, and just putting that back into the picture is very important, I think.
They are a group of people who have been neglected in our studies. There's a lot of people working on this, this isn't just me by any means. When we find them in the burials — well, when we think we find them, because it's extremely rare to find someone buried in their own right that we think might have been enslaved. But there's also the question of how do we tell? Unless somebody's sort of buried in chains or something, it's very hard.
But we do find — not often, but it's not that uncommon — that people have been killed in the course of funerals. You have a burial of a man or a woman, and then an extra body is in the grave, which has clearly been treated very differently. So their hands might be tied or they've been decapitated or something, and there's people who have very clearly been killed at the funeral.
Just the fact of that presumably means that they have a very different kind of status to the primary occupant of the burial. [They're] not necessarily enslaved; they could be prisoners or criminals. But there's been more recent studies looking at the diet of those people. You can use isotopes to study what people have eaten. [Editor's note: Isotopes are variations of elements. When people consume different foods and water, different amounts of certain isotopes are incorporated into their teeth and bones.] And in some cases, the people who've been killed at funerals have a much, much worse diet than other people, which implies that they have a much lower status and poorer nutrition and so on.
So the implication really is that they might be enslaved. So I think that's where we are with the burials of enslaved people.
LG: You spend an entire chapter on Viking Age children. What was it like to grow up in Scandinavia during this time, and what can we learn about their lives from grave goods and skeletal analyses?
NP: The first thing is that an awful lot of people didn't make it out of childhood at all. Putting numbers on this is a bit of a game, but probably less than half the population got past the age of 10. So child mortality is massive.
When we imagine the Viking Age or think back to it, remember that almost every single family will have lost children, with the psychological effects of that and the emotional effects and so on. And we shouldn't be entirely sure what those effects were, because if child mortality is so high, they have different coping mechanisms. But it still must have been utterly awful.
We don't find as many child burials as we should. There are a couple of written sources that mention that dead children are effectively discarded, and maybe this is connected with a coping mechanism for child mortality that people don't become sort of "full people" until they get to a certain age. We don't know.
But there are child burials and, quite often they're buried with scaled-down versions of the things that adults have. So young girls are buried with women's jewelry, but smaller. And they obviously had their possessions; they had their clothes and their jewelry, and we find toys, not in the graves, but on settlement sites — we find dolls, wooden animals, there's a fantastic horse on wheels that you can roll it about, lots and lots of little wooden boats that you can sail down. So they're thinking about boats quite early. I think their lives are quite recognizable up to a point, though very hard.
The age of maturity seems to be somewhere between about 14 and 16. After that, you're an adult, and then you're just out there with the rest.
LG: To us that seems young, but for them to make it that far would have been an accomplishment.
NP: And even in adults — you asked about skeletal analysis — there are an awful lot of adults that are malnourished as children, and it leaves traces in their bones.
There's also a rather grim set of data from a fairly small sample, but still — the proportion of adult women who were malnourished as children is much greater than the proportion of men. In other words, if food was scarce, they gave it to the boys. So it's also a glimpse of their priorities and the realities of their world.
LG: The Scandinavians settled in the Rus' in what is now Ukraine. What do we know about these people? Were they traders, warriors, or a mix of many things?
NP: I think [it's] a mixture. The identity of the Rus' is one of the big questions of the Viking Age. They used to be seen very simply as what the Vikings are called when they go east. And there's some truth to that. They seem to be culturally Scandinavian in the beginning, so we're talking the early ninth century or probably the eighth century.
Over time, as they travel on the eastern rivers, they become much more ethnically diverse. So it's a culture that grows up around an activity, rather than people from a particular place. Probably the closest parallel [is] if you think of the fur trade on the Canadian rivers and some parts of the states as well — the sort of 1600s and 1700s.
They're certainly militaristic though; they're armed traders. There's no doubt about that. And they found trading settlements, together with local people and other incomers as well. And they settle there. After a time, they're not actually [newcomers], they live there. And then, over time, quite late in the Viking Age and on into the Middle Ages, you get this Rus' state, with its capital of Kiev. But they range over a very large part of Eastern Europe and actually I think further east as well.
LG: You focus on this group of Rus' warriors, the Varangians, and you give the example of them leaving graffiti on a marble lion statue that's now in Venice. Can you tell us the story about these runes they carved?
NP: Yeah sure, it's a bit strange that the best monument to these guys is a lion that's much, much older than the Viking Age. It's from classical antiquity. It's outside the Arsenal now in Venice, but it used to stand in the harbor of Athens at a place called Piraeus.
The Varangians were kind of a subset of the Rus', but they're basically Scandinavians who take very clear contracted employment in the armies of Byzantium, the Eastern Roman Empire. So they're mercenaries, and they were very sought after, and there's lots and lots of written sources about them.
This lion, which once stood in the Athenian harbor, had three inscriptions in runes over its shoulders and legs and things. Two of the inscriptions are very fragmentary, so you can't get much from them. But the biggest one is a memorial to a guy called Haursi. It actually calls him Haursi the farmer, so it really does emphasize that you could be a farmer, but maybe you do a season in the army down in Greece and make a bit of money and go home. So people have professions and they have choices, and they do this for a bit, but then they go back and do what they did before.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- 'His urine goes on tour around Europe, showing the kings and queens this glowing pee': The weird world of alchemy before chemistry
- 'Call it Genghis Khan's final victory': Why the tomb of the 'Disturber of the Universe' remains hidden after 800 years
- He looked like Ramses the Great': How experimental archaeologists used ancient techniques to mummify a modern-day person
This inscription is written by this guy's friends or his comrades, and it specifically says that he was killed before he got paid. And it's kind of a hint. It's "So, pay up, because you owe him, or you owe his family."
You get this little vignette of a soldier's life. And also carving the inscription on this lion is a pretty major job. This isn't like scribbling on a wall or something — they're carving it, and so they're there a long time. And presumably have control of the harbor because you can't just chisel this thing on, you know, people are trying to stop you.
We can think of the Varangians being stationed in Athens or waiting for a ship or something like that. It's this wonderful snapshot.
LG: Your book is loaded with details about Viking Age people. What do you hope readers will take away from your work?
NP: That they were more than actual Vikings. The people of the Viking Age were individuals, every bit as varied and complicated as we are. So that's it.
This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

Laura is the managing editor at Live Science. She also runs the archaeology section and the Life's Little Mysteries series. Her work has appeared in The New York Times, Scholastic, Popular Science and Spectrum, a site on autism research. She has won multiple awards from the Society of Professional Journalists and the Washington Newspaper Publishers Association for her reporting at a weekly newspaper near Seattle. Laura holds a bachelor's degree in English literature and psychology from Washington University in St. Louis and a master's degree in science writing from NYU.

articles.title: NASA astronauts splash down after 100 million miles in space
articles.text:
NASA astronauts splash down after 100 million miles in space
- Date:
- October 8, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have returned to Earth after 237 days in space, traveling more than 100 million miles and completing over 3,792 orbits while conducting research to prepare for future missions to the Moon and Mars. The mission also made history with record-setting spacewalk achievements and experiments that could transform medicine both in space and on Earth.
- Share:
After spending more than seven months aboard the International Space Station, NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have safely returned to Earth. Their spacecraft splashed down Thursday in the Pacific Ocean near Los Angeles, bringing an extraordinary mission to a close.
The four astronauts spent 237 days in orbit, traveled more than 100 million miles, and completed thousands of trips around Earth while carrying out scientific experiments that could help shape future missions to the Moon and Mars.
NASA will host a news conference at 3:30 p.m. EDT on Thursday, Oct. 15, at Johnson Space Center in Houston, where returning crew members will discuss their experiences and research accomplishments.
"Jessica, Jack, Sophie, and Andrey spent 237 days living and working in orbit, traveled more than 100 million miles, advanced important science, and returned safely home because of the extraordinary expertise and competence of thousands across NASA, SpaceX, and our international partners," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "Building the capability, experience, and confidence to do this repeatedly is exactly what will allow us to go farther, and I am grateful to Crew-12 and their families for their service to humanity's greatest adventure."
NASA Astronauts Return After 237 Days and 100 Million Miles
The returning crew included NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev.
Their spacecraft touched down in the Pacific at 8:34 a.m. PDT. SpaceX recovery teams aboard specialized vessels reached the capsule shortly afterward and brought the astronauts and spacecraft aboard.
Following routine medical evaluations, the crew members will be transported to shore before traveling to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston.
"NASA's activities supporting the International Space Station -- transporting crew, conducting impactful research, and maintaining critical national assets -- enable the science, engineering, and risk‑reduction needed for future missions across the solar system," said Dana Weigel, manager of NASA's Low Earth Orbit Program at the agency's Johnson Space Center. "We're grateful for the dedication across the human spaceflight team that makes this possible, and we're thrilled to welcome Jessica, Jack, Sophie, and Andrey home."
Over the course of their 237-day stay, the astronauts circled Earth more than 3,792 times, accumulating over 100 million miles of travel.
For Meir and Fedyaev, Crew-12 marked their second journey into space. Hathaway and Adenot, meanwhile, completed their first space missions.
The crew launched on Feb. 13 at 5:15 a.m. EST, reaching and docking with the International Space Station the following day.
Space Station Experiments Could Help Future Moon and Mars Missions
Beyond the remarkable distance traveled, Crew-12 devoted hundreds of hours to scientific investigations designed to support future human exploration and improve life on Earth.
One research project explored ways to produce stem cells in space for potential use in cell-based medical treatments. Another demonstrated technology capable of producing IV fluids on demand, an ability that could become especially valuable during long-duration missions far from Earth.
The astronauts also investigated how pneumonia-causing bacteria may contribute to lasting heart damage. Understanding this relationship could offer new insights into cardiovascular health.
Other experiments focused on nutrition in space and how individual physical characteristics may influence blood flow during spaceflight. These studies could help researchers better understand the health risks astronauts face during extended stays in microgravity.
Together, the investigations provide valuable information about keeping humans healthy beyond Earth while testing technologies that may eventually support crewed expeditions to the Moon and Mars.
Historic Spacewalks Mark Crew-12 Mission
The mission also included significant milestones outside the space station.
Meir carried out four spacewalks during Crew-12, raising her career total to seven. That achievement places her third among NASA women for the most career spacewalks, behind former astronauts Peggy Whitson and Suni Williams.
Adenot also reached a historic milestone by completing three spacewalks. In doing so, she became the first French woman to venture outside the International Space Station.
With Crew-12 safely back on Earth, NASA has completed another extended mission that combined scientific research, international cooperation, and human spaceflight experience. The knowledge gained will contribute to preparations for more ambitious journeys beyond Earth's orbit.

articles.title: Các nhà khoa tìm ra loại oxy mới có đặc tính kỳ lạ
articles.text:
Các nhà khoa học ở Nhật Bản đã tạo ra hai dạng oxy mới có những đặc tính khác thường so với các lý thuyết phổ biến về cấu trúc nguyên tử.
Oxy-28, một trong hai đồng vị mới vừa được tạo ra trong phòng thí nghiệm, là đồng vị oxy nặng nhất mà chúng ta từng biết đến. Nó cũng hoạt động một cách kỳ lạ.
Hai đồng vị này đều là dạng oxy, luôn có 8 proton trong mỗi nguyên tử. (Ảnh minh họa: Sputnik)
Nhà nghiên cứu Yosuke Kondo tại Viện Công nghệ Tokyo giải thích trên tạp chí Nature số ra ngày 30/8 rằng nhóm của bà đã cho một số nguyên tố tiếp xúc với “điều kiện khắc nghiệt” để tạo ra oxy-28 và đồng vị oxy-27 nhỏ hơn một chút.
Hai đồng vị này đều là dạng oxy, luôn có 8 proton trong mỗi nguyên tử. Tuy nhiên, một nguyên tử có thể có số lượng neutron bất kỳ mà không làm thay đổi tính chất hóa học của nó.
Trước đây, số neutron nhiều nhất từng thấy trong hạt nhân oxy là 18. Đồng vị này được gọi là oxy-26 vì nó cũng có 8 proton bên trong.
Để hình thành các đồng vị oxy mới, nhóm của bà Kondo đã sử dụng Máy chùm tia đồng vị phóng xạ RIKEN đặt tại thành phố Saitama của Nhật Bản. Họ đã bắn một chùm đồng vị canxi-48 vào mục tiêu bằng berili để phá vỡ các mảnh canxi và tạo ra các nguyên tử nhẹ hơn. Trong số những chất được tạo ra có các nguyên tử flo-29 - có 9 proton và 20 neutron và nằm cạnh oxy trên bảng tuần hoàn.
Sau đó, các nhà nghiên cứu lấy nguyên tử flo-29 này và phá vỡ nó cùng với một nguyên tử hydro lỏng để biến flo thành oxy.
Kết quả, họ tạo ra được hai nguyên tử khác nhau bằng quy trình này: oxy-28 có 20 neutron và oxy-27 có 19 neutron.
Theo bài báo, những gì xảy ra sau đó đã khiến các nhà khoa học bối rối. Mặc dù họ nghĩ oxy-28 sẽ ổn định nhưng nó lại phân rã và trải qua sự phát xạ neutron tự phát.
Điều đó có nghĩa là nó nhanh chóng giải phóng bốn neutron và trở thành oxy-24. Oxy-27 cũng nhanh chóng phân hủy, mất đi ba neutron để trở thành oxy-24.
Các nhà nghiên cứu ban đầu tin rằng hai dạng oxy mới có tính chất ổn định dựa trên mối quan hệ toán học chi phối “lớp vỏ” của các hạt trong hạt nhân, trong đó bội số của 8 và 20 được coi là những con số “ma thuật” do có đặc trưng ổn định cao. Nhóm của bà Kondo kỳ vọng oxy-28 ổn định vì số đồng vị của nó là “ma thuật gấp đôi”.
Ví dụ, dạng oxy mà chúng ta hít thở ở đây trên Trái đất là oxy-16, là bội số của 8 và cực kỳ ổn định.

articles.title: 'The back of her head had been removed by a single blow from a sharp blade': Archaeological clues are revealing the horrific lives and deaths of the people enslaved by Vikings
articles.text:
'The back of her head had been removed by a single blow from a sharp blade': Archaeological clues are revealing the horrific lives and deaths of the people enslaved by Vikings
In this excerpt from "The Sea-King and the Sorceress," author Neil Price looks at the lesser known lives of the people enslaved by Vikings: the thralls.
Slavery has existed for thousands of years, permeating ancient and modern societies across the world. The Vikings were no different. Enslaved people were valuable commodities, being captured and then traded across the Vikings' vast networks. Legal texts and written sources show how enslaved people were sold at trading centers in the same vein as cattle.
In this excerpt from "The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age" (Basic Books, 2026), author and archaeologist Neil Price looks at the horrific lives of the "thralls" — the Viking term for the enslaved. In it, he highlights the inhumane treatment of enslaved people, from the raids to kidnap people into the slave trade to a woman who appears to have been killed as a tribute to a high-status man.
Neil Price interview: 'It gives us a glimpse of a different kind of Viking life': Archaeologist Neil Price on the sea-kings, sorcerers and Sámi who lived during the Viking Age
The vast majority of the Norse population were farmers, but there is another group of people who were almost as numerous, though very hard to find in the archaeological record: the enslaved. They have only recently begun to be properly acknowledged in our histories, partly because of the long-standing neglect of the marginalized and vulnerable in many cultures, but in the Viking world also due to a particular coincidence of terminology. For the Norse, the unfree were þrælar, translated into English as "thralls," which is too mild a word to convey its true meaning.
Today, we can be enthralled by a work of art or even a person, but we do not say that we're enslaved by them. Norse thraldom took many forms, some less severe or permanent than others, but all involved the loss of liberty and rights, and the subjugation of one person to another through servitude. A chapter here, even with tangential references in a few others, is nowhere near enough to do justice to this side of the Norse experience (or rather, often the non-Norse experience, since many of them were kidnapped abroad during raids and other campaigns). Archaeological recognition can at least restore some measure of individual dignity, though more comforting to us than to them.
Slavery, as both a practice and an integrated economic system, was an indivisible part of Viking-Age Norse society and had probably already become established in Scandinavia centuries or even millennia earlier. People could be born into slavery, or be forced into it through kidnap or war, and then find themselves sold on, sometimes through many hands and over great distances. Some free people might even temporarily sell themselves in a form of indenture, as a means of paying off debts or other obligations.
Thralls on Norse settlements were ranked in a hierarchical and quite specific nomenclature of service categories and forced to undertake all the tasks of the farm and household. In a few, rare cases, thralls could take on senior responsibilities of estate management, with a special title — bryti — to match. One such man ran the royal estate at Hovgården opposite the island town of Birka, and was allowed to raise a runestone to himself and his wife, though one wonders who paid for it. Nonetheless, the vast majority of thralls endured lives of drudgery.
The grim reality is summarized with derogatory terminology in the poem Rígsþula, the "List of Rígr" (another name for the god Heimdall, or perhaps for Odin): "They fixed fences, dunged fields, worked at the pigs, watched over the goats, dug the peat." Even their names are shaming, mocking their appearance or hygiene: they translate as Badbreath, Stumpy, Fatty, Bedmate, Craneshanks, Dumpy, and many more. Thralls were extremely vulnerable to sexual exploitation. The textual records of viking raids, coming from every culture that was attacked, emphasize that women were particularly targeted for kidnapping and enslavement.
In the ninth century, as the viking attacks escalated both in Western Europe and on the rivers of the east, the taking of captives came to be one of their prime objectives, feeding the lethal trinity of raiding, trading and slaving. In the words of Ibn Miskawayh, a Persian official who described a viking attack on the city of Bardha'a in what is now Azerbaijan in 943: "They kept the women and boys, whom they raped and enslaved [ . . . ] They dragged the women, boys and girls they wanted with them."
The repetition drives home the point, and little imagination is required to sense the undiluted horror. Some of these raids were informed by advance intelligence gathering and directed against high-profile targets for whom ransom could be demanded, but many were destined for sex trafficking, especially to the Arab world. Enslaved humans, particularly from the Baltic region, were among the main commodities exchanged eastwards along the Silk Roads.
In late ninth-century Scandinavia, the logistical needs of the escalating raids brought new demands on the workforce at an ever-larger scale, especially in all the many industries connected with shipbuilding (including textile production, timber management, tar manufacture, ironworking, and much more). This in turn drove the need for unfree labor to still greater levels.
As economic expansion enlarged the capacity for ship-borne aggression and released the agricultural workforce to crew these expeditions, the increased flow of human victims enabled its continuance in a vicious circle. Enslavement was one of the primary characteristics of the Viking Age: the raids were a key component of it and of the Norse diaspora that resulted.
To what degree these people are visible in the funerary record is hard to know. There were probably no diagnostic items that were used exclusively by thralls, so we cannot perceive them through specific objects in the graves. It also seems unlikely that those without rights and with few possessions, indeed with hardly any legal identity as individuals rather than chattel, would be accorded conventional burials. Ibn Faḍlān says that thralls who died while traveling were simply discarded, but this is unlikely to have been the case in settlements. When we do encounter them, it is often because they were killed as part of funerary rituals and their bodies deposited in burials. One example that we can explore here comes from an excavation at the site of Ballateare, in Jurby parish on the northwestern coast of the Isle of Man — the best preserved of all the Viking-Age graves on the island.
At Ballateare, it is instructive to see just how normal the initial funeral, and its circumstances, appear to have been, albeit for a high-status individual. By Viking-Age standards he was in his prime when he died in the early tenth century, somewhere between eighteen and thirty years old. He may have been among the early Norse settlers on Man. We have no reason to believe that the clothes he was buried in, and the things laid in the grave, are not reflections of his life and the international milieu he came from.
He had been interred in a wooden coffin, dug down quite deep into the ground. A sheathed knife was suspended on a lanyard round his neck and he wore a cloak held by an Irish ringed pin. Inside the coffin was a sword — probably from Norway, but with a belt from the British Isles — that had been cut into pieces before being sheathed in the scabbard; the hilt lay broken off beside it. A spearhead also lay in the coffin by the man's feet, snapped off because there was no room for the shaft. A shield, also deliberately damaged with two heavy blows to the boss, had been slid vertically down the outer side of the coffin; the shield board itself may have been smashed too. This was not battle damage; all his weapons were made unusable for reasons we can only guess. Fragments of the shield also revealed traces of paint: it had been decorated with white gesso, banded with black, with rows of red dots along the stripes. Two more spears had been laid across the top of the coffin.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- 'If it was a man, we would say that's a warrior's grave': Weapon-filled burials are shaking up what we know about women's role in Viking society
- 'Call it Genghis Khan's final victory': Why the tomb of the 'Disturber of the Universe' remains hidden after 800 years
- He looked like Ramses the Great': How experimental archaeologists used ancient techniques to mummify a modern-day person
The burial pit was then filled with fine white sand, and a mound was built on top — about 3 metres [10 feet] high and 22 metres [72 feet] in diameter. It was made of thick-cut turfs, which had been brought to the mound from a wide area rather than simply dug up in the vicinity. The earth of the mound seems to be an offering of the land itself, a territorial tribute to the dead man.
I do not wish to relate what happened next in terms of dramatized reconstruction; archaeological description must suffice. On top of the mound lay the body of a woman aged between twenty and thirty, who had been deliberately killed: the back of her head had been removed by a single blow from a sharp blade, probably a sword. Rigor mortis had set in, and some twelve to seventy-two hours had elapsed between her death and the time when her body was covered. She had either lain exposed on the mound for some time after her death, or been killed elsewhere (perhaps more likely, as the missing part of her skull was not present with the body). The woman seems to have died while kneeling, and had fallen forwards with her hands raised. A post was raised on top of the mound beside her body, presumably a grave marker.
A paragraph is not enough to convey what actually occurred, let alone to extrapolate the life that the woman had led before her death — possibly decades of servitude and enslavement, with all that this implies. Her corpse was covered by a very thick layer of cremated animal bone, including considerable numbers of oxen, horses, sheep and dogs. (Somewhere nearby must have been a truly massive cremation pyre.) The mound was finally sealed with turf, covering her body and the ashes of the animals.
Excerpted from The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age by Neil Price. © 2026 by Neil Price. Available from Basic Books, an imprint of Hachette Book Group, Inc.

Drawing on the latest archaeological research and scientific analysis, The Sea-King and the Sorceress brings us closer to understanding the lives and times of the Vikings. The era that bears their name will never seem so simple again.
Neil Price is distinguished professor and chair of archaeology at Uppsala University, Sweden. He has been researching, teaching and writing on the Vikings for nearly 40 years and is the author of several books on the history of the Viking Age, including "Children of Ash and Elm" (Basic Books, 2020). He lives in Sweden.
- Hannah Osborne Editor

articles.title: 5 mẹo dân gian khiến rắn sẽ không dám bén mảng tới gần nhà bạn
articles.text:
Ít ai ngờ rằng, những mẹo đơn giản dưới đây lại là khắc tinh của loài rắn, khiến chúng chạy xa chúng ta.
Chúng ta biết rằng, mùa hè là mùa sinh nở của côn trùng và tránh nóng của các loài rắn, rết. Bởi vậy không mấy lạ khi nhiều người dân chia sẻ rằng họ rất hoang mang khi phát hiện một chú rắn đang du ngoạn nhà mình, hay nằm thu lu ở góc nhà, trong máy giặt...
Chắc hẳn ai cũng giật mình, hoảng hốt khi thấy cảnh tượng này.
Mới đây nhất, người dân tại Tiền Giang vô cùng hoảng sợ khi chứng kiến cảnh tượng con rắn dài khoảng hơn 1 mét vùng vẫy trong phòng tắm tại nhà của một người dân.
Điều này khiến không ít người lo lắng, hoảng loạn. Bởi vậy, hãy nắm ngay những biện pháp phòng rắn vào nhà dưới đây để bảo vệ sức khoẻ, mạng sống của bạn và người thân.
Bột hùng hoàng (tên khoa học là: arsenic sulfide) được coi là khắc tinh của rắn. Chúng sẽ bỏ đi ngay lập tức khi đánh hơi thấy mùi này.
Thực chất, đây là một loại quặng trong tự nhiên, phân bố rộng rãi trên bề mặt trái đất. Trong tự nhiên, arsenic kết hợp với với oxygen, chlorine, và sulfur thành một dạng phức hợp arsenic vô cơ, và khá độc.
Bột hùng hoàng.
Arsenic sulfide gần như ít tan trong nước, nếu con người ăn phải hay hít phải sẽ ảnh hưởng tới dạ dày, tới các men tiêu hóa.
Đặc biệt, người hít phải với số lượng lớn bị ngộ độc. Do đó, khi rắc bột này quanh góc nhà, bạn cần đeo găng tay, khẩu trang, tránh để bột rơi vào thức ăn hoặc nguồn nước. Sau khi làm, cần phải rửa tay thật sạch sẽ. Do tính nguy hiểm, bạn chỉ nên dùng biện pháp này khi cấp bách mà thôi.
Ít ai biết rằng, một số loại cây không chỉ có ý nghĩa làm đẹp, trang trí cho ngôi nhà của bạn mà cũng có tác dụng xua đuổi những con vật nguy hiểm nữa đó.
Có thể kể đến một vài loại cây như: cây nén, cây sả, hoa lan tỏi... đó là những loại cây sẽ khiến rắn "né" nhà bạn từ xa. Đặc biệt, rắn lục đuôi đỏ cực nhạy cảm với mùi nên tác dụng của việc trồng cây sẽ càng hiệu quả hơn.
Cây nén có tinh dầu cay nồng nên rắn rất sợ.
Cụ thể, cây nén thuộc họ hành, thường được gọi là hành tăm, hành trắng. Đây là một loại gia vị đặc biệt do sở hữu tinh dầu trong củ, lá có mùi thanh và cay hơn so với hành/tỏi nên khi phát hiện mùi từ xa - các loài rắn sẽ tìm cách lẩn tránh và không dám đến gần.
Hoa lan tỏi...
Hoa lan tỏi là một loại cây có thân leo, hoa màu tím, vị ngọt, có tác dụng giải nhiệt, chống rôm sảy... và là một vị thuốc an thần tốt. Tuy nhiên, do lá cây này có mùi tỏi rất nồng, khó chịu, thậm chí nồng hơn cả tỏi nên lũ rắn mới tránh xa những khu vực trồng cây này.
...hay cây sắn dây có mùi khó chịu - khắc tinh với rắn.
Loài cây thứ 3 khá quen thuộc với chúng ta là sắn dây. Do phần nhựa tiết ra từ cây sắn dây có mùi khó chịu nên khiến rắn sợ và tránh xa.
Rắn cực ưa bóng tối, thích nơi mát mẻ. Do đó, để rắn không cư ngụ nhà bạn bất thình lình, bạn nên dọn dẹp những nơi tối tăm như gầm giường, gầm tủ... sạch sẽ. Đồng thời, cần thường xuyên chú ý tới những khu vực xung quanh bể nước, bồn tắm, máy giặt vì đây cũng là những khu vực mát, rắn thích trú ẩn.
Bạn nên dọn dẹp những nơi tối tăm như gầm giường, gầm tủ... sạch sẽ.
Điều này sẽ khiến rắn không có chỗ trốn và cũng để bạn có thể nhanh chóng phát hiện được sự đột nhập "bất hợp pháp" của loài vật nguy hiểm này.
Cùng với đó, đồ đạc trong nhà cũng cần phải sắp xếp gọn gàng, tránh tạo những nơi ẩm thấp, u tối - là nơi trú ngụ tuyệt vời của loài bò sát này.
Nuôi một chú chó hoặc một con mèo không chỉ để trông nhà, mua vui... mà chúng còn giúp bạn đuổi rắn.
Nếu rắn xuất hiện, những con vật nuôi sẽ giúp bạn phát hiện ra sớm.
Khi thấy rắn xuất hiện, những con vật này sẽ báo động giúp bạn có thể phát hiện sự xuất hiện của vị khách không mời.
Rắn có thể sợ và bỏ chạy, nhưng đôi lúc nó có thể tấn công lại vật nuôi. Dẫu vậy, khi nhận thấy sự bất thường, bạn cũng nên kiểm tra lại một lượt để tránh nguy hiểm bất ngờ có thể xảy ra.
Chắc chắn nhiều người sẽ cảm thấy bất ngờ vì bạn hoàn toàn có thể đuổi rắn bằng các nguyên liệu dễ dàng tìm thấy trong nhà bếp. Các loại cây gia vị như hành, tỏi, nén….là những cây gia vị có mùi nồng và kích thích khứu giác mạnh. Vì thế, rắn rất sợ những mùi hương này.
Vậy làm sao để đuổi rắn khỏi nhà bằng các nguyên liệu nhà bếp? Điều này hết sức đơn giản. Các bạn chỉ cần lấy 10 củ nén giã nhỏ trộn với 1 củ tỏi, 10 nhánh hành hương và một ít thuốc lá sợi, giã nhỏ, đựng vào một túi vải treo xung quanh nhà hoặc đeo bên mình. Mùi dược liệu bốc ra sẽ làm rắn tránh xa.
Đặc biệt đây được xem là cách đuổi rắn lục xanh đuôi đỏ hiệu quả và vô cùng tiện lợi trong thời điểm rắn lục hoành hành như hiện nay.
Rắn là loài bò sát thích ẩn nấp ở những chỗ ẩm thấp, mát mẻ và kín.
Rắn là loài bò sát thích ẩn nấp ở những chỗ ẩm thấp, mát mẻ và kín. Vì vậy, nếu phát hiện có rắn trong nhà, đơn giản là nó đang tìm một chỗ ẩn nấp cho nên đừng quá hoảng sợ.
Nếu phát hiện rắn ở trên mặt sàn, có thể dùng một tấm chăn, mền dày chụp lên nó.
Nếu con rắn ở một góc khuất nào đó như ngăn kéo, góc tủ thì hãy để yên nó.
Hãy dùng gậy dài hoặc vòi phun nước áp suất cao để đuổi nó ra khỏi khu vực gia đình. Nếu không, hãy tìm sự trợ giúp.
Mặc dù đã đuổi được rắn ra khỏi nhà, tuy nhiên thật khó có thể biết trước chúng có thể quay trở lại hay không, Vậy thì hãy chủ động áp dụng một số biện pháp để không cho chúng quay trở lại nhà nhé:
Thường xuyên cắt tỉa cây cối phát quang bụi rậm. Việc làm này để tránh tạo điều kiện tạo ra không gian trú ngụ cho rắn.
Loại bỏ các nguồn thức ăn của rắn, thức ăn của rắn thông thường là chuột, dế, các loài côn trùng… Để hạn chế rắn vào nhà bạn phải đảm bảo nhà không có chuột. Bạn cần dọn dẹp, vệ sinh nhà, tránh để thức ăn thừa ở bên ngoài để không chiêu dụ lũ chuột vào nhà.
Bịt kín các lỗ hỏng trong nhà bằng keo trám trét hoặc keo bọt nở. Các vết nứt hay lỗ hỏng này rất dễ trở thành nơi trú ngụ của rắn và việc bịt kín, trám lại sẽ khiến chúng không có chỗ ẩn nấp. Chúng sẽ không quay trở lại nếu không tìm được nơi an toàn trú ẩn.

articles.title: October’s night sky is full of cosmic tricks and treats
articles.text:
October’s night sky is full of cosmic tricks and treats
- Date:
- October 8, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- October’s skies are packed with celestial surprises, from Jupiter disappearing behind the Moon to two meteor showers lighting up the darkness. NASA highlights four must-see events, including shooting stars from Halley’s Comet and a glowing Hunter’s Moon just before Halloween.
- Share:
October is bringing a spectacular lineup of celestial events, including a disappearing planet, two meteor showers, and a bright full Moon just in time for Halloween. As autumn days grow shorter and darkness arrives earlier, the night sky offers more opportunities to witness some remarkable astronomical sights.
NASA has highlighted four events worth watching this month, ranging from Jupiter briefly vanishing behind the Moon to shooting stars created by debris from Halley's Comet. With crisp autumn evenings and a little luck, skywatchers can enjoy several of these displays without any special equipment.
Jupiter Disappears Behind the Moon on October 6
Before sunrise on Tuesday, October 6, skywatchers in parts of North America had an opportunity to witness an unusual celestial disappearing act. Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system, slipped behind the Moon's slender crescent and remained hidden for approximately an hour before coming back into view.
Astronomers call this phenomenon a lunar occultation. It happens when the Moon moves directly between Earth and a more distant object, temporarily blocking our view. Despite its mysterious-sounding name, occultation simply refers to one celestial object concealing another.
The event was visible to the naked eye, although binoculars offered a more detailed look. Observers using optical equipment could also potentially watch some of Jupiter's moons disappear behind the lunar edge and emerge again.
Viewing opportunities depended on location, with the occultation visible across parts of eastern and central North America. The timing varied geographically, with the event occurring during the early morning hours, around 4 a.m. EDT in some locations.
Draconid Meteor Shower Peaks October 8 and 9
The next celestial attraction comes on the evening of Thursday, October 8, when the Draconid meteor shower reaches its peak. Favorable viewing beginning around 9 p.m. EDT, and the display continues into the early hours of Friday, October 9.
Unlike many meteor showers that are best observed after midnight, the Draconids offer a convenient opportunity to see shooting stars soon after nightfall. That makes them particularly appealing to casual observers who would rather not stay awake until dawn.
Conditions are especially promising this year because the Moon is approaching its new phase. With little moonlight to brighten the sky, even relatively faint meteors should be easier to detect.
The shower gets its name from Draco, a constellation representing a dragon. Although the name might sound like something from a Halloween horror story involving a certain famous vampire, it actually refers to the constellation from which the meteors appear to originate.
The Draconids are generally a modest display, typically producing only a handful of visible meteors each hour. For the best chance of spotting them, head somewhere away from bright city lights, allow your eyes to adjust to the darkness, and scan the open sky for brief streaks of light.
Orionid Meteor Shower Brings Debris From Halley's Comet
Another opportunity to catch shooting stars arrives on October 21, when the Orionid meteor shower reaches its annual peak.
These meteors have a particularly fascinating origin. They are tiny fragments of material left behind by Halley's Comet during its journeys through the solar system. When Earth travels through this trail of ancient comet debris, the particles enter our atmosphere at tremendous speeds, creating bright streaks of light as they burn up.
For observers in suburban areas with some artificial lighting, NASA estimates that approximately 3 to 6 meteors may be visible each hour. People watching from darker locations could see somewhat more.
The Orionids take their name from Orion, the famous hunter constellation, because their meteors appear to radiate from that region of the sky. Orion is also home to Betelgeuse, an enormous red supergiant star recognizable by its reddish appearance (but don't say that name three times in a row!).
There is one potential obstacle to this year's display. The Moon will be in its waxing gibbous phase, meaning more than half of its visible surface will be illuminated. Its brightness could make some of the dimmer meteors difficult to spot.
Fortunately, viewing conditions should improve after the Moon sets at approximately 3 a.m. local time. By then, Orion will also be higher in the sky, creating a better opportunity to catch meteors during the hours before sunrise.
October's Hunter's Moon Lights Up the Halloween Sky
October's final major celestial highlight is the Hunter's Moon, which reaches its full phase on October 26 in Universal Time. For observers in much of North America, the Moon will appear full on the evening of Sunday, October 25.
The name Hunter's Moon comes from traditions associated with the changing autumn season. As crops were harvested, fields became more open, and daylight hours shortened, hunters could take advantage of the bright moonlight to locate and follow animals after sunset.
The Moon will remain a prominent feature of the night sky in the days following its full phase. As Halloween approaches, it will gradually transition into a waning gibbous Moon, with its illuminated portion slowly decreasing each night.
Its lingering glow will provide a fitting backdrop for the final evenings of October, bringing NASA's month of celestial tricks and treats to a memorable close.

articles.title: Nearly 30,000 people tested quit-smoking methods. One stood out
articles.text:
Nearly 30,000 people tested quit-smoking methods. One stood out
Nicotine e-cigarettes are more effective in helping people quit smoking than many conventional methods such as nicotine gums and patches and quitting with behavioral support or no support at all, an updated Cochrane review finds
- Date:
- October 8, 2026
- Source:
- Cochrane
- Summary:
- Nicotine e-cigarettes appear to help more smokers quit than patches, gum, and several other common approaches, according to a major review of 80 clinical trials. Researchers say regulated vaping products are not risk-free, but may be a significantly less harmful alternative for people who would otherwise continue smoking.
- Share:
An updated Cochrane review has found that nicotine e-cigarettes may help more people stop smoking than several commonly used approaches, including nicotine gum, nicotine patches, behavioral support, or trying to quit without assistance.
Smoking remains the world's leading cause of preventable disease and death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), it is responsible for more than seven million deaths each year, including 1.6 million deaths among non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke.
The findings come from a living systematic review, meaning researchers continually update the analysis as new evidence becomes available. The latest version included 80 randomized controlled trials involving 29,861 participants, with nine new trials added in this update.
Nicotine Vapes Outperform Patches and Gum
The researchers found high-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes produced higher quit rates than nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), such as patches and gum. For every 100 people, nicotine e-cigarettes resulted in about 4 additional people successfully quitting.
Nicotine e-cigarettes also performed better than non-nicotine cigarettes, leading to about 2 additional quitters per 100 people.
People given e-cigarettes also had higher quit rates than those who received no support or behavioral support (such as individual counseling and group programs). However, the researchers had less confidence in this comparison because of potential bias in how some of the studies were designed.
"We have very strong evidence that regulated nicotine e-cigarettes are substantially less harmful than smoking," says Dr. Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, senior author of the review from the University of Massachusetts Amherst. "Based on the consistency of the findings here, it's clear that they are a proven and viable option for people wishing to quit traditional cigarettes. This update includes 9 new trials and our main conclusions haven't changed."
What the Evidence Says About Vaping Risks
Researchers found no evidence that using e-cigarettes to quit smoking increased the risk of serious harm, although they emphasize that longer-term research is still needed.
The conclusions apply specifically to regulated, nicotine-containing e-cigarettes. Illicit products and e-cigarettes containing other substances, such as THC, may present different risks.
"It's worth highlighting that our review looks at regulated e-cigarettes containing nicotine, but many of those available on the market do not meet these standards," says Dr. Hartmann-Boyce. "Unlicensed e-cigarettes are potentially dangerous, with issues including unstable batteries and harmful chemicals. Anyone looking to use e-cigarettes to quit smoking should only purchase devices that have been tested and approved by their country's regulatory body. Lists of regulated devices are available from the FDA in the US and MHRA in the UK."
Major health organizations and agencies, including the WHO, continue to warn that e-cigarettes expose users to nicotine and other chemicals that can be harmful. Health officials have also raised concerns that e-cigarette use among children and young people can lead to nicotine addiction and later use of tobacco products.
A Step Away From Cigarettes, Not a Risk-Free Endpoint
The researchers stress that e-cigarettes may not be the best quitting method for everyone. People who want to stop smoking are encouraged to speak with stop-smoking support services or their clinicians about the most appropriate approach.
Vaping still carries health risks. However, the authors say those risks are much smaller than the dangers associated with continuing to smoke cigarettes.
Dr. Nicola Lindson, lead author of the review based at the University of Oxford, reflects that: "Quitting smoking is hard, and a lot of people who smoke will have tried many times to quit smoking and been unsuccessful. For that reason, it is important that there are a number of different options available to help somebody quit, which could encourage them to keep trying. Although nicotine vapes are unlikely to be completely risk-free, they are less harmful than smoking, and that is the most important comparison to make for people who are still smoking tobacco."
Dr. Hartmann-Boyce views switching to e-cigarettes as a possible stage in the process of moving away from smoking, rather than necessarily the final destination.
"For somebody who is already addicted to nicotine through cigarettes, having a safer alternative like an e-cigarette is something worth considering, especially when other quit aids have proven unsuccessful. We are currently working on a review of interventions to help people quit vaping, which could be the next step along for people looking to transition to a lower-harm product before quitting nicotine altogether."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cochrane. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Nicola Lindson, Jonathan Livingstone-Banks, Ailsa R Butler, Hayden McRobbie, Christopher R Bullen, Peter Hajek, Angela Difeng Wu, Rachna Begh, Annika Theodoulou, Claire Ma, Caitlin Notley, Nancy A Rigotti, Tari Turner, Thomas Fanshawe, Jamie Hartmann-Boyce. Electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2026; 2026 (8) DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD010216.pub11
