articles.title: Heineken Việt Nam chia sẻ chiến lược phát triển bền vững tại VCSF 2026
articles.text:
Từ nhà máy bia đầu tiên tại TP.HCM năm 1991, Heineken Việt Nam nay có 5 nhà máy, gần 3.000 nhân viên và hỗ trợ 167.000 việc làm trên toàn chuỗi giá trị. Song hành cùng định hướng phát triển của Việt Nam, Heineken Việt Nam đặt phát triển bền vững làm trọng tâm trong mọi hoạt động kinh doanh - sản xuất, giúp doanh nghiệp nâng cao hiệu quả, thúc đẩy đổi mới, tăng khả năng thích ứng và tạo nền tảng cho tăng trưởng dài hạn, chất lượng cao.
Phát triển bền vững tạo ra giá trị cốt lõi
Chiến lược toàn cầu EverGreen 2030 của Heineken đặt các chỉ tiêu phát triển bền vững và trách nhiệm quan trọng ngang với các chỉ tiêu tài chính. Nỗ lực này giúp công ty không chỉ đạt được những thành tựu xuyên suốt ba trụ cột: Uống có trách nhiệm, Môi trường và Xã hội, mà còn góp phần nâng cao năng suất, chất lượng tăng trưởng và năng lực cạnh tranh.
Cách tiếp cận này giúp doanh nghiệp hướng tới hiệu quả sử dụng tài nguyên và khả năng thích ứng tốt hơn, thúc đẩy những sản phẩm đổi mới, đáp ứng nhu cầu người tiêu dùng ngày nay như Heineken® 0.0, và củng cố vai trò đối tác dài hạn với các bên liên quan.
Đầu tư công nghệ và phát triển chuỗi cung ứng nội địa
Ông James Crampton - Giám đốc Ngoại vụ cấp cao Heineken Việt Nam cho biết: “Trong suốt 35 năm qua, Heineken Việt Nam luôn giữ vững niềm tin rằng, doanh nghiệp chỉ có thể thành công khi Việt Nam thành công. Tinh thần song hành cùng Việt Nam này được thể hiện qua việc phát triển cùng đối tác trong nước, tạo dựng hệ sinh thái lớn mạnh xung quanh doanh nghiệp và mang đến những giá trị lan tỏa”.
Tại nhà máy Bia Vũng Tàu, những khoản đầu tư liên tục vào công nghệ, tự động hóa và tối ưu tài nguyên giúp nhà máy vừa nâng công suất, vừa vận hành hiệu quả hơn và giảm tác động môi trường. Đội ngũ Heineken Việt Nam đã làm việc cùng các chuyên gia quốc tế và hiện có thể độc lập vận hành, bảo trì và tiếp tục nâng cấp những hệ thống tiên tiến tại nhà máy. Trong năm 2025, đội ngũ cũng đã đóng góp 28 thực hành tốt mới về hiệu quả sử dụng nước và năng lượng cho mạng lưới Heineken toàn cầu.
"Công nghệ có thể được đưa vào Việt Nam. Nhưng năng lực để hiểu và vận hành công nghệ đó phải được xây dựng tại Việt Nam, cho nhân tài Việt Nam”, ông James Crampton nhấn mạnh.
Hợp tác bảo tồn nguồn nước và tuyên truyền an toàn giao thông
Với nhận thức rằng các thách thức môi trường và xã hội cần sự chung tay của nhiều bên, Heineken Việt Nam xem hợp tác công - tư là một hướng tiếp cận trọng tâm trong chiến lược phát triển bền vững. Chương trình bảo tồn nguồn nước triển khai từ năm 2022 cùng Bộ Nông nghiệp và Môi trường, WWF-Việt Nam và các đối tác địa phương là một ví dụ tiêu biểu.
Trong giai đoạn I (2022 - 2025), chương trình tập trung vào ba lưu vực sông Hồng, Đồng Nai và sông Tiền. Đến cuối năm 2025, doanh nghiệp đã đạt mục tiêu cân bằng nước tại ba nhà máy ở Hà Nội, TP. Hồ Chí Minh và Tiền Giang. Chương
trình tiếp tục mở rộng triển khai tại lưu vực sông Cu Đê tại Đà Nẵng và Sông Ray - Đá Đen tại TP. Hồ Chí Minh, hướng đến tham vọng cân bằng 100% lượng nước sử dụng trong sản phẩm và bốc hơi tại cả 5 nhà máy vào năm 2030.
Bên cạnh môi trường, doanh nghiệp cũng kiên trì thúc đẩy văn hóa tiêu dùng có
trách nhiệm. Năm 2025 đánh dấu năm thứ 15 đồng hành cùng chương trình “Đã uống rượu bia thì không lái xe”, Heineken Việt Nam dành 15% ngân sách truyền thông của thương hiệu Heineken® mỗi năm cho các chiến dịch thưởng thức có trách nhiệm và giới thiệu Heineken® 0.0 đến với người tiêu dùng.
Đóng góp kinh tế của Heineken Việt Nam trong năm 2025
“Chặng tăng trưởng tiếp theo của Việt Nam đòi hỏi nhiều hơn nguồn lực, đó là những năng lực mới. Với Heineken, Việt Nam là nơi chúng tôi đầu tư, xây dựng năng lực và cùng phát triển với cộng đồng địa phương”, ông James Crampton chia sẻ.
Năm 2025, Heineken Việt Nam chi gần 22.000 tỷ đồng mua sắm từ doanh nghiệp trong nước, đóng góp tương đương 0,5% GDP quốc gia và nộp hơn 27.000 tỷ đồng tiền thuế, thuộc Top 5 doanh nghiệp đóng góp ngân sách lớn nhất theo bảng xếp hạng VNTax 200. Mỗi việc làm trực tiếp tại công ty hỗ trợ thêm 58 việc làm gián tiếp trong nền kinh tế.
Sau 35 năm, Heineken Việt Nam cam kết tiếp tục đầu tư, đổi mới và mở rộng hợp tác vì một Việt Nam tốt đẹp hơn.
(Nguồn: Heineken Việt Nam)

articles.title: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its vision-restoring chip, PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).
“The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said on stage. “We consider cochlear implants, retinal prostheses, motor prostheses, these are all different types of BCIs.”
Hodak outlined a vision in which BCIs expand into a wide range of medical technology applications, rather than simply being a way to control computers.
While PRIMA is commercially available in Europe for patients who’ve lost their sight to geographic atrophy, an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration, the company believes its approach can be applied to multiple diseases, including Stargardt disease, which is currently considered incurable.
Stargardt disease affects the outer retina, causing the gradual death of the eye’s light-sensing cells while potentially sparing the inner retina, the part that passes visual signals onto the brain. It causes a central blind spot that gradually enlarges over time. Approximately 150,000 people worldwide have lost vision due to the disease.
“One of the nice things about this device approach, when I was saying the brain’s a computer, vision is electrical potential, like electrical activity down the optic nerve,” Hodak said. “That’s all vision is to the brain, and so if you can get the optic nerve to signal the the rest of the brain correctly, then you can provide vision to it.”
The company says its first patient with Stargardt disease received the PRIMA implant in May as part of its ongoing trial at the Sydney Eye Hospital in Australia. During the patient’s first rehabilitation session, he saw a letter, and during the second, he was able to read a word.
To use the device, patients undergo an hour-long procedure that plants a small chip in the back of their eye, where the photoreceptors have degenerated. Then they wear camera-equipped glasses that transmit a view of the world to the chip. The implant essentially works like artificial photoreceptors.
“The device that this patient has is a two millimeter by two millimeter implant placed under the in the back of the eye, and so it’s like looking through a straw,” Hodak said. “It is not a big field of view color vision. It’s a patch in their central vision where . . .it’s black and white, but it is sharp. It’s high-contrast sharp, and so they can see a couple letters at a time. The next step is to make the field of view bigger. So to make a bigger implant, you have to deal with the curvature of the eye, and we need to make the electrodes smaller so that we get closer to native levels of detail.”
He continued, “I think we have a clear path. There’s a there’s a next ‘next generation’ that’s being worked on that’ll be in humans in the next year, and over the next five years, I think we’ll be able to get pretty close to native acuity.”
When Hodak founded Science Corporation in 2021 after leaving Neuralink, the company outlined plans to develop advanced neural engineering and brain-computer interface technology. But first, the company wants to prove its methods work and develop a sustainable business, which is why it’s working to restore vision with the visually impaired.
As for Science Corporation’s brain-computer interface technology, it has previously said that its sensor will be implanted inside the skull and rest on top of the brain, unlike a Neuralink device, which is inserted directly into brain tissue.
The company has said it believes the device could help address neurological conditions, such as possibly monitoring neurological activity in patients with brain tumors.
“In the near term, we’re going to be applying our first clinical indication, which hasn’t been announced publicly, is a neurodegenerative disease that everybody’s heard of,” Hodak said. “We’re also looking at stroke. For example, if you’ve lost part of your brain because it’s been dead due to stroke, if you can get connections into the deep brain in two different areas, you can imagine adding new cortical areas, just like adding new brain areas entirely — something simply not possible with conventional electrodes. But, I’d say longer term, the long-term mission of the company is to understand how the brain creates the mind and to learn to build engineered brains.”
Hodak went on to note that Science Corporation’s belief is that many people will eventually use some kind of BCI. While the company isn’t designing for “healthy 40-year-olds,” he said, it believes people will eventually need some kind of BCI by the age of 60 or 70.
“We want to figure out how do we extend not just lifespan but health span,” Hodak said.

articles.title: VIS 2026 quy tụ lãnh đạo toàn cầu, bàn cách hút vốn và đưa công nghệ Việt ra thị trường
articles.text:
Hội nghị Thượng đỉnh Đổi mới Sáng tạo Việt Nam 2026 diễn ra tại TP.HCM từ ngày 13 đến 15/10, tập trung vào thu hút dòng vốn đầu tư thế hệ mới, thương mại hóa công nghệ và nâng cao năng lực cạnh tranh của doanh nghiệp Việt trước các tiêu chuẩn xanh toàn cầu.
Trong cuộc cạnh tranh thu hút vốn quốc tế, câu hỏi với Việt Nam không còn chỉ là làm thế nào để có thêm đầu tư, mà còn là cách giữ lại nhiều giá trị hơn cho nền kinh tế. Đây cũng là một trong những vấn đề trọng tâm được đặt ra tại Hội nghị Thượng đỉnh Đổi mới Sáng tạo Việt Nam (VIS 2026), diễn ra tại TP.HCM trong ba ngày 13-15/10.
Với chủ đề “Critical Mass – The New Currents of Innovation: Vietnam at the Center of a Global Realignment”, sự kiện hướng đến kết nối cơ quan quản lý, doanh nghiệp, quỹ đầu tư và các trường đại học để thảo luận về dòng vốn, công nghệ và năng lực cạnh tranh quốc gia.
Theo số liệu được ban tổ chức dẫn từ Quỹ Tiền tệ Quốc tế (IMF), tăng trưởng kinh tế toàn cầu năm 2026 được dự báo ở mức 3%. Trong khi đó, Việt Nam ghi nhận GDP năm 2025 tăng 8%, xuất khẩu tăng 16,7% và vốn FDI giải ngân đạt 27,6 tỷ USD. Các dự báo được Ngân hàng Thế giới (WB) và Ngân hàng Phát triển châu Á (ADB) đưa ra cho tăng trưởng Việt Nam năm 2026 nằm trong khoảng 7,4-7,8%.
Tuy nhiên, việc thu hút vốn mới chỉ là một phần của bài toán. Việt Nam còn cần những cơ chế giúp chuyển dòng vốn, tri thức và công nghệ thành giá trị kinh tế thực chất.
Thu hút vốn và đưa công nghệ từ phòng thí nghiệm ra thị trường
Một trọng tâm của VIS 2026 là thảo luận về lộ trình xây dựng Khu Thương mại Tự do (FTZ) và Trung tâm Tài chính Quốc tế (IFC) tại TP.HCM, trong khuôn khổ diễn đàn “Capital Without Borders”.
Ông Ismail Al Naqi, thành viên Hội đồng Tiểu vương quốc Ajman, UAE, dự kiến chia sẻ kinh nghiệm vận hành mô hình khu thương mại tự do, bao gồm khung pháp lý cho phép sở hữu 100% vốn nước ngoài, cơ chế tự do hóa dòng vốn và chính sách thu hút nhân tài. Theo định hướng được ban tổ chức nêu, FTZ được kỳ vọng đóng góp 1/5 GDP TP.HCM vào năm 2045.
Bên cạnh dòng vốn, hội nghị tập trung vào khả năng thương mại hóa các công nghệ lõi như trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI), bán dẫn, Physical AI và sản xuất thông minh.
Một phiên thảo luận do Đại học RMIT Việt Nam đồng tổ chức, dưới sự chủ trì của GS. Scott Thompson-Whiteside, sẽ giới thiệu mô hình hợp tác “Ba nhà” giữa nhà nước, doanh nghiệp và trường đại học. Nội dung đáng chú ý là chiến lược cấp phép tài sản trí tuệ, được kỳ vọng tạo cầu nối để các nghiên cứu về robot và AI tiến gần hơn tới ứng dụng thương mại.
Đây là bài toán quan trọng với hệ sinh thái đổi mới sáng tạo: kết quả nghiên cứu không chỉ dừng lại trong phòng thí nghiệm mà cần có con đường đi vào sản phẩm và hoạt động kinh doanh thực tế.
Hơn 150 phiên kết nối đầu tư, doanh nghiệp đối mặt tiêu chuẩn xanh
VIS 2026 dự kiến tổ chức hơn 150 phiên kết nối giao thương trực tiếp 1:1, trong đó có chương trình ASEAN CrossConnect đồng tổ chức với Cradle Fund Malaysia. Các hoạt động diễn ra tại bốn khu vực chuyên biệt mang tên Inno, Beyond, Connect và Collab, tạo cơ hội để tập đoàn, quỹ đầu tư và doanh nghiệp công nghệ tìm kiếm đối tác.
Theo ban tổ chức, những phiên kết nối này hướng đến việc chuyển các cuộc trao đổi thành cơ hội hợp tác và thương mại hóa cụ thể, thay vì chỉ dừng ở thảo luận về đổi mới sáng tạo.
Một chủ đề khác là năng lực cạnh tranh của doanh nghiệp Việt trước các yêu cầu ngày càng khắt khe về phát triển bền vững. Các tiêu chuẩn môi trường, xã hội và quản trị (ESG), cùng cơ chế điều chỉnh biên giới carbon (CBAM), đang khiến việc tuân thủ tiêu chuẩn xanh trở thành vấn đề đáng chú ý đối với doanh nghiệp tham gia chuỗi cung ứng quốc tế.
Tọa đàm “Cạnh tranh bằng định chuẩn trong thời kỳ xoay trục kinh tế”, do Masterise Group đồng chủ trì, sẽ tập trung vào kinh nghiệm áp dụng tiêu chuẩn quốc tế trong hạ tầng và các dự án trọng điểm. Nội dung này đặt vấn đề nâng cao năng lực không chỉ ở từng doanh nghiệp mà còn trên toàn chuỗi cung ứng trong nước.
Diễn ra từ ngày 13 đến 15/10 tại Riverside Saigon Palace, TP.HCM, VIS 2026 đặt trọng tâm vào việc kết nối vốn, công nghệ và thể chế. Những vấn đề được đưa ra thảo luận đều xoay quanh một câu hỏi lớn: làm thế nào để Việt Nam không chỉ trở thành điểm đến của dòng vốn quốc tế, mà còn nâng cao khả năng tạo ra giá trị từ dòng vốn và công nghệ đó.

articles.title: Is Mini DisplayPort becoming obsolete? - Engadget
articles.text:
Is Mini DisplayPort becoming obsolete?
How Thunderbolt and USB-C replaced the need for a dedicated video port.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
For a while, Mini DisplayPort was one of the main options for video output on smaller devices. Apple announced it in 2008 to replace interfaces like VGA and DVI with a single, slimmer connector. While it was seen on most Mac models for several years, it's since become difficult to find computers with Mini DisplayPort — even Apple has removed the port from Macs.
But does that mean it's obsolete? Not exactly, although you won't see it as often as you used to. The DisplayPort standard remains popular, especially among workstations and gaming monitors, so it's not as if the technology itself has become obsolete. But we now have another small port that's favored.
Why Mini DisplayPort faded out
Mini DisplayPort is called "mini" for a reason. The full-size version (simply called DisplayPort) supports the same core specifications, but with a larger connector. Apple always opted for the tiny version because it fits better on smaller computers like MacBooks and the Mac mini.
It doesn't matter whether you use DisplayPort (DP) or Mini DisplayPort — both can transmit video and audio through a single cable. Compared to older connectors like DVI and VGA, one of the main advantages of DisplayPort is that it offers much higher bandwidth. Depending on the generation, DP can handle resolutions up to 8K and beyond, at high frame rates (144+Hz) depending on the resolution. Meanwhile, older connectors struggle with anything above 1080p.
When the Thunderbolt standard emerged, its first two iterations used the Mini DisplayPort connector. While a standard Mini DP port only carries video and audio, Thunderbolt also supports high-speed data transfers. That meant the same connector could be used for video, audio and data — perfect for accessories like Apple's Cinema Display.
In late 2015 and 2016, the Thunderbolt 3 standard arrived and switched to the USB-C connector. Apple and other PC manufacturers quickly moved to USB-C or HDMI, leaving the Mini DisplayPort connector behind. These days, USB-C has become the standard for nearly everything. Not only can it support high-speed data transfer, but it can also handle video, audio and even the Thunderbolt protocol — all in a single, small reversible connector. Not every USB-C port can handle the same tasks, but you'll see some version of it on almost every device.
To further push Mini DisplayPort down, USB-C also supports DisplayPort Alternate Mode, meaning a compatible USB-C cable and ports can carry the same DisplayPort signal through the more modern cable. PC makers have no reason to have people buy a Mini DP-to-DP cable when they can simply buy a USB-C-to-DP cable.
Where DisplayPort still makes sense
That doesn't mean DisplayPort is gone. Of course, you may still find older hardware with Mini DisplayPort, like past laptops and graphics cards. If you still have one of these, you can buy a Mini DP-to-DP cable to connect them to a modern monitor. Since the protocol is the same, they'll communicate with each other just fine. New hardware also continues to use full-sized version of DisplayPort. It's still the standard for many high-end monitors and graphics cards.
HDMI has come a long way in recent years and can now transmit video at incredibly high resolutions. Still, DisplayPort remains the gold standard for absurdly high resolutions and refresh rates, such as 4K at 240Hz. For comparison, while HDMI 2.1 offers up to 48 Gbps of bandwidth, DisplayPort 2.1 can reach 80 Gbps. This makes a difference for those looking to get the most out of the hardware they have. HDMI 2.2 offers 96 Gbps bandwidth, which may even the field a bit once compatible devices are widely available.
Of course, when using older hardware, not everything may work as expected. VR headsets, for example, can be picky about their video signal, and they don't always play nice with Mini DisplayPort when you use an adapter. The same goes for the old Apple Cinema Display — Apple makes it clear that it doesn't work through a Thunderbolt adapter. Still, it doesn't hurt to try if you have the right cables on hand.

articles.title: Bảo Tín Minh Châu lên tiếng về việc đại lý căng băng rôn đề nghị trả lại tài sản
articles.text:
Trong thông báo phát đi, Bảo Tín Minh Châu (BTMC) cho biết ngày 25/3, Cơ quan Cảnh sát điều tra Công an TP Hà Nội (PC03) đã tiến hành thu giữ hàng hóa, nguyên liệu tại các cơ sở kinh doanh của doanh nghiệp để phục vụ công tác xác minh, điều tra. Trong số hàng hóa, nguyên liệu bị thu giữ có tài sản của BTMC và tài sản của các đại lý.
Đến nay, số hàng hóa, nguyên liệu nêu trên vẫn đang trong quá trình được cơ quan chức năng xác minh, xử lý. BTMC chưa nhận được thông báo hoặc văn bản chính thức của cơ quan có thẩm quyền về phương án và thời điểm hoàn trả số tài sản này.
“Vì vậy, việc hoàn trả tài sản hiện vẫn cần chờ kết quả xử lý và hướng dẫn chính thức từ cơ quan chức năng”, BTMC cho hay.
Doanh nghiệp cũng khẳng định không né tránh trách nhiệm và luôn thiện chí phối hợp với đối tác cũng như cơ quan chức năng để xử lý vụ việc trên cơ sở hồ sơ, chứng từ và quy định pháp luật. Từ đó, thúc đẩy việc xem xét, giải quyết và hoàn trả tài sản trong thời gian sớm nhất có thể.
Cùng với đó, BTMC sẽ tiếp tục phối hợp, cung cấp thông tin và thực hiện các công việc cần thiết theo yêu cầu của cơ quan có thẩm quyền. Ngay khi có thông tin chính thức liên quan đến phương án xử lý, hoàn trả tài sản, BTMC sẽ kịp thời thông tin đến các khách hàng, đối tác trong phạm vi được phép.
Trước đó, ngày 2/4/2026, Cơ quan Cảnh sát điều tra Công an TP Hà Nội đã ra quyết định khởi tố ông Vũ Minh Châu, nhà sáng lập thương hiệu Bảo Tín Minh Châu, cùng 3 người khác để điều tra về tội Vi phạm quy định về kế toán gây hậu quả nghiêm trọng.

articles.title: Cerebras CEO says we're nearing a future where everyone has a personal AI assistant at home | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Cerebras Systems CEO and co-founder Andrew Feldman believes we’re nearing a future where everyone will have an AI appliance in their own home.
Speaking on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Tuesday, the chipmaker executive answered a question about what would need to happen for AI to become a home appliance, saying, “Actually, I don’t think that’s very far away.”
He pointed to the advances in consumer AI agents, like Meta’s Muse and Instinct, the startup now valued at $10 billion, as examples of how AI is finding its footing with everyday users.
As for home AI? He predicts that we’ll have personal AI assistants that run locally.
“Just like your cell phone, they’ll do some work on device and some work going back to the cloud,” Feldman explained. “But I think they will get to know you very well, and you will have a security perimeter around them. And they will certainly have access to credit cards and be able to buy things for you,” he continued. “I think they will make a meaningful impact in making our lives better.”
Of course, for an AI chipmaker, the vision of a home AI appliance, or at least widespread consumer adoption of agentic technology, is certainly appealing.
But Feldman isn’t just working on the hardware infrastructure; he’s a personal AI user himself, saying that he now uses “a collection of agents” to sweep his calendar, pull up information about the people he’s going to have a call with, and more. While AI is already doing many of the things we used to do manually, Feldman is most excited about the new possibilities — things that weren’t possible before.
He’s leaving it up to other founders to figure out what those might be, though.
“One of the reasons I love being in infrastructure is because I don’t need the consumer-facing idea … I like building the platforms that other people’s ideas take flight on,” he said.

articles.title: Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Has a Unique Perspective on Daddy Issues
articles.text:
Only one person agreed to be Alex Gibney’s new Elon Musk documentary immediately: Musk’s father. “We had Errol Musk at ‘hello,’” Gibney says.
Eventually, the director would speak with scores of Musk’s associates for his film. His first wife, Justine Musk, appears, as does his ex-girlfriend Ashley St. Claire. Journalist Kara Swisher, LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, myself, and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond also spoke to Gibney for Musk, which hits theaters nationwide on Friday. But landing Errol Musk, with whom the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has a complicated relationship, was a watershed.
“Everybody else took a lot of persuasion,” Gibney says. “It was very difficult to get people to appear because the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.”
Once Gibney interviewed all of his subjects, he had enough material to make a documentary that runs nearly four hours, including a 10-minute intermission. It’s a damning portrait of the trillionaire CEO, detailing how much of his genius is based on his formidable ability to promote his own mythology—and the stock price of his public companies.
Musk never agreed to an interview with Gibney. Instead, the director’s team researched every public comment Musk ever made and created a simulated Elon Musk who appears throughout the film.
I spoke with Gibney earlier this month about his experience making the film, why he decided to make his simulated Elon attractive, and what material he had to leave on the cutting room floor.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
ZOË SCHIFFER: Alex Gibney, thank you so much for being with us today.
ALEX GIBNEY: Good to see you, Zoë.
This shouldn’t spoil anything, but in the four years that you spent making Musk, Elon Musk never agreed to sit down with you for an interview. Instead, your team looked back through the archives of everything he has said publicly, and you put together a sort of simulated interview, which appears throughout the film as a through line. Basically, it plays into Musk’s idea that we are all, in fact, living in a simulation. How did you decide on this approach for the film?
Well, what were we gonna do? He’s the main character.
I actually thought because he’d been so outspoken about this idea of a simulation, that cinematically we should lean into that. We should play in Elon’s sandbox and have a simulated interview. As we began to develop that idea, by using his real words, his actual audio recordings, but placing them in a kind of avatar which we would design, I think there became all sorts of thematic reasons to do it.
One was because he himself had said we’re living in a simulation. But two was the importance of this notion in the Elon Musk story of the shifting sands between what is real and what is unreal. Then also, because a lot of the film deals with his issues of AI, that discomfiting relationship that we’re beginning to explore, all of us on planet Earth, with these AI LLMs and how we begin to project things on these computer interfaces, it felt like this might be something interesting to do.
By the way, you’ll notice that when Elon is talking to people in a normal interview situation, he rarely looks at the interviewer or at the camera. He’s always looking this way or that way. So we designed this in a very different way, where he’s looking right down the barrel of the lens directly at the viewer, and we thought that that would be OK. We’re gonna give Elon a break, and actually, I thought our avatar made him look pretty good compared to some of the recent images of him.
I have a question about that because your simulated Elon Musk—I think it’s fair to say—looks a lot hunkier than present day Elon Musk. He’s kind of chiseled and tan, and …
It is kind of a two-day growth of beard.
Exactly. Was that an intentional choice? And if so, can you just talk about why that was?
It was. I joke about this, but he’s the star of my movie, I want my star to look good. But I think also it would’ve been a mistake to go into slop AI territory, like some of the images that Elon’s fans are posting about me right now, to sort of denigrate him visually.
Also, to some extent, the story is also about image building, too. So I thought, “OK, let’s have some fun with that as well.” Because we had a lot of choices. I mean, we started out with the design firm, like how should he look? What should he be dressed in? You know, we put him in a gamer chair, a leather jacket. There were conscious choices.
That extends to some of the comments he makes, where I don’t find like the most bumbling comments that Elon ever made.
When we have somebody speaking about something, I want a rejoinder from Elon. We looked for the best rejoinders, like how can he come back at us? Now, later on in the film, his statements become more and more fantastical, but that also is part of what happens.
I think it really worked for the film. I’ve seen it a couple times and I think there are these famous images of Elon Musk. I’m thinking of the one where he’s on the yacht and he’s shirtless. There, it seems like if you had leaned into a less flattering image, you would’ve been playing on his turf, but in a way that would undermine the message of the movie. Whereas elevating his look allowed you to hold him quite accountable in a way that comes across pretty fair.
Yeah, we were respectful. We gave him a good look. And much better by the time we go to the archive, particularly the archive of the SpaceX IPO, when he’s begun to start looking like Kim Jong Il.
I’m curious about your thoughts on ethics. It’s not putting words in someone’s mouth, because these are all statements that Elon Musk has really made, and it’s not even like you’re particularly mashing stuff together.
But your decision, for example, to have him look right at the camera, you are making decisions for him in a way that you couldn’t with a live interview subject. So I’m just curious if you could speak to the ethical implications of that.
I think that goes to the heart of what’s different about a documentary like this and maybe a podcast interview in the sense that we’re rendering that image in a kind of broader cinematic context. The imagery itself is intended to either convey meaning or to raise questions for the viewer that they should start to think about.
As you know from being interviewed for the film, we interviewed you in front of a green screen and then placed you in a background, which we sort of reveal at different times in the movie. All of this had to do with this kind of strange unreality, real unreal world we’re living in right now.
Mm-hmm.
But also by shooting him looking into the lens I sometimes do that and I sometimes don’t. There is this interesting psychological relationship that you begin to have with a subject that I think is both real and unreal at the same time, which was part of this larger conceit in terms of trying to find a way to make the movie and the formal devices in the film itself reflect some of the thematic concerns.
Right. It also makes him feel like there is a fair amount of conviction behind what he’s saying, and there’s this relationship between him and the audience.
I feel like over the course of his public life, he doesn’t appear to have had an allegiance or ideology to one coherent political identity or to even his colleagues or close friends. These things are shifting and changing. So I am curious how that kind of came up for you in the making of the film of wanting to convey an Elon Musk in the simulated interview that represented, to the best of your ability, the quote-unquote, “true Elon.”
I mean, it’s a shape-shifting image and one which is, after all, confected, which is useful, particularly when you’re using it as a vehicle to put these statements in. I agree with your point that you just made about Elon’s ideology. I think there are a lot of wise and very perceptive books that have been written that in my view sometimes make one kind of critical flaw. They try to render a coherence about Elon’s thinking that I’m not sure is there. I think he’s far more of an improviser and shape-shifter. He has an image of himself that he wants to convey, but he’ll sculpt and change that image according to conditions and evidence, like the way he acted with Obama versus the way he acted with Trump.
I mean, there was a history there, but still they’re both serving the same purpose for him, which is, “How do I cadge the most amount of resources out of the federal government?”
I’ve thought about this a fair amount as well. I think his acquisition of Twitter now acts as a very clear example where in the moment it was clearly this impulsive decision, but now that it’s become this big source of political power for him, there’s this tendency to be like, “Oh, he was playing a complicated game all along.”
My view has always been that if Elon has a superpower it’s that he has a pretty high risk tolerance, and so he’s able to make impulsive, rash decisions and then deal with the fallout in a way that a slightly more cautious person might not be able to, for better or often worse.
He’s so comfortable with risk. It’s as though he goes through life on a canoe moving down the rapids. When he sees a rock there, he goes this way. He sees another rock or a shifting current, he goes that way. In the case of Twitter, as you pointed out in your book, he kind of bought the company on a dare, and he grossly overpaid for it and also abandoned all due diligence.
From the standpoint of a businessman, it was just dumb. But he didn’t care, and he had so many resources, what did it matter? Twitter, now X, was always a vehicle for his ambitions and his ability to court retail investors.
I don’t think it occurred to him until later when he had virtually destroyed the value of the company for the rest of us, that actually this would be a good propaganda platform for me. That’s what it becomes. Then suddenly it actually has enormous political and economic utility in a way that I don’t think he thought through at the beginning.
So Musk aside, plenty of people did speak to you for this film: Musk’s first wife, Justine; his former girlfriend, the influencer Ashley St. Clair, who he has a kid with; his father; former business partners; former colleagues; people he’s fired; the former ambassador to the United Nations, Samantha Power; Kara Swisher.
Walk me through the process of getting these people to say yes, to trust you. Specifically, was there anyone who really surprised you in their immediate willingness to say yes, and anyone who really needed extra time and conversation with you in order to be able to say yes?
Almost everybody who appeared in this film needed time to be able to process and accept appearing, in part because there was a sense of risk associated with it. Only one person agreed immediately, and that was Errol Musk.
Oh my gosh.
It was almost like, what’s that line from that great film “You had me at …”
“You had me at ‘hello.’”
We had Errol Musk at hello. “Hello, Errol, would you like to appear in this documentary?” “Yes.” We quickly rushed a crew over to his house. I did a remote interview in South Africa. It was the one interview we did that was not green screen, and he was remarkably revealing, sometimes in intended and sometimes in unintended ways.
Everybody else took a lot of persuasion. I was having conversations with Justine for over a year, I think, before she agreed to sit down. Even somebody as powerful as Reid Hoffman, same thing. So it was very difficult to get people to appear because Musk’s—the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.
In some cases I did talk to a lot of people, sort of powerful people in Silicon Valley, on background—some of whom had fond feelings toward Elon and some who didn’t. I found it interesting that there’s sort of like talking to people in a gentleman’s club, and one doesn’t talk about other people publicly.
While I did learn things when they were talking to me on background or off the record, I found that kind of revolting in a way. It’s like we’re dealing with a figure now who has enormous sway over all of us, and isn’t it important to weigh in on that kind of public debate?
But that wasn’t the view that they had. In fact, there’s a guy I know who is friends with Elon and treasures his friendship with Elon, and I said, “Let’s have a conversation off the record. You know, tell me what’s great about Elon and why you like him so much.” He said “I would never betray a friend like that.”
I got that for my book as well. I don’t feel as surprised. I think if we were talking about six, seven, eight, nine, 10 years ago, like, yes. But these are similar people to those who are flying to Washington, DC to pay fealty to Trump, and going directly against values that they were talking about not that long ago.
That’s right.
I do wanna talk about Errol Musk because you brought him up. There’s this very powerful interview in the film where he talks about his son. He seems to have had a very big impact on Elon Musk’s life, and not necessarily a positive one. This was kind of the central thesis of Walter Isaacson’s biography of Elon Musk.
It kind of came down to daddy issues. So I’m curious to get your perspective on Errol’s influence on Elon and how you balanced showing the hardship of his childhood without using that as an overly simplistic explanation for his behavior today.
I think that’s an important point. I do think that Errol Musk had a powerful impact on Elon, because of how Elon felt he was treated by his dad, sometimes cruelly, psychologically. We don’t know of any kind of physical abuse. But also I think, you know, by watching Errol, you grok—to use a term from the Heinlein book—the notion that the apple doesn’t fall far from the tree.
There’s an element you can see the character of Elon. We kept it in a kind of short contained section and as an element of how we can think about Elon Musk. But I think the Walter Isaacson conclusion, in a way, is a little bit too easy. There are a lot of people who’ve been bullied or abused by their parents who don’t end up becoming bullies or abusers.
And to say it’s a kind of a mechanical thing that happens is kind of letting Elon Musk off the moral hook. That was an issue I had with Walter’s book. To some extent, we’re all grateful for the fact that he was able to spend so much time with Elon. There’s an accretion of detail in the book that’s valuable.
But I think the conclusions were sort of a get out of jail free card for the performative cruelty that ultimately he engaged in. Yet you need to know about the origin story without—it can be an explanation without being an excuse, I guess is what I would say.
I would imagine that in the making of a film like this, there is an open question at the beginning in particular about whether you’re actually going to get enough access for this to work. It’s certainly a question with features that we write. I’m curious if there was a particular interview, maybe with someone close to him, where you knew like, “OK, we’re, we’re gonna be able to do this. I think we’re gonna have enough.”
Well, weirdly, it didn’t happen until very late, and I would say it was the Justine Musk interview. I mean, the Ashley St. Clair interview is powerful as it is, and it is powerful, and it gives you a front-row seat to the election of 2024. The Justine Musk interview gave me insights into his personality that were very powerful in both understanding him as a person, but also understanding some of what he did thematically.
Because I asked her—and this answer is not in the film, but it helped to guide me—“What was it that attracted you about him back in college?” They met in college in Canada. And she said it was his enormous confidence. And then the other thing she said that’s powerful that is in the film is that she learned about gaslighting from Elon Musk.
That gaslighting thing, the idea of trying to convince somebody that the truth is other than what it is, and to suggest that you’re crazy and if you don’t go along, is a super important insight into who Elon is. And confidence, of course, is what allows that to happen.
Justine’s was such a powerful interview in the film. There are multiple moments where she cries or is near tears. She comes across as just so genuine, and I think she also seems like someone who doesn’t appear to be in it for attention or power or money. Like, there’s a point in the film where I think she says, “I really wanted to have a say in how this story was told.”
I’m thinking specifically of when their first child died in a SIDS-related incident, and Elon Musk tweets that he was holding the child. The child died in his arms. And Justine says, “No, this was one of the most defining moments of my life. He died in my arms.” You really just see how Elon has hurt her over the years.
That’s right. That gets me kind of emotionally worked up even as I think about it, because of course that moment was deeply painful for Elon, which is what Walter Isaacson spent some time on in the book. But to credit-grab in the midst of a tragedy like that seems so petulant and small and, you know, talk about main character syndrome.
One of the defining things about Elon Musk is that over time, as he increased more and more power, there was only one character in all his companies, and that’s Elon Musk, and only one character in all of his marriages. That’s Elon Musk. Everyone else recedes into the background. It’s interesting.
Justine is a storyteller. She’s a talented novelist. I went deep into reading her blogs and also the article that she wrote for Marie Claire. You know, her ability to be a storyteller is actually quite profound precisely because she’s reaching for a deeper truth.
I think when Elon is a storyteller, he’s actually reaching for fiction. He’s reaching to mythologize in a way that undoes the truth, that steers us away from that kind of hard work of getting to the stuff that is really deep and painful because it’s true.
I am curious about your take on this because it’s a question that I have had about Elon Musk: Does he actually believe what he’s saying or is he knowingly lying?
I think it’s closer to the former, and I’ve dealt with a number of characters who are like this. Sam Harris in the film makes a distinction between liars and bullshitters, and liars, of course, have to assiduously keep track of the truth in order to know when and how they’re lying.
Bullshitters just say what comes to their mind. It’s a kind of—it’s on the right track, but sort of insufficient. I think for somebody like Elon Musk—or people in the past like that I’ve dealt with, like Elizabeth Holmes or the guys at Enron or even somebody like Lance Armstrong—in the moment, because you feel a kind of righteousness about your cause, you feel you’re kind of entitled to make things up, You feel over time so entitled and so corrupted by this notion that the end justifies the means, that some kind of psychological trick is played inside your own mind where in order to be forceful and confident about what it is you’re saying in the moment, you have to believe it.
I reckoned with that with Lance Armstrong, where he could look people in the eye at a press conference and say with great force, “How dare you say that I, as a cancer survivor, would ever use performance-enhancing drugs?” And then he’d get down off the podium and do a bag of blood.
But I think in the moment he did believe what he said, because that’s how you come off as being effective. You see it particularly for people who become kind of addicted to a growing power that they have, and they see that also they have an ability to convince, like Elizabeth Holmes did.
It’s a psychological quirk that kind of takes over, and it’s peculiar, but I think it’s real.
It’s so hard to remember when talking about Elon Musk that this goober in an Occupy Mars T-shirt who’s thrashing around with a chainsaw waxing poetic has had this undeniable impact on so many people’s lives and livelihoods, and a lot of that impact has been negative.
The part of your film about DOGE, Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, which is a short-lived stint in Washington, DC where he fired, I think, 300,000 federal workers to, quote-unquote, “solve the federal deficit.” Spoiler alert, he didn’t even come close. That was probably one of the hardest moments to watch.
Samantha Power, former ambassador to the UN, spoke specifically about the lives lost, thousands and thousands, and millions more projected, after he shuttered USAID. I’m curious, given all you know about Elon Musk at this point, and the reporting you did on DOGE, what do you think that period and that experiment was really about for him?
It wasn’t about waste, fraud, and abuse. There was an aspect of glee and performative cruelty that we tried to represent in the film by showing the DOGE cuts as a kind of first-person shooter game, juxtaposed of course, with the sober testimony of Samantha Power, who talks about how many children died as a result.
But I think in many ways the waste, fraud, and abuse was kind of the magician’s sleight of hand to say, “This is what we’re doing.” But what he was really doing was something very self-serving, which as a big tech baron, was literally destroying the regulatory state.
If there was a lot of collateral damage, people died, disease went up, who cared? It was the destruction of the inspectors general, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. He called everything corrupt without any evidence and so forth and so on.
The other thing, and the more controversial thing, which we’re all still chasing in a way, is the fact that the DOGE boys, who were clueless about the agencies they went into, nevertheless seemed to know an awful lot about data extraction and data access.
And they were granted, according to one head of IT at a federal agency I talked to, super admin status, which you know better than I, allows them to break through all sorts of silos that are intended to be erected to either protect classified information or protect our private data.
So the DOGE boys had access to vast amounts of data that no one has ever had access to in history. All of that didn’t go unnoticed, but it was the flash over the chainsaw all of the press conferences kind of hid a lot of what was really going on, I think.
Yeah, if you’re really worried about waste, fraud, and abuse, then there’s a certain level of care that you would take in your auditing. The DOGE boys were posting on X this kind of, quote-unquote, “wall of receipts” where they would talk about contracts that they’ve slashed, not understanding that in procurement paperwork, oftentimes you’ll put the total lifetime amount that could ever be spent on a contract, which is sometimes quite different, millions of dollars different, from the actual amount that was spent.
So they were claiming savings that were nowhere close to what had actually been saved. There was another, and this is in the film as well, moment where Elon Musk was talking about how they were finding tons of people who were getting Social Security benefits who were 150 years old, not understanding that when you don’t have a birthday for someone in the Social Security system, which is built on very arcane technology, really old code, it defaults to a birthday that shows someone as 150.
Anyone who had worked in SSA would’ve been able to tell them that, but they didn’t seem, to me, to be particularly interested in the details, which again, if you’re really worried about waste, fraud, and abuse, that’s all about details.
Correct. And indeed the detail that you mentioned about Social Security was actually posted on the Social Security website. So they could’ve read the website. But it goes to this kind of performative cruelty where it almost didn’t matter to them, you know?
One of the more chilling interviews, which I got from a deposition, was with one of the DOGE boys, a kid named Nate Cavanaugh.
Mm-hmm.
The questioner asked him, “Did you not care about the lives that were being affected by all of these mass firings and, and the kind of pain and suffering that would cause?” And he said, “Well, no, because we thought it was more important to reduce the federal deficit.” Next question: “Did you reduce the federal deficit?” “No.” But, you know, for a guy who’s supposed to be such a genius, you would think there would be some analysis done.
But that parallels what happened at Twitter, as you know better than anybody. In other words, they would fire people at Twitter who had actually critical jobs, without even knowing what they did.
Ezra Klein has talked about this. I think it’s really true. Like at Twitter, when you make a rash decision or you fire people, the feedback loop with the company or social media is pretty small. You can see the effects of that pretty quickly. The site starts to get glitchy.
In government, the feedback loop is really long. You don’t get to see immediately the impact of those decisions, and to me that appears to be a large reason why the effects were just so much more devastating, and honestly, while he has admitted publicly DOGE was a failure, it seems like there was no move made to kind of correct any errors.
I think even as a failure, it was sort of an intended failure in the sense that it was an attempt to really fire cannons at the government, particularly the regulatory state, so that the castle couldn’t be repaired.
Yeah, I guess I should say the stated goal of the budget deficit was a failure, but the implicit goal was quite successful.
That’s right. It was really successful. The other thing that is so disturbing about the DOGE moment is that in a lot of cases they were literally warned about the damage that was done, and that, that was certainly the case at USAID. You can make a decision as a country that we’re not gonna give aid to developing countries anymore, but money had already been appropriated by Congress. Indeed, food had been bought to send to starving children, and in some cases, boats were literally stopped to prevent that food from going to the children, who then subsequently died while they ended up burning the food on pallets someplace, literally wasting food that had already been bought and paid for.
So the cruelty had a kind of performative quality to it, which was meant, I think, to speak to the roiling anger that Musk is so good at fomenting on X and which the MAGA movement is so good at exploiting politically.
Toward the end of the film, Geoffrey Hinton comes on and says, quote, “It’s fairly clear to me Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections. If you want to corrupt those midterm elections and you want to use AI, what you’d need to do is get detailed information on US citizens. And what DOGE did looked to me like just what you would do if you wanted to get data on US citizens.”
Basically, he’s saying Musk appears to have already gathered up the data Trump would need to meddle in the upcoming election. We’re now less than a month out. So based on the interviews that you conducted and the information that you have coming out of this project, I’m curious what you are most worried about, and what is the concern in terms of what Musk may have been cooking up, and how do you see this playing out?
The first thing I should say is I don’t really know.
You guys are doing a lot of interesting reporting now about where the money is going and how much of it is going to focus on negative advertising versus pro-candidate stuff. But also, what kind of stories are people particularly susceptible to? We know from years of having our data mined by Facebook and X and others that it’s really useful to know what people respond to and what people think, and you have enormous data about them, then you can message certain things in order to be able to reach those soft points psychologically.
I would have to say at this moment, because it does look like we’re not far away from the election, and it looks like it’s gonna be a blue wave. We’ll see. But if it is, my bigger concern is over a disinformation campaign, aided and abetted by Elon Musk, with massive amounts of data that would try to undermine people’s confidence that the election was free and fair.
That’s what I fear most at this moment.
The documentary comes in at just under four hours.
Three hours, 45 minutes, but there’s a 10-minute intermission.
OK. The documentary comes in just under four hours, but I know from talking to you and being a little bit involved in the project that there was a ton that you left on the cutting room floor. So I’m wondering if you can speak about what parts you had to cut that were the hardest, what you wish you could’ve kept in, and how you ultimately made those decisions.
There are sections that I wish I could have kept at their expanded length. One of them is Twitter, where we had a lot more detail about the chaos of Twitter. DOGE also. There were a lot of things I would’ve liked to have expanded rather than have to condense to their essence.
The SolarCity story was one that we left out, which was a really interesting story. There was a Russian influence story that was quite powerful, though we never got to a kernel that would indicate exactly the dimensions of it.
There was a counterintelligence investigation, the whole SEC thing about the tweets, and then we got an incredible deposition. I love depositions. They show so much about people sometimes, particularly people in power who are being held to account in a deposition.
So there was a lot of wonderful detail that was left on the cutting room floor. Maybe someday for all of us geeks, we’ll release it.
We’ll get the six-hour cut.

If you’re on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

articles.title: Đây là xếp hạng thương hiệu điện thoại Android từ "tệ nhất đến tốt nhất": Huyền thoại ở Việt Nam xếp chót bảng?
articles.text:
Trong khi các thương hiệu Trung Quốc như Xiaomi, OnePlus, Honor giành được xếp hạng cao thì một cái tên "huyền thoại" với người dùng Việt Nam lại ở vị trí cuối cùng.
Cuộc tranh luận kinh điển giữa Android và iPhone đã kéo dài suốt nhiều năm qua và thực sự dần trở nên nhàm chán khi ai cũng đã chọn xong "phe" cho riêng mình. Điều đáng quan tâm hơn ở thời điểm hiện tại chính là những gì đang diễn ra bên trong thế giới Android. Bởi nếu từng dùng qua hai chiếc điện thoại Android đến từ hai hãng khác nhau, bạn sẽ thấy chúng mang lại trải nghiệm hoàn toàn khác biệt.
Người dùng Samsung luôn quả quyết thiết bị của họ là hoàn hảo nhất. Tín đồ Vivo lại cho rằng máy của mình chụp ảnh đẹp hơn. Trong khi đó, những người trung thành với Motorola chỉ cần pin ba ngày là đủ, chẳng mấy bận tâm đến các tính năng thời thượng.
Tổng hợp dữ liệu từ các bài đánh giá công nghệ, diễn đàn thảo luận và phản hồi từ người mua thực tế đã mang lại nhiều góc nhìn bất ngờ.
Có những thương hiệu đạt thứ hạng cao hơn hẳn so với danh tiếng vốn có, trong khi một số cái tên sở hữu bảng thông số kỹ thuật "trong mơ" nhưng lại gây thất vọng về mặt trải nghiệm phần mềm. Suy cho cùng, mỗi người dùng đều hướng tới những giá trị riêng, và đó cũng chính là nét quyến rũ của hệ điều hành Android: mang đến sự lựa chọn gần như vô tận.
Dưới đây là bảng xếp hạng các thương hiệu Android từ tệ nhất đến tốt nhất do người dùng đánh giá, được trang BGR tổng hợp, phản ánh chính xác những tiêu chí được người dùng coi trọng nhất, từ độ bền phần cứng, giao diện mượt mà, tốc độ cập nhật phần mềm cho đến chất lượng dịch vụ chăm sóc khách hàng.
Lưu ý, bảng xếp hạng này chỉ mang tính chất tham khảo và theo phép tổng hợp riêng của trang BGR nên có thể gây ra những ý kiến tranh cãi.
10. Motorola
Motorola chinh phục người dùng nhờ giao diện Android thuần gọn nhẹ, không bị chiếm dụng dung lượng bởi ứng dụng rác hay các tùy biến rườm rà. Dòng cao cấp Razr Ultra sở hữu viên pin dung lượng lớn cùng hiệu năng ấn tượng, chứng minh năng lực sáng tạo phần cứng của hãng, trong khi các dòng máy tầm trung duy trì mức giá dễ tiếp cận và thời lượng pin ổn định.
Mặc dù vậy, điểm trừ lớn nhất khiến cộng đồng công nghệ thường xuyên phàn nàn là tốc độ cập nhật phần mềm rất chậm trễ. Dù các kênh hỗ trợ vẫn duy trì đầy đủ nâng cấp như cam kết, thời gian chờ đợi bản vá bảo mật quá dài khiến nhóm khách hàng chỉ còn biết chấp nhận thực tế này để đổi lấy độ bền phần cứng và hiệu năng ổn định.
9. Huawei
Sở hữu năng lực phần cứng hàng đầu, Huawei từng gây chú ý khi ra mắt chiếc Mate XT gập ba mở rộng thành màn hình 10,2 inch cùng hệ thống ống kính linh hoạt thay đổi khẩu độ.
Tuy nhiên, rào cản lớn nhất lại nằm ở hệ điều hành HarmonyOS NEXT khi nền tảng này đã loại bỏ hoàn toàn gốc Android. Mặc dù AppGallery sở hữu hàng chục nghìn ứng dụng, việc thiếu hụt các dịch vụ phổ biến của phương Tây và các sự cố văng ứng dụng hay chậm thông báo khi cài đặt bên ngoài khiến trải nghiệm người dùng quốc tế bị ảnh hưởng đáng kể. Dù phục hồi mạnh mẽ tại thị trường nội địa Trung Quốc, các rào cản về tính tương thích vẫn khiến Huawei khó tiếp cận người dùng phổ thông toàn cầu.
8. Vivo
Vivo khẳng định thế mạnh ở khả năng nhiếp ảnh di động nhờ hệ thống camera chất lượng từ dòng flagship X200 Pro cho đến các dòng giá rẻ Y30. Mặc dù vậy, thương hiệu này nhận về nhiều phản hồi trái chiều do sự cố giật lag khi quay video 4K, hiện tượng quá nhiệt hay khựng khung hình ở tần số quét cao trên một số mẫu máy.
Điểm trừ lớn nhất thuộc về giao diện Funtouch OS khi yêu cầu các điều khoản thu thập dữ liệu khắt khe ngay cả với ứng dụng cơ bản, đi kèm lượng lớn ứng dụng cài sẵn khó xóa và mức độ trượt giá nhanh chóng chỉ sau vài tháng mở bán.
7. Oppo
Oppo tiếp tục tập trung mạnh mẽ vào công nghệ chụp ảnh với đại diện Find X8 Ultra đạt thứ hạng cao trên các bảng đo kiểm uy tín, kết hợp thuật toán AI và khả năng chụp đêm ấn tượng trên dải sản phẩm tầm trung.
Tuy nhiên, giao diện ColorOS nhận nhiều chỉ trích vì tích hợp sẵn hơn 20 ứng dụng bên thứ ba cùng tính năng tự động tải thêm phần mềm rác. Chính sách cập nhật của hãng cũng phân hóa rõ rệt khi dòng cao cấp Find nhận được tới 5 bản nâng cấp Android lớn, trong khi các dòng máy phổ thông chỉ được hỗ trợ từ 2 đến 3 năm với mức giá thường nhỉnh hơn đối thủ do chi phí vi xử lý thương mại.
6. Sony
Dòng Xperia của Sony duy trì một tập khách hàng trung thành nhờ việc giữ lại cổng cắm tai nghe 3.5mm, hỗ trợ âm thanh độ phân giải cao và phím chụp ảnh thủ công chuyên nghiệp.
Mặc dù sở hữu phần cứng cao cấp, chính sách hỗ trợ phần mềm lại là điểm yếu cố hữu khi các mẫu máy có giá trên 1.000 USD trước đây thường chỉ nhận được 2 bản cập nhật Android lớn.
Mức độ phổ biến hạn chế tại các thị trường lớn cùng thị phần sụt giảm khiến Sony trở thành lựa chọn mang tính thói quen cho người mê âm thanh hoặc nhiếp ảnh, thay vì là một đề xuất mua sắm phổ quát.
5. Honor
Honor khẳng định vị thế tối ưu về giá trị bằng các sản phẩm sở hữu cấu hình mạnh mẽ, sạc siêu nhanh cùng thiết kế mỏng nhẹ như dòng màn hình gập Magic V5. Dịch vụ hỗ trợ phần mềm của hãng ghi nhận bước tiến lớn khi cam kết tới 7 năm cập nhật cho dòng Magic cao cấp, tiệm cận các thương hiệu hàng đầu. Dù giao diện MagicOS đã gọn gàng hơn, hạn chế lớn nhất của Honor vẫn nằm ở hệ thống phân phối chưa phủ rộng toàn cầu, mạng lưới bảo hành khiêm tốn và giá trị bán lại chưa cao.
4. Nothing
Gia nhập thị trường muộn hơn, Nothing tạo ấn tượng mạnh nhờ ngôn ngữ thiết kế mặt lưng trong suốt kết hợp hệ thống đèn Glyph Interface độc đáo. Các dòng máy như Phone (2) hay Phone (3) chạy hệ điều hành Nothing OS mượt mà, tiệm cận Android thuần và không chứa ứng dụng rác.
Hãng cam kết thời gian hỗ trợ phần mềm dài hạn lên tới 7 năm cho các dòng máy mới. Dù vậy, do tuổi đời thương hiệu còn trẻ, hệ thống trung tâm bảo hành và nguồn linh kiện thay thế ngoài các thị trường trọng điểm vẫn là rào cản đối với người sử dụng.
3. Xiaomi
Thế mạnh của Xiaomi nằm ở việc cung cấp cấu hình chuẩn flagship với mức giá tầm trung, sẵn sàng cạnh tranh trực tiếp ở phân khúc cao cấp lẫn phân khúc điện thoại chơi game với dòng Blackshark.
Người dùng luôn nhận được vi xử lý mạnh mẽ, dung lượng pin lớn và màn hình chất lượng cao trên chi phí đầu tư tối ưu. Mặc dù vậy, giao diện HyperOS vẫn duy trì việc hiển thị quảng cáo trong ứng dụng hệ thống và cài sẵn nhiều phần mềm không cần thiết. Độ trễ cập nhật phần mềm giữa phiên bản nội địa và quốc tế cũng là yếu tố khiến trải nghiệm người dùng chưa thực sự đồng nhất.
2. OnePlus
OnePlus duy trì danh tiếng "sát thủ flagship" nhờ mang lại hiệu năng cao và cụm camera chất lượng với mức giá hợp lý. Giao diện OxygenOS nhận được nhiều lời khen ngợi từ cộng đồng công nghệ nhờ sự mượt mà, độ trễ cực thấp và khả năng tùy biến linh hoạt.
Bên cạnh việc nâng cấp chất lượng ống kính, chính sách 4 năm cập nhật Android lớn và 5 năm vá lỗi bảo mật giúp OnePlus giữ vững vị trí hàng đầu về mặt trải nghiệm tổng thể.
1. Samsung
Samsung tiếp tục giữ vị trí số một về mức độ hài lòng của khách hàng và thị phần toàn cầu nhờ sự toàn diện trên mọi phương diện. Các dòng flagship Galaxy S series và Galaxy Z Fold liên tục đặt ra tiêu chuẩn về màn hình, khả năng chụp ảnh và hiệu năng.
Hãng sở hữu mạng lưới chăm sóc khách hàng rộng khắp, chính sách hỗ trợ phần mềm tới 7 năm và giao diện One UI tích hợp hệ sinh thái đa thiết bị vượt trội. Dù mức giá phân khúc cao cấp tương đối đắt đỏ, Samsung vẫn là lựa chọn Android hoàn chỉnh và đáng tin cậy nhất hiện nay.
Theo BGR, bảng xếp hạng trên được xây dựng dựa trên dữ liệu thị phần thực tế kết hợp cùng quá trình phân tích đánh giá từ nhiều nguồn. Các thảo luận trên diễn đàn Reddit cung cấp góc nhìn thực tế về trải nghiệm sử dụng dài hạn, trong khi chuyên mục bình luận tại các trang tin công nghệ phản ánh chi tiết các sự cố kỹ thuật.
Bên cạnh đó, điểm số xác thực từ người mua hàng trên các nền tảng bán lẻ lớn được tích hợp nhằm đảm bảo kết quả phản ánh chính xác góc nhìn của đại chúng thay vì các thông số quảng cáo đơn thuần.

articles.title: The Biggest Pro-AI Super PAC Network Has Poured Millions Into Nevada Shell Companies
articles.text:
The Spanish Springs shopping center in Sparks, Nevada, hosts many businesses, including a Spirit Halloween, a hearing aid supplier, and a Vietnamese restaurant. It’s also home to a consulting agency that’s received millions of dollars from one of the biggest pro-AI super PAC networks ahead of November’s midterm elections.
The problem is that the company—Lantern Production Consultants LLC—doesn’t seem to exist anywhere beyond a post office box in the Spanish Springs shopping complex.
Lantern Production Consultants has been paid around $20 million since last year by Think Big, part of a network of pro-AI super PACs funded by the Leading the Future PAC, for a wide array of services, including polling, digital advertising, research, and strategy, according to federal campaign finance records reviewed by WIRED. Backed by major AI investors, Leading the Future has taken a main role in supporting candidates who back what it calls “an AI innovation policy agenda.”
It is just one of four mysterious LLCs based out of Nevada that have received payments from super PACs in the Leading the Future PAC network, including Think Big and American Mission. The network, which is also based in Nevada, has raised over $140 million to influence political campaigns that align with AI-industry priorities in the midterms.
Summit Ridge Media Group LLC, which received around $13 million between December 2025 and September 2026 from American Mission, lists an address at a mail center in a Reno strip mall. Blue Horizon Compliance Consultants, which also appears in the filings, has its address listed as a Staples location in Reno. And Prusik Partners LLC’s listed address is at a strip mall in Henderson, Nevada, sharing a building with a chiropractor and a beauty salon.
Nevada’s secretary of state told WIRED that they were unable to locate any records for the businesses.
| Got a Tip? | 
|---|
| Do you know about what’s happening here? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at tessowen.77. | 
Election watchdogs argue that these LLCs are shell companies, designed to mask the identities of strategists, consultants, and production companies who are working with Leading the Future. “This is about hiding where the money is going,” claims Shanna Ports, senior legal counsel at the Campaign Legal Center.
In May, the Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the FEC, which enforces campaign finance laws, alleging that Think Big and American Mission had broken federal law by using shell companies in this way. Specifically, lawyers with the Campaign Legal Center alleged that super PACs in the Leading the Future network had violated the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) by failing to disclose the actual recipients of their payments. The LLCs, they wrote in their complaint, “function as mere extensions of the super PACs they serve.”
In an emailed statement to WIRED, Leading the Future spokesperson Jesse Hunt wrote, “We comply with all applicable laws and this is merely a desperate ploy for attention from Public First, Anthropic, and the groups aligned with their outside organizations who see our message resonating with the public and policymakers.”
WIRED reached out to Anthropic and Public First—a pro-AI super PAC focused on transparency and safeguards that has significant backing from Anthropic leadership—to ask about Leading the Future’s charge. “I have no idea what they’re talking about,” said Public First spokesperson Anthony Rivera-Rodriguez. “We unequivocally had nothing to do with this complaint.” Anthropic did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The Campaign Legal Center said in a statement to WIRED that the suggestion they “filed this complaint at the direction of, on behalf of, or in consultation with any outside entity is absolutely false.”
The Campaign Legal Center doesn’t expect its case to be heard by the FEC anytime soon, given that the FEC is essentially toothless at the moment. The FEC has six commissioner seats, all presidential appointees. To make a decision on a legal complaint, the FEC needs a quorum of four commissioners, which it hasn’t had since May 2025. Meanwhile, Think Big and American Mission have continued to pour millions of dollars into the Nevada LLCs.
Leading the Future has piqued a lot of public interest, not just because it has the most cash of any pro-AI group—thanks to Silicon Valley bankrollers like billionaire Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI president Greg Brockman—but also because it funnels money into super PACs that support both Republicans and Democrats. Think Big overwhelmingly funds Democrats, and American Mission funds Republicans.
The fact that the Leading the Future network is playing both sides of the aisle, supporting AI-friendly Democrats and Republicans, has generated speculation from experts as to why it’s spending so much on shielded vendors. Typically, political strategists and consultants cater to Democrats or Republicans, not both. “If you’re running in a Democrat primary and Think Big comes to spend in your race, and they drop half a million on your congressional district doing positive ads while using Republican vendors and strategists—that’s news,” speculates Kyle Morse, deputy executive director of Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit advocacy group that’s critical of big tech.
There are plenty of reasons why a super PAC may want to hide its vendors, ranging from benign to nefarious. In this instance, it's possible businesses don’t want to be publicly associated with a pro-AI campaign. But with the FEC lacking a quorum for the foreseeable future, “We are not fundamentally equipped to figure out what’s happening here,” says Morse.
Leading the Future isn’t the only PAC accused of shielding vendors by using shell companies. Earlier this year, Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the FEC against pro-gun YouTuber Brandon Herrera, who is running for Congress in Texas District 23, alleging that more than 99 percent of his campaign’s disbursements were funneled through Texas Strategy Group, which was, the complaint claimed, “being used as a shell entity.” When reached for comment, Herrera’s campaign directed WIRED to conservative personality Matt Braynard, who runs Texas Strategy Group. Braynard strongly denied the Campaign Legal Center’s accusations, calling the complaint “meritless” and “little more than a recycled legal theory from a partisan advocacy group.”
Campaign Legal Center also filed a complaint with the FEC against Lead Left PAC, a pop-up super PAC that was funded by Republican operatives while posing as a Democratic entity with the presumed goal of meddling in Democratic primaries. Campaign Legal Center accused it of paying shell companies to avoid being linked to Republican strategists.
Ports says that this marks a disturbing trend in campaign finance, at a time when dark money in politics already reigns. “There’s no way of tracing the source behind the money, and that’s bad enough on its own,” says Ports. “Now there’s this new component, where groups are playing games to hide where the money is being spent. As a result, voters really lack fundamental information about where the money is coming from and where it’s going.”
Updated 2:15 pm ET, 10/13/2026: This story has been updated with further comment from Nevada's secretary of state and the Campaign Legal Center.
