articles.title: Shopify opens its catalog up to more AI agents
articles.text:
More AI agents will soon be able to browse and purchase from Shopify listings, marking an expansion of the company’s agentic commerce ambitions.
Shopify opens its catalog up to more AI agents
Shopify previously announced a partnership with Meta’s Muse for AI-powered shopping and checkout.
Shopify announced Tuesday it will let shoppers configure their AI agents to purchase products on their behalf, giving more agents access to over a billion listings in Shopify’s catalog. (The catalog consists of both items on and off Shopify storefronts.) In September, Shopify announced it was partnering with Meta to allow its Muse agent to browse and purchase items on a human’s behalf; now, shoppers can use any agent without a partnership integration.
To set up the feature, customers connect an agent with their account on Shop, a Shopify-owned platform that consolidates orders, tracks packages, and recommends products. Like the Muse partnership, customers use the one-click Shop Pay feature to check out within the conversation with the agent. Orders placed through the agent are funneled back to the Shop app. Shopify is marketing the feature as a “personal shopper” that humans can give rules to, like setting budget guardrails or only displaying products with fast shipping. Buyers must approve each purchase.
E-commerce has become one of the battlegrounds in the era of AI — it’s no coincidence that many demos of agentic tools end with a transaction, whether it’s buying clothing, booking a flight, or ordering takeout on a human’s behalf. The tech industry, including big commerce players like Google and Amazon, are investing in AI-driven shopping tools where the end goal is an “agent” purchasing things for a human user. It’s also the basis of an ongoing fight between Amazon and AI companies like Perplexity — and more recently, Meta’s Muse — over whether agents should be able to shop on a customer’s behalf.

articles.title: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Rockets are, infamously, a real pain in the butt. Our old friend physics forces rockets to be built with almost no room for error, and even then only a small fraction of their weight makes it to orbit.
There are, at least in theory, other ways to do the job — space elevators, centrifuges, or a big chain hanging from a satellite in space and scooping up cargo from Earth. (Blue Origin spent some time thinking about that one before the idea wound up in a Neal Stephenson novel.)
And then there’s an idea dating all the way back to Jules Verne: Use a big gun to shoot a projectile into space.
Longshot Space Technology, a startup based in Alameda, California, is working on exactly that. The co-founders, CEO Mike Grace and CTO Nato Saichek, see an opportunity to take a technology that has already proven its worth and apply it to the pressing need for space launch. The startup has raised about $20 million from venture investors in service of its mission.
When it comes to frontier technology, Grace says, “you can build something that has a lot of novelty, or you can do something really hard. You don’t get to do both.” He points to SpaceX as an example of a company that has “taken classically de-risked technology and scaled it aggressively.” What SpaceX did with NASA rocket research, he says, Longshot will do with multi-injection guns — designs that give a projectile extra boosts as it moves down the barrel — built for World War II and during 1960s research programs.
The idea is to take all the work done by the first stage of a launch vehicle and collapse that into a reusable accelerator on the ground. Picture a steel pipe mounted horizontally over the ground, with tanks of high-pressure gas attached at ports spread across its length. When a projectile is fired and moves down the barrel, the tanks fire off at precise times to accelerate it — to speeds as high as Mach 4, thus far.
The company is currently firing a 70-foot gun with a six-inch diameter at its test site near Barstow, California, and says it can accelerate projectiles up to near-hypersonic speeds. Soon, it expects to start firing a 140-foot-long gun with a 30-inch diameter at its Alameda test site. After that, the company is preparing to build out a 30-inch diameter gun that is 328-feet long, with plans to extend it to about 3,000 feet — making it the largest gun on the planet. It will be capable of launching 220-pound payloads up to speeds of Mach 8, the team says.
These guns will let Longshot keep proving its technology works while also generating revenue from performing hypersonic testing for the U.S. military, which has awarded the company several contracts. Grace envisions building one of his guns on a U.S. military installation like Fort Bliss, where it could be part of the infrastructure for testing the next generation of U.S. interceptors. (And no, the guns don’t need to point up at an angle. Longshot’s projectile is a lifting body, meaning its shape generates lift, so it will aerodynamically gain altitude once it exits the barrel.)
“If you want to practice shooting down a Chinese or Russian hypersonic missile, wouldn’t it be nice not to pay $30 million for that?” Grace asks. “This is a way for half a million, a quarter of a million bucks, of doing hypersonic clay pigeons, throw them and shoot them down, and do it really fast and really cheap.”
The ultimate goal, however, is putting large payloads into space. The team is confident it can scale up its current design to accelerate payloads to as much as five kilometers per second (more than 11,000 mph). That’s fast enough to get into space if the payload, which effectively serves as the second stage of a rocket, has its own propulsion system. But doing that would require a gun 10 kilometers (about six miles) long and nearly 10 feet in diameter. As you might imagine, one problem the company faces is simply finding suitable worksites.
“The hard part is not building the thing, it’s finding a place where they will let you build the thing,” Saichek jokes.
But if Longshot can realize its vision, the math is very attractive: The system is cheap to construct and to fuel, and is highly reusable. Grace expects that if everything works out, they can send payloads to space for a hard-to-believe $50 per kilogram (about $22 per pound). Considering that the much-hyped orbital data center industry needs prices to fall to around $300 per kilogram to get off the ground, that leaves Longshot plenty of room to offer a competitive price.
It will require some modification to launch spacecraft in this form factor and conditions, but at that price point, satellite operators will be willing to try.
If you want to learn more about Longshot from the company itself — while also checking out dozens of startups, hearing their pitches, and listening to guest speakers on four different stages — join us this week at Disrupt, Tuesday to Thursday, in San Francisco. Learn more here.

articles.title: Everything announced at Apple's 'Welcome Home' event - Engadget
articles.text:
Everything announced at Apple's 'Welcome Home' event
All about the HomeView, HomePod mini 2, Apple Home Collection and more.
Apple is making a bigger push into the smart home domain. The company invited press and creators to a "Welcome Home" event in New York City on Tuesday to reveal a batch of fresh products, and we'll break it all down for you right here.
Among those was the long-anticipated HomeView — Apple's first smart home hub. In addition, we saw refreshed versions of the Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini. That's not all, because Apple talked up a whole ecosystem of smart home products.
We've had a chance to try Apple's new products. So, be sure to check out our hands-on coverage of the HomeView, Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 for our initial impressions.
Let's dive into everything Apple announced at its Welcome Home event.
HomeView smart home hub
We've heard rumors for years that Apple was working on an iPad-style display from which you'd be able to manage smart home devices. It was described as the company's answer to Amazon's Echo Show or Google's Nest Hub. Reports suggested it would be called the HomePad, but thankfully Apple steered clear of causing any confusion with the HomePod. Instead, the device is called the HomeView.
The HomeView has a tilting, seven-square-inch Liquid Retina touch display — perhaps paving the way for the touchscreen MacBook that's said to be coming very soon — that's attached to a base with a speaker. There are two variants. You can place one on a table or countertop and mount the other to a wall.
The display itself has two full-range drivers, which complement the down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators in the base of the countertop model. The wall-mounted version doesn't have a base, but Apple says its audio is tuned for wall placement. The screen has a maximum brightness of 500 nits and that can drop down to 0.3 nits (useful if you're using HomeView on a nightstand next to your dozing partner).
The device is powered by Apple Intelligence and has Siri AI baked in. (Reports suggested that Apple had put HomeView on ice until the delayed Siri AI was ready.) You can start a conversation with the assistant on HomeView, and continue on another Apple device. You'll also be able to handoff things like music and recipes from your iPhone to HomeView as well.
HomeView can recognize the face of the person who's interacting with it (up to six people), and automatically switch from a shared household screen to a customized interface for that individual. This should mean the user will have access to their own notifications and calendar, as it can tap into their personal data from their iPhone or iPad. You'll be able to have Apple Watch-style custom "faces" on HomeView that have four adjustable widgets and can feature things like weather details, some favorite photos and Snoopy animations.
Among other things, HomeView supports FaceTime calls thanks to a 12MP front-facing camera. Entertainment options include music, podcasts and video streaming, and Apple says you can follow recipes while you're cooking.
Apple says it designed HomeView to keep users' information secure and separate. The company stressed that it doesn't track or sell your data to others.
The HomeView runs on the A18 chipset, the same one that powers the iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16e and MacBook Neo. It costs a surprisingly reasonable $299 for both the tabletop and wall-mountable versions. The countertop version comes in four relatively muted color options: silver, starlight, rose pink and space gray. The wall-mounted model is available in space gray and silver. Pre-orders open today and it'll ship on November 13.
HomeView is initially available in English in the US, Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa and the UK. Apple says it'll add Canadian French support later via an update.
Apple TV 4K (2026)
The newly refreshed Apple TV 4K runs on the A19 chipset, the same one the company used in the iPhone 17 and iPhone 17e. Since Siri AI can pull from personal context on your iPhone, you can ask the assistant to do something like "play that show my sister texted me about" and the Apple TV 4K should fire it up. The assistant may offer suggestions to refine your searches and it can display responses to your questions on screen. Of course, you can control smart home devices using Apple TV 4K as well.
The set-top box has far-field microphones that'll let you talk to Siri AI hands-free. It can pair with up to four HomePod mini 2 speakers for surround sound. You won't have to bother tuning them manually, as the system will automatically calibrate the speakers for your space.
If you misplace the updated Siri Remote (or a family member has), you can use a voice command to trigger an audio alert to help you locate it. It has Find My support with Precision Finding as well.
Pre-orders for the latest Apple TV 4K open today and it costs $299 ($100 more than the previous model even after a price hike earlier this year). It'll ship on November 13.
Apple says Siri AI is available in beta on the last two versions of the Apple TV 4K as well (as in the models it released in 2021 and 2022). Folks in the US, Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa and the UK can use the assistant on their set-top box in English.
The fourth-gen Siri Remote will also available to buy separately. It works with Apple TV HD and Apple TV 4K, just in case you happen to lose the thing a bit too often and want it to play a sound so you can track it down.
HomePod mini 2
Rather than an A-series chip, Apple opted to slot the S10 into the HomePod mini 2. That's the same chipset that the Apple Watch Series 10, Series 11, SE 3 and Watch Ultra 3 run on, and it means you can use Siri AI with the speaker. Apple says that, along with answering questions that spring to your mind, Siri AI can help you get things done, such as adding items to a family calendar.
However, Apple notes that the latest version of the voice assistant won't be available on the HomePod mini 2 right away. The company will add Siri AI to the device with "a future software update."
The speaker is available in new colors — pink, blue and green to match iMac — as well as white and midnight. The lights on top of the HomePod mini 2 can match the album art of whatever song you're playing at that moment and pulse in time with the beat. Apple calls this feature Sound Glow. What's more, you can use the HomePod mini 2 as a default speaker for your iMac (or two of them for proper stereo sound).
The HomePod mini 2 costs $149. As with the new Apple TV, pre-orders open today. You'll be able to set it up in your home (at least if you're in a region where the original HomePod mini is currently available) starting on October 30.
Apple Home Collection
Apple has supported an ecosystem of smart home devices for well over a decade through the HomeKit framework, and now it's expanding on that. The company is working with LG and Schneider on devices that fall under an umbrella called Apple Home Collection. The initiative speaks to Apple stamping its own branding more prominently on smart home devices.
The lineup includes indoor and outdoor cameras, a video doorbell, smart door lock, thermostats and temperature sensors. Some will be available in December and others will begin to arrive early next year.
They can all be set up with a tap and managed through the Home app on an iPhone. You'll be able to manage them using Siri and devices like HomeView as well, of course. You'll be able to set up scenes for your smart home devices that can, for instance, change the thermostat, tilt an indoor camera down as you're getting dressed and play music.
All of products support Thread, so they should remain connected if your Wi-Fi network conks out. The devices will also automatically connect to your new Wi-Fi network if, for instance, you change routers or move home.
Data is encrypted, meaning neither Apple, LG nor Schneider can access it. Apple says you'll need to be running the latest version of iOS to use NFC pairing. It adds that some features require a hub like the Apple HomeView, Apple TV or a HomePod.
LG's cameras support up to 2.5K video capture and can recognize people, familiar faces, pets, vehicles and packages. Video is stored using iCloud, so you won't need a separate subscription. Event video history is saved for up to 10 days. On certain iCloud+ plans, Apple Intelligence can generate video descriptions and allow you to search clips using natural language. The cameras have built-in storage too.
The $250 Video Doorbell Wired has two cameras and a built-in spotlight. You can switch between the top view (which offers 2.5K resolution) and the full HD camera on the bottom. Its chime can play over HomeView, HomePod and HomePod mini.
LG's $400 Floodlight Cam has dual adaptive floodlights that switch on when the device detects motion and low-light color night vision. The Outdoor Cam ($300) supports low-light color night vision as well. As for the $200 Indoor Cam, that can automatically tilt up and down when you access the camera remotely and tilt back down when someone comes home. You can tilt the camera as you wish via the Home app too.
The $350 Smart Deadbolt Lock can connect to the Ultra Wideband chip on your iPhone or Apple Watch, so it can unlock automatically as you approach the door. If you'd rather tap your iPhone or Apple Watch, use a PIN or unlock the door with an actual key, you can do that too. You can also open the door via the Home app. If you have the doorbell and smart lock, you can speak to a visitor who buzzes you and unlock the door for them if you wish. If your Wi-Fi network goes down, the lock will still work locally thanks to Matter and Aliro compatibility.
LG and Schneider will each offer smart thermostats ($200 each) that can automatically adjust the temperature depending on whether someone's home, getting ready for bed or out somewhere. They can tap into sensors from LG and Schneider that monitor temperature and humidity ($40 each) and as well as those built into HomeView, HomePod and HomePod mini. These thermostats and dedicated sensors are Matter compatible and work with several HVAC systems, Apple says.

articles.title: Google says Gemini 4 Argon is a 'powerhouse' AI model, and anyone can pay for it
articles.text:
Google has released Gemini 4 Argon globally to paying users, in the Gemini app, in Search and through the API. The $2 and $10 per million token prices are a launch discount against standard rates of $4 and $20.
Google has released Gemini 4 Argon to anyone willing to pay for it. The model is live globally in the Gemini app, in Search, and through the API.
Developers pay $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, Google said on Tuesday. Consumers need a Pro subscription, which starts at $19.99 a month.
Those prices are temporary. Argon’s standard rates are $4 and $20, and the launch discount runs for at least a month with no stated end date.
Tulsee Doshi, Gemini product lead at Google DeepMind, called it a “powerhouse” and the first of a family, she told Business Insider. Google says it ranks first on the Vals Index, which measures finance, coding, legal and tax work.
The first users were not developers. Argon went to a small group of cyber defenders without its guardrails, through a programme Google calls Fairwind.
That group is now growing to hundreds of partners. Wiz has been using the model to scan critical infrastructure, and says it found a bypass exposing a master key in healthcare software.
Europe has a name for this category. Cyber offence is one of four systemic risks the AI Office must police, alongside bio-attacks, loss of control and mass manipulation.
It polices them with 36 people. The office has had trouble getting access to some frontier models, and can fine up to 3% of global turnover when it does.
Google’s own numbers are reassuring, and they are Google’s. External bio red teaming unlocked under 1% of the sub-tasks it tests for, and shortcut attempts in coding fell to 2%.
It also runs a monitor that reads the model’s reasoning as it works, to catch a run going wrong before it finishes. Prompt injection attacks succeeded 0.7% of the time.
The internal gains come through Antigravity, Google’s agent tool. Agentic code submissions rose more than 35%, rollbacks fell by nearly a third, and a Chrome refactor took weeks instead of months.
The science claims are larger. Google says Argon helped find counterexamples to a 1967 conjecture about fusion reactor magnetic fields, and taught a humanoid to play cornhole by watching a video.
The tool behind those results is not in the $19.99 tier. Antigravity needs an Ultra subscription from $99.99 a month, and Google moved free users to its smallest model four days ago.

articles.title: Gia Lai gắn tiến độ dự án ngoài ngân sách với đánh giá KPI lãnh đạo
articles.text:
Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh Gia Lai Phạm Anh Tuấn vừa ký ban hành Công văn số 12543/UBND-PVHCC yêu cầu tháo gỡ vướng mắc, đẩy nhanh tiến độ các dự án đầu tư ngoài ngân sách, phục vụ mục tiêu tăng trưởng hai con số.
Theo đó, các cơ quan, đơn vị phải chuyển mạnh từ theo dõi thủ tục sang đánh giá kết quả thực tế. Với từng dự án, phải xác định rõ vướng mắc, cơ quan, người chịu trách nhiệm xử lý, thời hạn hoàn thành và mốc khởi công, tạo khối lượng hoặc đưa vào hoạt động.
Các thủ tục về đất đai, giải phóng mặt bằng, quy hoạch, xây dựng, hạ tầng kết nối phải được chủ động chuẩn bị. Những phần việc pháp luật cho phép thực hiện đồng thời cần triển khai song song để rút ngắn thời gian.
Lãnh đạo tỉnh trực tiếp theo dõi, tháo gỡ vướng mắc dự án
Các Phó Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh được phân công trực tiếp theo dõi, chỉ đạo, đôn đốc các nhóm dự án quy mô lớn, dự án quan trọng.
Lãnh đạo tỉnh trực tiếp làm việc với nhà đầu tư, sở, ngành và địa phương để tháo gỡ khó khăn. Đối với dự án chậm tiến độ hoặc còn vướng mắc lớn, việc tổ chức làm việc, kiểm tra, xử lý có thể thực hiện cả ngày thứ Bảy, Chủ nhật khi cần thiết.
Đáng chú ý, kết quả theo dõi, tháo gỡ vướng mắc và tiến độ các dự án được phân công sẽ là một trong những căn cứ đánh giá KPI đối với từng Phó Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh và các sở, ngành, địa phương liên quan.
Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh cũng yêu cầu kịp thời chấn chỉnh trường hợp cán bộ né tránh, đùn đẩy trách nhiệm, xử lý công việc máy móc, thiếu chủ động hoặc làm chậm tiến độ dự án do nguyên nhân chủ quan. Trường hợp cần thiết, đề xuất cấp có thẩm quyền xem xét điều động, bố trí, thay thế.
Đối với các dự án có tổng vốn đầu tư trên 50 tỷ đồng đến dưới 1.000 tỷ đồng, Tổ công tác của Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh trực tiếp theo dõi, xử lý, đôn đốc; Sở Tài chính là đầu mối chung. Các dự án từ 50 tỷ đồng trở xuống do Chủ tịch UBND xã, phường nơi có dự án trực tiếp theo dõi, giải quyết những khó khăn thuộc thẩm quyền.
Rút ngắn thời gian xử lý, theo dõi tiến độ hằng tuần
Nhằm rút ngắn thời gian xử lý hồ sơ, các cơ quan, đơn vị được lấy ý kiến về những nội dung liên quan đến xử lý dự án phải có ý kiến trong thời hạn một ngày làm việc kể từ khi nhận được văn bản. Quá thời hạn không có ý kiến được xem là thống nhất với nội dung lấy ý kiến và phải chịu trách nhiệm về nội dung đó.
Các sở, ngành tập trung rà soát, tháo gỡ vướng mắc đối với những dự án năng lượng, nông nghiệp, nông nghiệp công nghệ cao, chăn nuôi, khu kinh tế và khu công nghiệp, nhất là những dự án có khả năng khởi công, tạo khối lượng hoặc đưa vào hoạt động trong năm 2026.
Sở Tài chính được giao phối hợp với Thống kê tỉnh và các sở, ngành liên quan lượng hóa khối lượng thực hiện, năng lực sản xuất tăng thêm và đóng góp dự kiến của từng dự án vào tăng trưởng quý IV và cả năm 2026, đồng thời phục vụ xây dựng kịch bản tăng trưởng năm 2027.
Các sở, ngành, địa phương phải cập nhật tiến độ và kết quả tháo gỡ vướng mắc đối với từng dự án. Sở Tài chính và Ban Quản lý Khu kinh tế tỉnh có trách nhiệm tổng hợp, báo cáo Chủ tịch và các Phó Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh hằng tuần.
Những vấn đề cấp bách hoặc vượt thẩm quyền phải được báo cáo ngay để kịp thời xem xét, giải quyết, không chờ đến kỳ báo cáo định kỳ.
Bình An

articles.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world | TechCrunch
articles.text:
If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable.
“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”
Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.
“Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.
Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon, October 13.
Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas.
“I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said.
Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.
“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said.
At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world.
The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale.
Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom.
Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision.
“It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.”
While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop.
“They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said.
Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world.
“There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.”
Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Japanese trucking manufacturer Isuzu and Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto.
Nvidia is also a customer, says Sun. The two companies, alongside T-Mobile, are working together on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses.
Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals.
Chief among its rivals is Applied Intuition, a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation. Isuzu is also one of Applied’s customers.
Sun isn’t too worried. He believes Laplace’s core methodology of using AI to test AI is a “new paradigm that changes the testing of physical AI entirely,” turning it into a “dynamic interactive testing process.”
“That will be the biggest moat,” he said.

articles.title: Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports
articles.text:
Retro gaming is going through a wild time at the moment, thanks to decompilations and recompilations that are letting gamers port classic titles to new devices, or merge code from two different games into a single new experience. Microsoft has witnessed skateboarding being modded into Call of Duty and Halo being played in a web browser, and the company is now officially embracing the chaos of this new AI-powered era of game modding.
Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports
Microsoft has created a new Xbox Labs group to experiment with decompiling and recompiling games.
Microsoft is putting together a new Xbox Labs group to explore the rapid emergence of these mods, many of which use AI models to help modders remix games in ways we’ve rarely seen before. Xbox Labs will be a “small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience,” says Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. “We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.”
Sharma thinks the experiments we’ve seen in recent weeks, where Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside browsers, “challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games.”
“While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators,” says Sharma. “These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.“
Modders are now doing the type of work that Microsoft has been doing for decades with its Xbox backward compatibility program, letting old games run on modern hardware. But they’re doing it without the business model restrictions that Microsoft is tied to. It’s starting to feel like we’re just a model or two away from even more breakthroughs that decouple more modern games from their intended hardware.
Sharma clearly sees an opportunity here, particularly for AI agent use at Xbox. “I think Xbox has an important role to play here,” says Sharma. “Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide.”
Xbox Labs is clearly a way for Microsoft to experiment with how AI will shape where games are played, and Xbox will share any tools and learnings with developers. The bigger question is how Microsoft will respond to decompiles and recompiles of games where modders take its precious IP and make it freely available. Modding is fun, but I can’t see Microsoft and other publishers seeing the fun side if modern console games start to appear where they shouldn’t.
I asked Microsoft to comment about unauthorized IP use, but the company didn’t respond in time for publication.
Here’s Sharma’s full memo:
Team,
The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we’ve helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.
In recent weeks, we’ve seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we’ve seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.
These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models. To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.
I think XBOX has an important role to play here. Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We’ve spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible. As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.
Our priorities aren’t changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology without abandoning the work already underway.
Asha

articles.title: What happens to an EV battery after it's removed from your car? - Engadget
articles.text:
What happens to an EV battery after it's removed from your car?
Your old EV battery may end up trading its daily commute for a stationary role.
An EV battery's life is far from over once it leaves a car. When the owner is done with the vehicle, for whatever reason, there are varying degrees of battery health and usefulness to consider. It may not be able to supply the original range any longer, may have developed a fault or it could have been damaged in a crash. But even if a car owner decides it's time to replace their EV battery, the battery still has more to offer, and specialists (usually called EV battery diagnosticians or technicians) will inspect, test and determine what comes next in the battery's lifecycle.
Occasionally, repair is possible. An EV battery pack contains several individual cells, typically grouped in modules. Depending on the design, a tech may be able to replace a module or component, instead of tossing the entire thing into the recycling or repurposing pile. A safe and reliable used EV battery can potentially be reused in a compatible vehicle. However, it doesn't always work out that way because some EV packs are really difficult to repair, especially if the vehicle was in a particularly nasty accident, the kind that results in a total loss.
For the most part, an EV battery will enter a repair or reuse operation post-removal. Its condition will determine its future, whether it becomes stationary energy storage or goes to a recycler. There's no singular answer here, only a list of possibilities, depending on the battery's status.
A second life off the road
Just because an EV battery no longer delivers the range the owner wants doesn't mean it's no longer useful. Retired EV batteries can potentially retain as much as 70 to 80 percent of their original capacity, assuming they aren't damaged. Basically, it boils down to what it can be used for next. Pretty simple, really. One of the popular options is placing them in stationary energy storage. Instead of powering an EV, it supplies backup power for a building or helps balance electricity supply and demand on the grid. For example, California is using Nissan Leaf and Honda batteries to store solar energy.
Though the battery's commute is long over, the work goes on. Repurposing isn't always a simple process, however. Once a tech has thoroughly inspected the battery, they integrate suitable components and any controls and safety equipment needed for its new or future home. It's a costly process as well, so there's no guarantee that a viable battery won't face recycling if the cost is more than the return.
What happens to EV batteries when they no longer work?
Repair and repurposing are nice, but neither is suitable in some cases. Fortunately, that doesn't spell the end of an EV battery's usefulness. If repair or repurposing aren't on the docket, the pack is prepared for safe processing and dismantled. Materials like steel, aluminum and copper are stripped out and recovered. Cell processing typically involves shredding and separation that produces a mixture of "black mass." This black mass contains electrode materials that will eventually go through even more processing to recover valuable ingredients.
The battery's chemistry dictates the next stage, which may include heat or chemical solutions to extract more. Since not all batteries are identical, the outcomes will include varying amounts of material, most of which will return to manufacturing. Again, the recycling process is costly. It requires a lot of energy and results in losses during the procedure. But it does result in less demand for mined resources, which means less environmental impact.

articles.title: Europe trails US on AI adoption
articles.text:
Europe is falling behind the US on AI use at work, and the main reason is not technology, according to a new report.The report from Sifted, sponsored by London Business School, says Europe has an organisational gap rather than a tech gap. Firms struggle with skills, management, trust and the cost of fitting AI into how they work.
“Doing a fun thing with ChatGPT and running your whole business on AI are two very different things,” Celonis executive Rupal Karia told Sifted.
The numbers
About 43% of US workers used AI for their jobs in early 2026, against 32% across Europe, a St Louis Fed analysis found. US workers spent more than three times as many work hours using AI as those in Germany, France and Italy.
Only 20% of EU firms use AI at all, up from 13.5% a year earlier, Eurostat data shows. Denmark leads at 42%, while Romania sits at 5.2%.
Even where firms use AI, few have gone all in. The report cites McKinsey data showing 88% of organisations use AI somewhere, but just 7% have fully scaled it.
“There is no inherent roadblock to Europe leading in AI adoption,” said Nicos Savva, a professor at London Business School.
Stuck in pilot mode
Karia, who runs northern Europe and the Middle East for German software firm Celonis, said many companies had underestimated the human side of change. Adoption has been slower than expected, he added.
Executives cited unreliable outputs, cyber risk and running costs as reasons for caution. Some firms are now limiting AI use as they weigh cost against benefit, LBS deputy dean Gary Dushnitsky told Sifted.
Returns are also hard to find. The report cites research from marketing firm Whito showing 75% of firms using AI see productivity gains, but only 12% see more revenue.
Paul Maker, technology chief at UK firm Aiimi, put it bluntly.
“Everyone’s been given a hammer and now they’re desperately looking for nails,” he said.
Fear and slow change
Fear of job losses is also slowing take-up, said LBS professor Lynda Gratton.
“If you feel AI will destroy your work, then you won’t want to adopt it,” she said.
LBS dean Sergei Guriev warned that rushing could backfire if people stop learning to think for themselves. A quick start, he said, could undermine longer-term adoption.
Some of the delay is normal. The report cites Goldman Sachs economist Elsie Peng, who found the PC took about 15 years to show up in productivity data.
Where it is working
Adoption is fastest in law and banking. More than 85% of banks supervised by the European Central Bank now use AI, the report says.
Belgian startup Oper built an AI agent to check mortgage paperwork for underwriter Creafin. It is named after Herman Verdoodt, a Creafin credit technician, who said his team spends far more time fixing data than writing mortgages.
Factories are slower. Many cannot shut down for days to rewire their systems, said Dan Hobbs, chief executive of Irish safety firm Protex AI.
Europe’s own route
The report argues Europe should not try to copy the US on frontier models. More than 75% of advanced AI computing power sits in the US, against less than 4% in Europe, it says.
Instead, it points to startups that place engineers inside client firms, much like Palantir does. It also highlights AI roll-ups, where startups such as Dwelly buy traditional businesses and rebuild them around AI.
Some European AI firms are also choosing to stay independent. UK avatar startup Synthesia reportedly turned down a $3bn offer from Adobe last year, the report notes.
Dushnitsky said Europe’s pitch could rest on control and resilience rather than price.
“Perhaps the European value proposition should be built around resilience, confidentiality and privacy,” he said.
That echoes founders who want smarter AI rules, not fewer. The report concludes that good rules can speed adoption by giving firms the confidence to try.

Get the most important tech news in your inbox each week.

articles.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security, says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said.
Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet.
Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach.
Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense.
Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating.
That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts.
When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway.
“In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.”
Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying.
“We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said.
In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools.
To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do.
What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation.
“We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained.
The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium, a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers.
She said 70% of Pluto’s sales pipeline now comes from inbound interest, although she didn’t break down how much of that comes directly through Plutonium.
Pluto said it plans to invest the new capital in developing its product, expanding its security research efforts, and growing its presence in the U.S. It has 40 employees in the U.S. and Israel.

articles.title: What is the difference between a rearview and a backup camera? - Engadget
articles.text:
What is the difference between a rearview and a backup camera?
Not all backup cameras can give you an ongoing live feed while you drive.
Backing up in a vehicle without proper visibility can present drawbacks ranging from annoying, like dinging your bumper on a pole, to devastating, like backing-over accidents involving children or pets. To prevent this, new vehicles sold in the United States and the European Union are required to come equipped with backup cameras, which activate when a driver shifts into reverse and often include both a wide-angle view and guidance lines for safer maneuvering.
In addition to backup cameras, which help with parking and reversing out of driveways, there is also a demand for rearview cameras, which offer a live video feed of the road behind a vehicle and can record accidents and help maintain awareness of the traffic surrounding your car on the road. So, what is the difference between the two cameras, do all cars have them, and what features and benefits does each come with?
What is a backup camera vs. a rearview camera?
A backup camera is positioned on the back of your vehicle and offers a live video feed directly to your dashboard of what is behind you. It is only activated when your car shifts into reverse and is meant to help with maneuvering into tight parking spaces and preventing accidents, including backing into poles and other obstacles or tragic incidents involving pets or children. The display often includes guidance lines and sensors that beep when you get too close to a potential obstacle. Typically, these cameras use a wide-angle lens that offers a 150- or 180-degree view of the immediate surrounding area.
How do you know which cars come already equipped with backup cameras? Well, if it is a model from 2018 or later, it is required to have one. That's because, in the interest of promoting road safety, in May 2018, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration issued a federal mandate in response to years of advocacy surrounding back-over accidents involving children and the elderly. A similar law was passed in the European Union that took effect in 2022. But these requirements only apply to backup cameras.
Rearview cameras, on the other hand, are not automatically included in new vehicles. Rather than activating exclusively for backing up, these devices offer a continuous feed at all times of the traffic behind your car. Unlike backup cameras, rearview cameras typically use a narrower lens that replicates standard vision rather than a fisheye lens for wider visibility. These cameras are included in some models automatically but can also be purchased and installed manually.
What can you use these cameras for?
Backup cameras are useful for anyone who ever has to reverse a car, parallel park, or back out of a tight spot — which is to say, all drivers. Plus, this sort of car safety tech has been proven to save lives. If your vehicle was produced before 2018 and doesn't have a backup camera built in, you can have one installed or buy an add-on wireless camera for prices ranging from $40 to more than $400. Monitors for these add-on cameras can be clipped to a rearview mirror to make the backup process more seamless (you can even re-use old tablet devices for this purpose).
As for dedicated rearview cameras, these devices are especially useful for large vehicles like RVs or drivers who often haul cargo or trailers that can block a standard rearview mirror. They can also be purchased and installed wirelessly in a car. This can be particularly useful if your car already lacks a backup camera, as a rear dash cam can be used as a backup camera. While it may not have the guidelines or sensors included in pre-installed backup cameras, the rear dash cam does offer a view of your vehicle backing up for safer driving overall.

articles.title: Chuyên gia VFS nhận diện 'điểm tụ' của dòng vốn trong chu kỳ đầu tư lớn
articles.text:
Dòng vốn đang chảy về đâu?
Theo ông Nguyễn Minh Hoàng, Giám đốc Phân tích Chứng khoán Nhất Việt (VFS), Việt Nam đang bước vào chu kỳ đầu tư lớn vào hạ tầng, năng lượng, logistics, sản xuất và công nghệ nhằm tạo động lực tăng trưởng dài hạn. Dòng vốn này cần được huy động và giải ngân trước khi phản ánh dần vào kết quả kinh doanh của doanh nghiệp.
Minh chứng rõ nét là ở lĩnh vực hạ tầng, hàng loạt dự án trọng điểm đang được đẩy mạnh như sân bay Long Thành, đường sắt tốc độ cao Bắc - Nam, các tuyến cao tốc và cảng biển. Song song đó, định hướng thu hút FDI giai đoạn 2026 - 2030 và Nghị quyết 57 cũng ưu tiên dòng vốn vào công nghệ cao, bán dẫn, trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) và năng lượng sạch, đồng thời thúc đẩy tính liên kết với các doanh nghiệp nội địa.
Số liệu thực tế cho thấy đà tăng trưởng dòng vốn đang rất tích cực. Trong 9 tháng đầu năm, vốn đầu tư khu vực Nhà nước tăng 17,3%, khu vực ngoài Nhà nước tăng 14% và khu vực FDI tăng 14,5% - tất cả đều vượt mức trung vị giai đoạn 2015 - 2025. Đặc biệt, dòng vốn huy động qua thị trường chứng khoán cũng ghi nhận mức tăng ấn tượng 85,6%.
Nhận diện những nhóm ngành tiềm năng đáng theo dõi trong năm 2027
Mặc dù các con số thống kê rất vĩ mô, nhưng đối với nhà đầu tư, điều cốt lõi không chỉ là nhìn thấy dòng vốn chảy qua, mà phải xác định được nó sẽ "đọng lại" ở đâu. Để giải bài toán này, chuyên gia VFS đã đưa ra khung phân tích theo chuỗi: Chính sách - Vốn - Đầu tư - Backlog/Hoạt động - Doanh thu - Lợi nhuận.
Trong chuỗi giá trị này, chính sách đóng vai trò định hướng và mở đường cho dòng vốn. Cơ hội thực sự sẽ thuộc về những doanh nghiệp sở hữu backlog (đơn hàng tồn đọng) lớn hoặc đang chủ động mở rộng quy mô đầu tư, từ đó tạo ra động lực tăng trưởng doanh thu và lợi nhuận thực tế trong tương lai.
Từ khung phân tích trên, VFS gợi ý các nhóm ngành đáng theo dõi trong năm 2027 dựa theo hai đầu của dòng vốn:
· Đầu nguồn dòng vốn: Nhóm ngành Ngân hàng và Chứng khoán.
· Nơi dòng vốn được giải ngân: Năng lượng - Dầu khí; Điện và thiết bị điện; Cảng biển - Logistics; Khu công nghiệp; Công nghệ; và một số nhóm Vật liệu có tính khan hiếm.
Tuy nhiên, chuyên gia VFS lưu ý, đây là các nhóm ngành tiềm năng được phân tích theo chu kỳ đầu tư để nhà đầu tư đưa vào danh sách theo dõi, chưa phải là khuyến nghị mua cụ thể đối với từng mã cổ phiếu.
Bài toán chọn mắt xích đầu tư
Đi sâu vào chi tiết, câu trả lời cho bài toán lợi nhuận không nằm ở tên của một ngành chung chung mà nằm ở từng mắt xích cụ thể. Thực tế trên thị trường, không phải doanh nghiệp nào thuộc ngành được hưởng lợi từ chính sách cũng có thể chuyển hóa dòng vốn đầu tư thành giá trị cho cổ đông.
Tại mỗi mắt xích của chuỗi giá trị, khả năng doanh nghiệp giữ lại được dòng tiền thực tế sẽ được sàng lọc qua 4 yếu tố cốt lõi: Biên lợi nhuận, Quyền định giá, Chi phí vốn, và Dòng tiền. Nghĩa là doanh nghiệp phải chứng minh được phần lãi còn lại sau chi phí, khả năng duy trì giá bán, gánh nặng lãi vay thấp và lượng tiền thực tế thu về.
Sự phân hóa giữa các doanh nghiệp trong cùng một ngành là lý do vì sao chiến lược của VFS cho năm 2027 tập trung vào việc "chọn đúng mắt xích hưởng lợi" thay vì mua dàn trải theo ngành.
Kiên nhẫn chờ đợi tín hiệu từ thị trường
Bên cạnh các cơ hội, VFS cũng đưa ra khuyến nghị thận trọng cho nhà đầu tư. Giai đoạn chờ đợi “giá của tiền” (chi phí vốn) tạo đỉnh có thể kéo dài hơn kỳ vọng nếu môi trường lãi suất trong nước, quốc tế cùng áp lực bán ròng của khối ngoại chậm cải thiện. Trong bối cảnh thị trường tiếp tục phân hóa mạnh, việc kiên nhẫn quan sát các tín hiệu xác nhận từ dòng tiền thực tế sẽ an toàn hơn là hành động quá sớm dựa trên kỳ vọng.

Với phương châm “Giải pháp vừa vặn - Đầu tư thông minh”, VFS hướng đến đồng hành cùng nhà đầu tư, cung cấp các giải pháp phù hợp với nhu cầu và mục tiêu đầu tư. articles.title: Google will let anyone publish an app to the Play Store, for free
articles.text:
Google will let anyone over 18 with a Google account publish privately listed Android apps built in its AI Studio, with no paid developer account. Apple spent this year tightening its own store against the same kind of software.
Google will let anyone over 18 with a Google account publish an Android app to the Play Store. There is no developer account to buy and no fee.
The apps have to be built in Google AI Studio and are privately listed, Bloomberg reported, so they do not appear in the store’s search or recommendations.
The barrier it removes is small but real. Google charges $25 once for a developer account, Apple charges $99 a year, and both review new submissions before release.
Sam Bright, who runs Google Play and its developer ecosystem, demonstrated it with a tracker for his children’s local sports team, splitting jersey money, umpire fees and post-game pizza across 15 families.
Apple has gone the other way. Submissions to its store jumped by 84% in a quarter as vibe coding spread, and it began removing apps that change behaviour after review.
Its review queue went with them. Approval times moved from a day or two to between one week and more than a month by March, and Replit and Vibecode had updates blocked.
The security question is the obvious one. AI-generated code passed Veracode’s tests 56% of the time last year, on raw models without guardrails.
The weak spots are the ones that matter in a phone app. Cross-site scripting passed 15% of the time and log injection 12%, though Google says AI Studio runs its own checks.
Europe is the part Google did not mention. The Commission issued binding measures in July requiring Google to give rival AI assistants the same Android access Gemini has.
Those obligations start in 2027, alongside a requirement to share search data with rival search engines and chatbots at regulated prices.
Google is also making the route around its store harder. Since 30 September, apps installed through participating stores on certified devices must be registered to a verified developer.
That is live in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand, and goes global in 2027. The workaround needs a trip into developer options, a restart and a 24-hour wait.
So the free door opens and the side door narrows in the same year. Both lead through Google, which is the company Brussels has just finished writing Android rules for.

articles.title: MIT startup says it can turn diesel trucks into cheaper hydrogen haulers — see it at Disrupt | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Diesel fuel powers everything from shipping to agriculture, and with prices hitting record highs in recent weeks, governments around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout.
For now, that’s meant releasing fuel from stockpiles, but in the coming years, the answer might be a new technology from an MIT startup called LNK Energies.
LNK has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from the price spikes that result from geopolitical instability like the war in Iran. “If you look at total cost of ownership of a Class 8 truck, it’s 13% cheaper than diesel,” Alexis Huynh, chief technology officer at LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. (Class 8 is the heaviest category of trucks, including big rigs.)
Automotive companies have been exploring the use of hydrogen in long-haul trucking in part because refilling a hydrogen tank is faster than recharging the massive batteries those trucks require. But hydrogen is challenging to move to refilling stations, and the pressure tanks required to store it on the truck are large and costly.
LNK’s approach is to carry hydrogen chemically attached to another compound. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers, or LOHCs, are liquids that can absorb and later release hydrogen, and they have been widely studied, but mostly for moving large quantities of hydrogen from refineries to fueling stations. The equipment needed to separate hydrogen from the LOHC, known as a reactor, has been too big to fit onto a truck.
“A lot of the reactors that LOHC companies have today are really large. They’re about the size of a shipping container,” Huynh said. “We have shrunk that basically to the size of a mini fridge.”
Moving the reactor onto the truck saves a surprising amount of energy. When hydrogen is stored on a truck, it must be pressurized to more than 11,000 psi (800 bar), roughly 800 times normal air pressure, and squeezing it that hard takes a lot of power. Because LNK’s fuel carries the hydrogen in liquid form and releases it on board as needed, that step goes away. “We’re eliminating the expensive compression step,” Sayandeep Biswas, co-founder and CEO of LNK Energies, told TechCrunch.
In LNK’s system, once the hydrogen is released on the truck, it can be burned in a conventional internal combustion engine, the kind in today’s diesel trucks, with just a few modifications. The company uses waste heat from the engine to help power the on-board reactor. Or, if the trucking company wants to fully eliminate combustion emissions, it can use fuel cells instead, which convert hydrogen into electricity to power electric motors.
The LOHC can be stored in a traditional fuel tank and dispensed using pumps, just like diesel. “The entire hydrogen infrastructure doesn’t need to exist,” Biswas said. “It’s just a standard diesel station.”
Biswas and Huynh have a demonstration reactor working in the lab that can power an engine from a lawnmower. In 18 months, they plan to install a larger version in a commercial truck.
The trucks will cost more up front, but promise to be cheaper to operate. The duo are confident that they can undercut diesel at a price of $6.50 per gallon after they’ve made just 50 to 100 trucks. None of their projections include government subsidies. “The idea isn’t to have a technology that is cheaper at scale, but one that is cheaper even during that adoption period,” Biswas said.
LNK will present live onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco, as part of our Startup Battlefield pitch competition. Come join us in San Francisco and take part in the action.

articles.title: Russian bot farms are still trolling, even after Ukraine’s drone strikes on Yandex
articles.text:
Days after Ukrainian military drones took down several Russian data centers, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that the campaign had hurt Russia’s disinformation efforts. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms,” Zelenskyy said Monday. “There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations.”
Russian bot farms are still trolling, even after Ukraine’s drone strikes on Yandex
Zelenskyy celebrated ‘less division’ on social media after the strikes but the data isn’t backing that up yet.
Zelenskyy isn’t the first to assert that the drone operation, which targeted data centers belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex, has cut down on spam and disinformation campaigns fomented by Russian bot farms. Social media users have claimed they’ve noticed less traffic on posts by MAGA-affiliated accounts, as well as those associated with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Some have even said they’ve noticed a steep drop in spam calls and messages.
But these people are wrong. The drone strikes appear to have affected Yandex’s web crawlers, not any disinformation or political operations.
In fact, the account antibot4navalny, which tracks state-sponsored troll farms, reports that bot traffic is steady as ever. On Monday, the same day Zelenskyy claimed that disinformation had died down, antibot4navalny reported that several Kremlin-aligned accounts posted videos falsely claiming that experts are demanding the European Union lift the ongoing sanctions on Russia. Danish analyst Valdemar Osted said interactions on MAGA and AfD accounts have actually increased since the strikes. And the charts purportedly showing a decline in bot activity appear to be AI-generated.
Ironically, claims that the drone strikes hindered Russian disinformation campaigns appears to be a form of disinformation itself, no matter what Zelenskyy says.

articles.title: NASA's Perseverance rover breaks record for off-world driving distance - Engadget
articles.text:
NASA's Perseverance rover breaks record for off-world driving distance
The nuclear-powered buggy has now traveled 28.10 miles, besting NASA's Opportunity rover.
NASA's Perseverance Mars rover just broke the record for the farthest distance traveled by any vehicle on another world, the space agency announced. The six-wheeled, nuclear-powered buggy has now traveled 28.10 miles (45.22 km) as of October 11th, besting NASA's Opportunity rover that rolled 28.06 miles (45.16 km) across the red planet's surface. Perseverance managed the feet in just five and a half years, compared to nearly 15 for the plucky Opportunity.
Last we checked with Perseverance, it was officially a marathon finisher with 26.2 miles under its pock-marked metal wheels. While the 28.1 miles it's covered to date may not seem like much, it's pretty good considering the vehicle's maximum speed is a glacial 0.1 mph. It's also impressive considering the challenging terrain it's been tasked to transit, as NASA showed in the video below.
The 2,260 pound rover attained the milestone traveling to a region called Idubi, where it will investigate a feature called "Lac de Charmes" with some of the oldest terrain ever explored in our solar system. "The rocks and terrain of Lac de Charmes are so ancient that their Earthly equivalents have long since been erased by erosion and plate tectonics (Mars doesn't have tectonic plates), and Idubi is where the science team hopes to find traces of ancient hydrothermal systems," NASA explained.
Perseverance's longevity can be chalked up in part to smart navigation decisions powered by its autonomous AutoNav system. Using that, the rover can image terrain and find hazards in real time while driving automatically between waypoints chosen by its planners. By processing 600,000 measurement points with each glance, it has been able to travel more than 90 percent of its total distance autonomously.
Thanks to a recent software update, Perseverance can now roll more and steer less to save wear on parts, while checking its own position against orbital maps in mid-drive. Next, the team wants to overcome camera glare issues from sunlight that impede its vision, so the rover can work longer days.
Perseverance may have out-driven Opportunity, but the Curiosity rover is still exploring Mars as well and has traveled 38.15 km (23.7 miles) to date. The next most traveled US vehicles are the manned rovers from the Apollo 16, 17 and 18 missions — of those, Apollo 17 rover went the farthest at 35.74 km (22.21 miles).

articles.title: Volkswagen’s US EV sales collapse 90% in a quarter
articles.text:
Volkswagen sold 1,421 electric cars in the United States in the third quarter, a 90% fall, after ending ID.4 production and halting imports of its electric minivan. In Europe battery electric cars took 29% of new registrations in August.
Volkswagen sold 1,421 electric cars in the United States between July and September. That is 90% fewer than a year earlier.
The ID.4 accounted for 989 of them, down 92.1% from 12,470, and the ID. Buzz for 432, down 82.5%, InsideEVs reported. Total US sales fell 10.9% to 78,179.
This is a supply number, not a demand one. For most of this year Volkswagen has been selling whatever was left on dealer lots, and InsideEVs calls it among the biggest drops of any electric carmaker in the market.
The ID.4 left production in Chattanooga in April, so the plant could build the petrol Atlas instead, and ID. Buzz imports stopped, leaving only 2025 cars.
Europe went the other way. Battery electric cars took 29% of new registrations across the continent in August, and Volkswagen is now taking more orders for electric cars than petrol and diesel in Germany.
Four budget models built in Spain have drawn about 100,000 orders between them. Volkswagen cancelled extra shifts at Wolfsburg as combustion demand fell, and added them at Emden and Zwickau.
Its European problem is a different one. Chinese brands took a record 10.9% share of the European market in June, roughly double their share a year before.
That is costing Volkswagen its best sellers. The Tiguan plug-in hybrid went from Europe’s top-selling plug-in to fourth in a year, behind the BYD Seal U.
Chief executive Oliver Blume wants Brussels to act, saying there is no time to lose. Existing EU tariffs of up to 35% cover battery electric cars from China but not plug-in hybrids.
The American replacement borrows the name. The ID. Tiguan arrives next year with a front boot and more physical controls, and the minivan returns as a 2028 model with a native NACS port.
Until then the lots are the lineup. The ID.4 has been discounted by up to $12,500, while the ID. Buzz still starts at $61,545 for a range topping out at 234 miles.
Washington removed the help. The ID.4 sold 248 cars in the final quarter of last year, once the federal tax credit expired, and tariffs contributed to a 53% drop in Volkswagen’s profit.
The contrast is sharper in China. Volkswagen’s joint venture there sells a plug-in hybrid saloon from about $17,175, under a third of what the minivan costs in America, with no plan to bring it west.

articles.title: Cảng hàng không Quảng Trị chuẩn bị chuyến bay kiểm tra an toàn tĩnh không
articles.text:
Dự án Cảng hàng không Quảng Trị được xây dựng theo phương thức đối tác công tư (PPP), do liên danh Công ty TNHH Đầu tư và Phát triển hạ tầng giao thông T&T (thành viên T&T Group) và Công ty Cổ phần Tập đoàn CIENCO4 làm chủ đầu tư.
Đặt mục tiêu vận hành thương mại vào tháng 3/2027
Theo Ban Quản lý dự án Cảng hàng không Quảng Trị, ngày 15/10, lãnh đạo tỉnh Quảng Trị cùng đại diện các sở, ban, ngành và chủ đầu tư sẽ kiểm tra, đánh giá các hạng mục khu bay đã hoàn thành. Đồng thời, chủ đầu tư phối hợp với Công ty TNHH một thành viên Trắc địa Bản đồ (SAMCOM) tổ chức chuyến bay kiểm tra tĩnh không và chướng ngại vật tại hai đầu đường cất, hạ cánh. Chuyến bay dự kiến kéo dài khoảng 60 - 90 phút.
Theo Công ty CHK Quảng Trị, tổng khối lượng thi công dự án đến nay đạt trên 80%. Trong đó, đường cất hạ cánh, sân đỗ, các hạng mục phụ trợ, sơn kẻ tín hiệu, dải bảo hiểm dọc đường băng và đường lăn đã hoàn thành thi công. Khu vực nhà ga hành khách và đài kiểm soát không lưu đang tiếp tục được hoàn thiện, với khối lượng đạt trên 90%.
Thời gian tới, các đơn vị thi công sẽ tiếp tục tập trung nguồn lực để hoàn thiện, bàn giao mặt bằng và hạ tầng kỹ thuật, bảo đảm điều kiện lắp đặt các hệ thống thiết bị quản lý, điều hành bay và thiết bị ngoại trường. Sau chuyến bay kiểm tra an toàn tĩnh không, chủ đầu tư sẽ phối hợp với các cơ quan chức năng tổ chức các chuyến bay đánh giá phương thức bay và hiệu chuẩn thiết bị.
Cùng với đó, Càng hàng không (CHK) Quảng Trị đang trao đổi với TCT Cảng hàng không Việt Nam (ACV) về phương án quản lý, vận hành và khai thác sân bay trong giai đoạn 2027-2032; phối hợp với Cục Hàng không Việt Nam và các đơn vị liên quan để hoàn thiện phương thức bay, hệ thống tài liệu, quy trình khai thác và hồ sơ cấp phép theo quy định. Mục tiêu đặt ra là đưa CHK Quảng Trị vào vận hành, khai thác thương mại trong tháng 3/2027, trước dịp kỷ niệm 120 năm Ngày sinh Tổng Bí thư Lê Duẩn (7/4/1907–7/4/2027), đồng thời đón đầu cơ hội từ Năm Du lịch quốc gia 2027 do tỉnh Quảng Trị đăng cai.
Hạ tầng chiến lược trên vùng đất giàu giá trị lịch sử
Quảng Trị là vùng đất mang trong mình chiều sâu văn hóa và lịch sử đặc biệt của dân tộc. Từ Thành cổ Quảng Trị, đôi bờ Hiền Lương – Bến Hải đến Địa đạo Vịnh Mốc, mỗi địa danh đều gắn với những năm tháng chiến tranh khốc liệt, sự hy sinh của các thế hệ cha anh và khát vọng hòa bình, thống nhất đất nước.
Ngày nay, những địa chỉ lịch sử ấy tiếp tục trở thành sức hút riêng cho du lịch Quảng Trị. Nghĩa trang Liệt sĩ quốc gia Trường Sơn, Nghĩa trang Liệt sĩ quốc gia Đường 9, đảo Cồn Cỏ, Trung tâm Hành hương Đức Mẹ La Vang cùng hệ thống cảnh quan thiên nhiên và di sản trong khu vực tạo nên tiềm năng phát triển đa dạng các loại hình du lịch lịch sử, tâm linh, sinh thái và trải nghiệm. CHK Quảng Trị khi hoàn thành được kỳ vọng trở thành một mắt xích quan trọng, góp phần rút ngắn khoảng cách địa lý và mở rộng khả năng tiếp cận vùng đất giàu truyền thống này.
Không chỉ có ý nghĩa đối với du lịch, sân bay còn gắn với vị trí địa kinh tế chiến lược của Quảng Trị. Nằm trên trục giao thông Bắc – Nam và hành lang kinh tế Đông – Tây (EWEC), địa phương có điều kiện kết nối với Lào, Thái Lan, Myanmar và các thị trường trong khu vực thông qua hệ thống cửa khẩu quốc tế. Các tuyến giao thông đường bộ, đường sắt, đường thủy, cảng biển cùng Khu kinh tế Đông Nam tạo nền tảng để phát triển thương mại, công nghiệp và logistics. Sự xuất hiện của một cảng hàng không được kỳ vọng sẽ bổ sung phương thức kết nối quan trọng cho mạng lưới hạ tầng này. Khi đi vào hoạt động, sân bay có thể tạo điều kiện thuận lợi hơn cho việc đi lại của người dân, đón khách du lịch, kết nối các hoạt động kinh doanh và vận chuyển hàng hóa bằng đường hàng không, qua đó nâng cao sức hấp dẫn của địa phương đối với các nhà đầu tư.
Kỳ vọng tăng trưởng hành lang kinh tế Đông - Tây và khu vực miền Trung
Dự án CHK Quảng Trị được xây dựng trên địa bàn xã Gio Linh và Cửa Việt, với quy mô hơn 316 ha, tổng mức đầu tư trên 5.800 tỷ đồng. Theo thông tin từ T&T Group, quy hoạch sân bay đã được điều chỉnh lên cấp 4E vào tháng 7/2026, cho phép tiếp nhận các dòng máy bay thân rộng, hiện đại như Boeing 777, Boeing 787 và Airbus A350. Công suất thiết kế đáp ứng nhu cầu khai thác khoảng 5 triệu lượt hành khách và 25.500 tấn hàng hóa mỗi năm.
Theo ông Đỗ Quang Hiển, Nhà sáng lập, Chủ tịch Điều hành T&T Group, Tập đoàn dành nhiều tâm huyết cho Quảng Trị, huy động tối đa nguồn lực để hoàn thành sân bay, đưa dự án trở thành động lực phát triển kinh tế địa phương, tăng cường kết nối với các địa phương trong cả nước.
Đại diện T&T Group cũng cho biết, tập đoàn đang nghiên cứu đầu tư Tổ hợp công nghiệp hàng không – Trung tâm thương mại tự do – Đô thị khoa học đổi mới sáng tạo và đô thị sân bay Quảng Trị, định hướng phát triển theo mô hình tích hợp, lấy sân bay làm hạt nhân, kết nối công nghiệp hàng không, logistics, thương mại tự do, khoa học công nghệ và đô thị.
Cùng với các dự án quy mô lớn khác trong lĩnh vực năng lượng, hạ tầng và bất động sản đang triển khai, T&T Group mong muốn tiếp tục đồng hành cùng Quảng Trị, góp phần thực hiện mục tiêu xây dựng địa phương trở thành một cực tăng trưởng quan trọng trên hành lang kinh tế Đông - Tây và khu vực miền Trung.
