articles.title: Abu Dhabi will use Ultrahuman's smart ring know-how to boost its public health app - Engadget
articles.text:
Abu Dhabi will use Ultrahuman's smart ring know-how to boost its public health app
But the system won't mandate the use of Ultrahuman's smart rings.
The Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre is teaming up with Ultrahuman to bring the latter's algorithms to its Sahatna app. Sahatna is the nationwide healthcare app enabling individuals to manage their health, including speaking to doctors and accessing health and genetics records. As of now, the app will also tell users their biological age (as opposed to their chronological age). That comes from Ultrahuman's Ultra Age metric, which analyzes your sleep, cardiovascular and blood markers into a single metric. You won't need to be an Ultrahuman user to get the benefit, as Sahatna's system is device agnostic.
Historically, wearables have received short shrift from doctors and regulators but it's clear the trend is shifting. The ADPHC, for instance, hopes the system will help people gain a better understanding of how lifestyle factors influence their long-term health. It adds that the model, which combines clinical and wearable data, will support "earlier interventions, more targeted prevention strategies and more personalized recommendations." It's not clear at this point if that means officials will be able to target and identify individuals who are deemed to require direct intervention, or if this will be left down to the user.

articles.title: Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
articles.text:
Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO’s secretive robotics project.
Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
Ford’s former EV and software chief will run Rivian’s robotics startup at a time of maximum hype for physical AI.
Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan. He left Tesla in 2018 and rejoined Apple. In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year.
Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing. While the company has yet to show off any of its robots in public, the startup says its robots are being designed with “dexterity and physical reasoning” that’s required for industrial work.
“Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products, and I couldn’t be more excited to be building Mind with him,” Scaringe said in a statement. “He has an incredible ability to foster great teams that take on big, complex ideas and deliver products that reset expectations. That’s exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.”
Field joins Mind Robotics at a major turning point for the field of robotics, with rapid advances in physical AI colliding with major hurdles in hardware and software development. Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions.
Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots.
Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup.
“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”
Correction October 13th: Mind Robotics is a partner of Rivian, but not a spinoff. A previous version of this story misstated the relationship between the companies.

articles.title: Google Play now lets anyone build private, vibe-coded apps that run on Android | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private.
These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator.
The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android.
Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use.
These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android.
Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up.
“That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.”
In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store.
And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews.
Related to AI’s impact on app development, Google said it’s also building better ways to curate the Google Play experience — for instance, by leveraging Google’s AI to create a personalized game recommendation engine, called Game Finder. The feature, first available in the U.S. in English, will be based on what the user likes to play combined with Google’s knowledge derived from its game community’s 1.2 billion players.
Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates.
Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations.
The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience.

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 13/10: Thế giới tăng cao, trong nước sắp điều chỉnh
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Giá dầu quốc tế trong phiên giao dịch đầu tuần (12/10) tăng mạnh. Giá dầu Brent vượt mức 106 USD/thùng.
Chốt phiên giao dịch 12/10, theo Reuters, giá dầu Brent tăng 1,84%, lên mức 106,7 USD/thùng, mức cao nhất kể từ ngày 15/9. Còn giá dầu WTI chốt phiên ở mức 93,74 USD/thùng, tăng 2%.
Đầu phiên giao dịch hôm nay (13/10), giá dầu WTI đảo chiều đi xuống.
Theo dữ liệu từ Oilprice, vào lúc 7h ngày 13/10 (giờ Việt Nam), giá dầu Brent vẫn được niêm yết ở mức 106,7 USD/thùng. Trong khi giá dầu WTI được điều chỉnh xuống mức 93,16 USD/thùng, giảm 0,62% so với phiên liền trước.
Giá dầu thế giới đi lên sau các vụ tấn công của lực lượng Houthi ở Yemen vào Saudi Arabia, làm gia tăng lo ngại về nguồn cung dầu từ Trung Đông.
Lực lượng Houthi do Iran hậu thuẫn đã nhận trách nhiệm về vụ tấn công ngày 10/10 vào sân bay quốc tế King Khalid ở thủ đô Riyadh của Saudi Arabia khiến 13 người thiệt mạng và hơn 300 người bị thương. Các cuộc tấn công vẫn tiếp diễn trong ngày 11/10, làm gia tăng nguy cơ xung đột lan rộng và ảnh hưởng đến hoạt động khai thác, vận chuyển dầu của Saudi Arabia.
Cùng với đó, trong tháng 10, nhiều tàu chở dầu tiếp tục trở thành mục tiêu tấn công khi đi qua eo biển Hormuz.
Cơ quan Điều hành Thương mại Hàng hải của Vương quốc Anh cho biết, một tàu chở dầu bị máy bay không người lái tấn công tại khu vực Sohar của Oman, trong khi một tàu khác bị hư hại khi đang di chuyển qua eo biển Hormuz.
Những diễn biến này đe dọa làm suy yếu sự phục hồi xuất khẩu dầu thô của Trung Đông.
Trước những rủi ro về nguồn cung, ngân hàng Goldman Sachs (Mỹ) đã nâng dự báo giá dầu Brent trong tháng 12 từ mức 85 USD/thùng lên 90 USD/thùng. Ngân hàng này ước tính giá dầu đang bao gồm mức phụ phí rủi ro hơn 20 USD/thùng do căng thẳng địa chính trị.
Goldman Sachs cũng nhận định giá dầu WTI tiếp tục thấp hơn dầu Brent do chi phí vận chuyển dầu từ Mỹ sang châu Âu ở mức cao. Giá dầu WTI trung bình được dự báo đạt 81 USD/thùng trong tháng 12/2026 và 73 USD/thùng trong năm 2027.

articles.title: Jio Platforms attracts more than $20B in bids ahead of record India IPO
articles.text:
Jio Platforms has drawn more than $20B in bids for what would be India’s largest listing, with Fidelity, Allianz and Capital Group indicating interest. The company is now seeking about $108B, against the $170B bankers discussed last November.
Jio Platforms has drawn more than $20B in bids for what would be India’s largest listing. The share sale is expected to open next week, with the listing completed before 30 October.
Fidelity, Allianz and Capital Group have indicated interest, Bloomberg reported, with the final anchor list due within days. Allianz is German, and Akash Ambani’s roadshow ran through London as well as Hong Kong and New York.
The price has come down a long way. When Jio filed in June, analysts put the company between $131B and $180B.
It is now seeking as much as 10.3 trillion rupees, about $108B. Bankers were discussing a figure as high as $170B last November, so the ask has fallen by roughly a third.
The timing explains some of it. Databricks’ chief executive called 2026 a terrible year to go public, and his company has stayed private.
His reason was competition for the same pool of money. SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI are seeking more than $200B from public investors between them, and institutional allocation budgets are finite.
Bankers read it the other way. BNP Paribas told TNW in June that liquidity attracts liquidity, and that the American wave would pull European listings along with it.
Jio is the first real test of which reading is right. Twenty billion dollars of demand is a strong book, but it was assembled only after the price came down.
The money has somewhere to go beyond the balance sheet. Jio is planning a 1,650-satellite constellation for Indian broadband, at an estimated cost of $10B to $15B.
Most of the proceeds go to debt. About 275 billion rupees will prepay external commercial borrowings at Reliance Jio Infocomm, the telecom subsidiary.
Several of those lenders are European. BNP Paribas and Barclays sit alongside ANZ, Bank of America and Citibank on the facility being repaid, so a slice of an Indian listing lands on European balance sheets.
Nobody is cashing out. The offer is entirely new shares, and Meta, Alphabet, Mubadala and Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund are all staying in, according to the draft prospectus.
At the top of the band the sale raises about 302 billion rupees. India’s record is Hyundai’s local unit, at roughly 279 billion rupees in 2024.

articles.title: X bundles Premium, Grok and Cursor under a single monthly subscription - Engadget
articles.text:
X bundles Premium, Grok and Cursor under a single monthly subscription
One membership will give you access to SpaceXSI’s products.
SpaceXSI has announced a unified membership scheme across its products called the X Subscription. The company was formerly known as SpaceXAI until its CEO Elon Musk announced that he would rename it, following President Donald Trump's push to use the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence. An X Subscription plan will include access to Grok, Grok Bot, Cursor and X Premium, depending on the tier you're paying for. If you'll recall, the company acquired coding startup Cursor back in August.
We've unified plans across Grok, Cursor, and X Premium.
Introducing The X Subscription. pic.twitter.com/SvkrVvBa0p
— SpaceX Super Intelligence (@SpaceXSI) October 12, 2026
The $8-a-month Plus tier for individuals will provide you access to Grok Chat, Voice, Imagine and Build, as well as Grok API and to Cursor for coding. You'll also get X Premium features, including a checkmark, fewer ads on your X timeline, enhanced creator tools and advanced analytics.
Meanwhile, the $30-a-month Premium tier will get you all those, as well as access to Grok Bot and the latest Grok models, the ability to make AI images and videos thru Grok and faster chat responses. On Cursor, you'll get access to code hosting, cloud agents and automations. And on X, you'll get ad-free scrolling and the ability to secure your preferred handle.
The $100-a-month Super tier includes everything in Plus and Premium, along with priority access to Grok models at peak times. Finally, the $200 Ultra tier includes the earliest access to all products and models, as well as 20 times the usage capacity of Plus. The Premium, Super and Ultra plans are also available for teams, while enterprise customers can get customized plans from the company.

articles.title: I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
articles.text:
The other day I whizzed past several people while running in the park, my playlist blasting at full volume. The next morning, I smiled at a barista while ordering a caramel apple-flavored matcha latte. Afterward, I sat on a park bench reading a book, called up a pal to chat about her recent trip to Prague, and then asked my Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses what meetings were coming up on my calendar. The chipper AI voice said I hadn’t connected my Google Calendar yet (I had) and asked if I would like help connecting. I sighed and then asked it to play an upbeat song. It picked Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us.”
I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
It’s harder to be a perv in these audio-only glasses, but removing the ick does make them less ‘useful.’
These past few days, dozens of people have seen or interacted with me while wearing smart glasses. Not a single person noticed. Probably because these audio-only versions look just like normal glasses. They come in a retro Clubmaster look — like the ones pictured in this review — or a more Wayfarer-esque Burbank style. Honestly, people usually don’t notice when I wear camera glasses either. But for once, I didn’t feel like a creep.
The Good
- I don’t feel like a creep wearing these
- Long battery life
- Lightweight
- Stylish
- Good for open-ear audio
The Bad
- Expensive for what they are
- Still not convinced AI is the killer app for these
The audio-only Ray-Bans aren’t a novel concept. Seven years ago, I strutted around Manhattan taking calls and listening to tunes in the Bose Frames, which also combined Bluetooth audio with stylish sunglasses. Nobody noticed me in the Bose back then, either. What makes this pair notable is that it’s 2026, they’re made by Meta, and, well, there’s been vigorous discourse about whether smart glasses are a form of spyware.
Let’s get privacy out of the way. During setup, all the privacy and data opt-out disclosures were much more prominent than when I’ve previously tested Meta glasses. A screen explained how visual data from AI experiences is handled. (You can opt out of Meta using that data to improve AI; voice data, however, is still used.) There’s no visual data from these glasses — this is simply the new messaging for any pair of Meta glasses. You can also opt out of sharing “additional data” with Meta as well, which is enumerated in a separate document online. This is a good thing, though it doesn’t address what makes people uncomfortable about smart glasses: the uneasy feeling that someone else is recording you.
You know what sort of does, though? Removing the camera. The Bose Frames never triggered the same level of distrust because they were “just” sunglasses-shaped headphones. That applies here too. Frankly, I felt much lighter wearing these out into the world precisely because I couldn’t record footage of anyone. (Even if I feel lame saying “Hey Meta” in public.)
I can imagine people still distrusting these Ray-Bans because they have always-listening capabilities for waking up the AI assistant. However, you can disable the wake word in settings and use a customizable button on the right temple arm instead. (This automatically feels 10 percent less silly if you “must” talk to AI assistants outside the home.) There’s no native way to record a conversation directly from the glasses. Any other audio-based feature, like live translation, has to be manually started.
I’m not saying these can’t be modded or used for evil out of the box. Where there’s a perverse mind and ill will, there’s a way. I’m saying it’d take more effort because these glasses simply don’t do very much.
At least, not yet.
Meta’s Muse AI is eventually coming to the glasses, but it’s not available right now. Right now, the glasses ship with the less powerful Muse Spark model. It’s better than what was on the Ray-Bans in 2023, but it’s still meh unless you’re using it for accessibility reasons. In which case, these glasses may not be the best use of $350. A camera-equipped model is more helpful for low-vision and blind users. For hard-of-hearing users, the FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature isn’t available yet, and for deaf users, the Meta Ray-Ban Display may be more useful because they support live captioning.
For everyone else, Muse Spark is nerfed without the camera but can still come in handy. For example, granting access to your messaging apps, Google Calendar, and email lets it do some light scheduling and correspondence on your behalf. If you enable location sharing, you can send where you are to the group chat. It’s fine for these tasks, but not great. It’s adept at short queries like “What’s my next calendar event?” or “Set a reminder to update my editors at 12PM.” With more complex asks, I’ve found Muse Spark gets confused, and it’s faster to whip out my phone. I ended up mostly asking it to set reminders for to-dos I remembered while in the middle of something else.
Muse Spark can also give you local recommendations and turn-by-turn audio directions while walking. As I’ve written before, that’s great if you’re traveling. Less so if you’re familiar with your local haunts. In my neighborhood, I already know which coffee shops have the best Wi-Fi and snacks — and it wasn’t the one Muse Spark suggested. As for walking directions, they’re not something I need that often. When I did, I found using Google Maps on my phone more helpful for getting my bearings.
I’m sure Muse will open up more possibilities when it arrives later this year. Then again, I’ve seen demos, and I’m still skeptical that agentic AI will be the thing that convinces people to buy smart glasses.
So what do I like about these? They’re simply a good pair of open-ear headphones.
I said good, not great. Sound quality is decent, but you’re still dealing with all the tradeoffs that come with this form factor. They struggle at louder volumes. The trebles start to get tinny, and bass can sound distorted. There’s inevitably sound leakage. My spouse frequently reminded me that they could hear everything I was listening to, all of the AI’s responses, and my phone calls. Conversely, even at top volume, ambient noise can still drown out your content. These won’t cut it on a loud subway, for instance.
Still, it’s nice to listen to audiobooks around the house without jumping out of my skin anytime my spouse or cats want my attention. On my daily walks, I’m less afraid of my maniac neighbors mowing me down in their murder mobiles. (New Jersey drivers, man.) It’s not mind-blowing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to my day-to-day routine. And I don’t have to think too hard about it.
At 43 to 47g, these are also much comfier than every other pair of Meta glasses I’ve tried. So far, I’ve worn them for two full days, including a 30-minute run and multiple walks, with zero issues. My Clubmaster review unit also has nose pads — huzzah for anyone with a low nose bridge. That also made for a huge improvement in call quality since the mic for calls wasn’t smushed up against my schnoz. The temple tips can also be adjusted for a better fit.
I usually ding smart glasses for not supporting my -10 prescription and severe astigmatism. These support a range of -12 to +6 — I’m still waiting on a prescription pair, but at least my garbage eyeballs don’t preclude me from wearing these as my daily glasses. All in all, these glasses will fit a much broader range of faces and vision needs.
Battery life is also phenomenal. I was able to eke out two full workdays without sticking the glasses back into the case.
Okay, I lied — one more gripe. These feel expensive for headphone glasses that don’t do much yet. The Meta Glasses, for example, now start at $250 and technically do more. These are $100 more for what, exactly? The Ray-Ban branding? The privilege of not worrying about freaking out other people? If these were $150 or $200, I’d say these would be a no-brainer. Starting at $350 without prescription lenses, without the hearing assistance features, without Muse? That feels off.
But pricing complaints aside, I didn’t miss the camera. (I only ever use it to take cat videos anyway.) Muse Spark isn’t what I’d call the most compelling AI model, but it’s useful now and then. For the casual user, the headphones are the most useful part of smart glasses.
I wish I could just thrust these into the air and declare that nixing the camera solves the privacy problem. I can’t. Yes, I’m relieved that I don’t have to worry about people punching me in the face if I wear these out and about. I don’t think most people want more than this right now. Still, I’d be lying if I said I didn’t personally know several people who would miss the camera. Not because they’re perverts, but because they find them to be genuinely useful tools for candid home videos, content creation, accessibility, or multimodal AI. For those people, this type of smart glasses isn’t a real option.
Besides, who’s to say Meta won’t add more ambient listening features down the line? Then what? The lack of a camera is only a comfort for now. It doesn’t negate the need for continued, thoughtful discussion about AI wearables, the definition of recording, and what role these gadgets ought to play in our lives.
Photography by Victoria Song / The Verge
Agree to Continue: Ray-Ban Meta Audio
Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.
To use the Ray-Ban Meta Audio smart glasses, you’ll need a Meta account and the Meta AI app downloaded onto your phone. A Meta account works across platforms like Meta, Instagram, and Quest and comes with its own terms of service and privacy policy. Should you decide to integrate with services like WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, Apple Music, Apple Health, Garmin, Strava, Amazon Music, and Spotify, you also agree to those terms and privacy policies. You may also be asked to give permissions related to Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, location services, and voice data. If you choose to get a pair of prescription lenses, you may also be asked to share that information with Ray-Ban and/or LensCrafters.
If you are concerned about privacy, you can access the Glasses Privacy menu in the glasses’ settings. There you can view the voice activity log as well as the “Share additional data” toggle. To access the visual data opt-out toggle, go to the glasses’ settings and navigate to the Meta AI menu.
The smart glasses also come with supplemental terms of service and privacy policies / notices, including:
Final tally: Two mandatory agreements, eight supplemental agreements and notices, and several optional agreements.

articles.title: SpaceX and Google both said no. Now his software is riding a SpaceX rocket next to Google’s | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The way Rama Afullo tells it, he saw orbital data centers coming.
The Kenyan American engineer previously worked in Google’s cloud computing business before a brief stint at SpaceX’s Starlink communications network in 2024. His experiences convinced him that there was untapped potential for computers in space.
“When I was at SpaceX, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no. When I was at Google, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no,” he tells TechCrunch.
So he left SpaceX and co-founded Satlyt, a new company with headquarters in Sunnyvale, California, and Nairobi, to build software for satellites that he hopes will let many satellites share the work of large computing jobs in space. The company has raised an $8 million seed round, Afullo exclusively told TechCrunch.
The timing looks good for him. SpaceX has since gone all-in on orbital data centers, and Satlyt’s software is set to launch Thursday on a SpaceX rocket alongside the first prototype for Google’s space data center effort, Project Suncatcher.
Unlike SpaceX, Google, or startups like Starcloud and Cowboy Space Company, Satlyt isn’t planning to build its own spacecraft. Afullo’s team is building the software to operate AI models on satellites, comparing his approach to VMware and Snowflake — companies whose platforms let users run complex software without worrying about the underlying infrastructure.
“The folks like SpaceX who are doing orbital data centers — if they are the iPhone, we’ll build Android as a horizontally integrated, open ecosystem,” he said. In other words, Satlyt wants to offer software that works across many companies’ satellites.
Satlyt has already flown its software on two demonstration missions. The initial focus is finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft, which typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise. Sending data back to Earth, known as downlink, is expensive and often slow, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings, either when resolving anomalies or by processing sensor readings on the spacecraft instead of on the ground.
Earlier this year, Satlyt deployed Google DeepMind’s Gemma AI model onboard a spacecraft operated by Momentus. The model cut the size of a transmission about onboard software errors by more than 60%, the kind of efficiency that Afullo says can save hundreds of thousands of dollars per satellite each year.
A launch will put Satlyt’s software to work onboard a spacecraft built by TakeMe2Space, an Indian startup that builds computing hardware for satellites. The mission involves three customers: NASA, which is paying the company to test protocols for cloud computing in space; Stellerian, a startup focused on space surveillance (tracking objects in orbit) that wants to test image processing workloads; and TakeMe2Space itself, to show the satellite can host other companies’ software.
Right now, few high-powered GPUs are in orbit. For now, the most likely opportunity lies in the kinds of workloads Satlyt is working on. But the company’s next project is to show that it can create a shared computing system — a cloud — spanning two different satellites, which it expects to attempt next year. If successful, it will allow the company to build a true compute cloud in orbit as a third-party provider to spacecraft builders.
The way to think about it is that we turn your satellite into a revenue-generating managed service,” Afullo said.
Satlyt’s seed round was led by Houston-based Non Sibi Ventures, where partner Bernard Harris, who served as a NASA astronaut for more than 20 years, helped ground the firm’s conviction in a novel, space-based business.
One reason the firm invested was that Satlyt doesn’t depend on a highest-octane vision of space data centers, which faces uncertain economics and a launch bottleneck. “We don’t need data centers in space for Rama to be wildly successful, right?” Non Sibi partner Kent Lucas told TechCrunch. “It can just be driven by the number of satellites going up.”
Afullo’s hope is to be live on 20% of satellites by the end of the decade, when he expects virtually every spacecraft builder to be putting GPUs and similar advanced processors in their satellites.
“If you’re putting up a satellite without putting up a GPU on it, at the very least, you’re doing yourself a disservice, right?” he says.
This story was originally published on October 1. Satlyt is among dozens of other startups vetted by TechCrunch and appearing at Disrupt as part of our broader Battlefield competition happening this week in downtown San Francisco. It all kicks off on Tuesday. Learn more here.

articles.title: Apple launches $299 HomeView hub alongside new smart home range
articles.text:
Apple has launched HomeView, a $299 smart display built around Siri AI, with shipping from 13 November in eight markets. The European Union is not one of them, because Siri AI is still blocked on iOS there.
Apple has launched HomeView, a $299 smart display built around the new Siri, with pre-orders open and shipping from 13 November. It is not for sale in the European Union.
Apple says so itself, in the last line of the pricing section of its own announcement. The reason it gives is that Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS in the EU.
That block is four months old. Apple said in June that EU regulators had rejected every proposal it made, and gave no timeline for Siri AI on iPhone or iPad.
The dispute is about interoperability. Apple says the Commission’s reading would force it to give rival assistants the same deep access to messages, files and purchases that Siri has.
Europeans have paid for this before. The iPhone 18 Pro shipped in September at the same $1,199 price everywhere, without Siri AI in the EU and with a smaller battery.
This time there is nothing to buy. HomeView goes on sale in eight markets, the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India, Singapore and South Africa, where Siri AI runs in English and in beta.
The risk was flagged in July. TNW reported then that the hub’s case rested on Siri, and that European buyers might get the hardware without the assistant that justified it.
The hardware is ambitious. A seven-inch display recognises up to six faces, gating each person’s messages and calendar behind their face and a recently unlocked iPhone, with camera data held in an isolated part of the A18 chip.
Diplomacy has not shifted it. Tim Cook and the EU’s digital chief Henna Virkkunen held a constructive exchange by video in June, with no agreement announced.
Cook is now executive chairman, a role that includes engagement with policymakers. John Ternus became chief executive on 1 September.
The accessories arrive anyway. Apple Home Collection, a line of cameras, thermostats and a lock, was built with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
Schneider Electric is French. Its Schneider Home arm also makes the three wall mounts for a device that cannot be sold in France.
Apple says it is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward. It has said versions of that since June.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says it’s evaluating allegations that Tesla’s 1,000 or so robotaxis using its automated driving system are exceeding “posted speed limits in active school zones.” Waymo’s robotaxis have also faced similar inquiries, including for illegally passing school buses and hitting a child near a California elementary school.
The feds are looking into reports of Tesla’s robotaxis speeding through school zones
NHTSA has received a petition requesting an investigation into Model Y and Cybercab vehicles exceeding active school zone speed limits.
NHTSA:
The Office of Defects Investigation (ODI) received a DP on September 23, 2026, requesting an investigation into model year (MY) 2026 Tesla Robotaxis (Model Y and Cybercab) with the Automated Driving System (ADS) engaged. The Petitioner alleges that the ADS exceeds posted speed limits in active school zones.
The Cybercab launched earlier this year, and is already under investigation for its lack of side mirrors, pedals, and a steering wheel. articles.title: Singapore third-quarter GDP growth softens from four-year high but beats estimates
articles.text:
Singapore's economic expansion decelerated in the third quarter of 2026, with GDP growth dropping to 5.4% after hitting a four-year high in the last quarter.
However, the GDP print beat expectations of a 5% growth from economists polled by Reuters.
Government data showed a decline in the country's manufacturing sector, although this was offset by an expansion in construction. Manufacturing is one of the city-state's largest sectors, contributing about 20% of its GDP.
Singapore back in August had lifted its annual economic growth forecast as AI-related sectors and exports powered its economy to beat expectations for the first two quarters of the year. This forecast is still mantain
GDP growth for 2026 is expected to come in at 4.5% to 5.5%, more than double the lower end of its previous forecast of 2%-4%.
This has been the second time Singapore has upgraded its growth estimates. At the start of the year, the country's ministry of trade and industry had estimated growth at 1%-3%.
The GDP numbers come as the Monetary Authority of Singapore held its monetary policy steady, marking a pause after two straight rounds of tightening.
The city-state had tightened its policy in back to back in April and July, citing inflation risks due to higher energy prices.
The MAS still projects inflation will remain high in the near term due to higher energy and food prices, then ease from mid-2027 "as import costs ebb and domestic price pressures stay subdued."
"The Singapore economy should continue to expand at a firm pace in the immediate quarters ahead, and moderate thereafter as the AI cycle eases from its exceptional pace and global financial conditions tighten," the MAS added.
Singapore does not use an interest rate to set monetary policy. Instead, it manages the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies belonging to the country's major trading partners, allowing the exchange rate to fluctuate within an undisclosed policy band.

articles.title: Goldman says investors are looking for 'profitable' Chinese business growth overseas
articles.text:
BEIJING — Equity investors are skeptical of Chinese companies' rapid expansion overseas, according to Goldman Sachs.
The "market wants to look for profitable expansions," Trina Chen, co-head of Greater China equity research at Goldman Sachs Research, said on a podcast that the investment bank published Tuesday.
Sluggish consumer demand in China has pushed many companies, such as electric car brands, to accelerate plans for entering other countries. Automaker Geely is one of the latest Chinese companies to push further abroad, announcing Friday it plans to enter Canada next year.
Chinese companies' overseas market share will likely reach 31% by 2035, up from around 18%, Chen and her team predicted in a Sept. 14 report. Their analysis covered more than 10 sectors, including express delivery, industrial robots and so-called white goods such as air conditioners.
Chinese businesses often find higher profit margins abroad than they would at home, enabling the companies to charge lower prices than local competitors.
Investors need to be convinced the global expansion "does not end up with something similar to involution, where the price actually gets killed because of competition," Chen said Tuesday, adding that geopolitics and market access restrictions also weighs on stock performance.
Involution refers to race-to-the-bottom competition in China, which regulators have attempted to address in recent years.
That uncertainty means Chinese companies have very little of their global expansion opportunity priced into their stocks, Chen said.
But on the flip side, she noted that investors are "ruthless" when incumbent companies lose their market share: A 10% to 15% loss could shrink market capitalization by 50% to 80%.
The Chinese players are not just looking at the U.S. and Europe. Goldman Sachs noted some of the most rapid growth is in emerging markets, as the businesses also pursue areas underserved by competitors.
"Chinese brands are no longer simply market challengers," Euromonitor said in a report last month. "Brands are becoming long-term, embedded competitors capable of reshaping market dynamics across Latin America.

articles.title: Here's where Jim Cramer stands on this newly public AI infrastructure stock
articles.text:
There's a new picks-and-shovels play on the artificial intelligence build-out, but CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday that investors should keep the stock at arm's length.
The "Mad Money" host gave two primary reasons for holding off on Accelevation Holdings: He's becoming more cautious about data center stocks ahead of the midterm elections and prefers established companies with proven track records. That's why Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio run by the CNBC Investing Club, instead owns shares of AI infrastructure players such as gas turbine maker GE Vernova and electrical equipment supplier Eaton.
"Accelevation has an exciting story, but after it came public with a whimper, I'm not too eager to jump on this one," he said. "For now, I say let's put Accelevation on our watch list and see if management can deliver before we pull the trigger."
Accelevation, which makes and installs electric, cooling equipment and support structures inside data centers, priced its offering on Sept. 29 at $18 per share, below its proposed offering range. Shares debuted the next day and closed at $17.95. They have since fallen to just over $15, a disappointing first couple of weeks for a company benefiting from surging demand for AI infrastructure.
Cramer's first concern extends beyond Accelevation. With the midterm elections just three weeks away, he expects political opposition to data center construction to remain a headwind for the broader industry. The enormous electricity demands of these facilities and their potential impact on energy costs have become political flashpoints, making Cramer reluctant to recommend buying into the sector before voters head to the polls.
"If you're going to buy a data center supplier, I think you should wait three weeks until after the election — that's when I expect some of the political heat to die down," he said.
His second concern is specific to Accelevation. While the company's growth has been impressive, Cramer is less confident in its ability to consistently turn that demand into profits, particularly as it competes with larger industrial players.
Accelevation's revenue surged 147% in 2025, while sales jumped another 176% year over year in the first half of 2026. However, higher labor costs and project inefficiencies weighed on gross margins during that period. "That tells me some of this work has been much harder to execute profitably than these guys expected," Cramer said.
He also expressed concerns about Accelevation's competitive position, citing Vertiv and Eaton as established companies that pursue overlapping segments of the data center infrastructure market. "There are a ton of different ways to play this story," he said. "I'd rather go with the ones that have earned my confidence."

articles.title: Anthropic urges court in Washington, D.C. to rehear appeal of Pentagon blacklisting
articles.text:
Anthropic is asking a federal court in Washington, D.C. to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models.
"The Secretary of War branded Anthropic — an American AI company whose models help defend the nation— a national-security 'supply chain risk' because it declined to permit its models to be used for mass surveillance of Americans or lethal autonomous warfare and publicly explained those AI-safety commitments," Anthropic attorneys wrote in the petition filed on Tuesday. "A divided panel upheld that extraordinary designation."
The Defense Department, led by Pete Hegseth, applied the supply chain risk label in March, a move that blocked defense contractors from using the company's technology in their work with the agency. That came after a breakdown in negotiations about how the military could use Anthropic's Claude AI models.
Anthropic sued the Trump administration in an effort to undo that action. In September, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting. The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional.
Anthropic's attorneys wrote in the Tuesday filing that the court ignored "straightforward evidence the designation was retaliation for Anthropic's speech about AI safety."
Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed.
A representative from Anthropic declined to comment beyond the filing. The Pentagon didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this report.

articles.title: Jim Cramer isn't giving up on semiconductor stocks despite the sell off. Here's why
articles.text:
Semiconductor stocks have been getting crushed in recent days, but CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday there's a compelling reason not to give up on the group.
The VanEck Semiconductor ETF has fallen 7.2% over six consecutive sessions, and Cramer warned that rising oil prices and interest rates could prolong the sell off. However, he argued chip stocks are increasingly trading together regardless of their individual fundamentals, obscuring the strong demand that fueled the sector's remarkable rally earlier this year.
To illustrate his point, Cramer described a recent visit to an Apple showroom, where he saw devices featuring a more personalized Siri and advanced smart home technology. The experience highlighted how increasingly sophisticated consumer products require more computing power and memory, creating additional opportunities for chipmakers.
"Before you decide to bail from the semis because you can't take the pain, go to the showroom," the "Mad Money" host said. "Go see where these chips are used. They appear in places that you'd least expect them. Don't watch the semiconductor index, watch the devices."
Cramer pointed to memory chip maker Micron as an example of a company whose fundamentals are being overshadowed by the broader sell off. The company has become one of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence build-out, with demand for memory chips far outstripping supply. Cramer highlighted its 26 long-term customer agreements, which currently cover about 35% of revenue through 2030, with negotiations already underway for 2031. Those take-or-pay contracts require customers to honor their financial commitments, he said, giving Micron greater visibility into future revenue. "If Micron had no agreements I would be worried," Cramer said.
And the demand story isn't limited to memory chips. Cramer also highlighted Intel and AMD, which "make the CPUs that are basic building blocks for practically every machine under the sun."
Cramer acknowledged that the group could face further losses after its enormous run, but said investors shouldn't dismiss the fundamental demand behind those gains. "It's reasonable to expect a sharp pullback after how far these stocks traveled," he said. "I just think that when you see the devices, when you know the exploding use cases, you can understand why Micron or Intel or AMD have been moving up."
"It wasn't all Situational Awareness, the wayward hedge fund that took so many semis up to unsustainable levels with borrowed money," Cramer said. "A lot of this is just raw demand."

In Asia, Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 0.62%. Japan's Nikkei 225 added 0.32%, while South Korea's Kospi rose 0.82%.
A drift downward in chip stocks weighed on the major averages Tuesday, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) falling for a sixth straight session over growing fears of an AI spending bubble and rising anxieties around competition out of China.
A swath of big banks posted strong quarterly results, but shares ended the day lower, with Goldman Sachs and Citigroup falling. The market's reaction suggested businesses have a higher bar to clear during the third-quarter earnings season — especially in tech where semiconductors are expected to be the largest contributor to year-over-year earnings growth.
S&P 500 companies are expected to post a blended earnings growth rate of roughly 30%, while semiconductors and semiconductor equipment are set for growth of 130%, according to FactSet data.
"The business fundamentals are very strong. It's very hard to argue with the demand side of the story for chips," Marta Norton, chief investment strategist at Empower, told CNBC's "Closing Bell: Overtime." "I don't know if we necessarily question how good those business fundamentals are as much as we question how much valuation is left in the space."
Investors are awaiting the September reading of the U.S. consumer price index Wednesday morning. Economists polled by Dow Jones anticipate inflation to have risen by 3.6% on a year-over-year basis, up from 3.4% in the prior reading.
The results arrive as oil prices remain elevated and consumers pay more for gasoline, which is averaging at $4.34 a gallon, compared to $3.08 per gallon a year earlier, according to AAA. Last week President Donald Trump announced he would temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports, but analysts don't believe the deal will do much to lower fuel prices for truckers and farmers.
Earnings season continues, with more big bank results from Bank of America and Morgan Stanley out Wednesday morning U.S. time. Dutch semiconductor company ASML also reports.

articles.title: United Airlines is making it harder to reach its top frequent flyer status in 2027
articles.text:
United Airlines is getting rid of one path to achieve elite status in 2027 and making its top tier harder to reach.
The Chicago-based airline is removing the ability for MileagePlus members to earn status partially based on flight segments flown in a calendar year for 2027. Instead, starting Jan. 1, United will only consider the number of points members earn based on Premier qualifying points earned from eligible flight spending, award travel and eligible United credit card spending.
United announced the change Tuesday in emails to MileagePlus members and on its website. The change aims to simplify how customers earn Premier status, according to the email obtained by CNBC that United sent to members.
Previously, members could gain status in the lowest elite tier, Premier Silver, with a combination of 15 flight segments and 5,000 points earned in a year, or with 6,000 points. Now, customers will only be able to achieve the status through points at the 6,000 point threshold.
The number of Premier qualifying points it will take for members to reach the Premier Gold and Platinum tiers through points will also stay the same as the previous points-only option. However, to reach United's highest rewards tier, Premier 1K, members now need 32,000 qualifying points, up from 28,000 in 2026.
Flyers earn one Premier qualifying point, or PQP, per dollar spent on United base fares and upgrades, and for every 100 miles they redeem for travel on United flights. United Chase cardholders also earn points when they spend money with their card.
MileagePlus members will still have to take at least four flights on United or United Express jets in a year to be eligible for Premier status.
In an interview with travel website The Points Guy, United's President of MileagePlus Jarad Fisher called the flight segments metric an "old relic," saying that the airline "thought it made more sense for them to have one consistent metric ... that they could focus on across the board between their flight activity, their engagement in the airline."
United also announced Tuesday that United cardholders who have Premier status will get a head start by automatically receiving 5% of the points needed to reach the status level they earned the previous year when a new year begins.
United earlier this year overhauled the way travelers earn miles to reward customers holding its credit cards. The carrier also slashed earnings for basic economy flights, following earlier changes to the same practice by American Airlines and Delta Air Lines. United previously upped the thresholds required to earn Premier status in 2024 for the 2025 qualification year.

articles.title: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI employee who allegedly planted recording device in conference room
articles.text:
An OpenAI employee was arrested after a "sophisticated recording device" was discovered inside its executive conference room, according to the Department of Justice and a post by the company.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9 in connection with the matter, the DOJ said in a release on Tuesday.
The company said an employee planted the device a few days before it was found, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation "moved quickly to make an arrest," the post said. The employee was terminated.
FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology."
Alfozan is also listed as a partner at Raed Ventures, a venture capital firm that focuses on the Middle East and North Africa, according to its website. The firm announced on Feb. 6, 2025, that H.H. Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, had joined the firm as a venture partner. Alfozan was announced as a venture partner two days later.
The Raed announcement for Alfozan lists Meta, Microsoft and SAP as previous roles and said he studied computer science and engineering at MIT.
Raed, which is headquartered in the Saudi capital of Riyadh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI said in the post. "We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance."
Alfozan was not authorized to access the executive conference room where the device was found, according to the DOJ. The department said footage showed him near the conference room on multiple days before the device was discovered. The DOJ said that on Oct. 5, he went into the room.
The DOJ said a bag was also found in the OpenAI building on or about Oct. 5 that belonged to Alfozan. Inside the bag, security found his wallet, ID and another recording device similar to the one that was in the executive conference room.
The department said a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse that "shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan's own chatbot account" was used to get information about continuous audio recording and Wi-Fi. The DOJ said promps were submitted related to "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device."
The device was concealed in toilet paper, and its contents were encrypted, according to the DOJ.
This security incident comes as the ChatGPT-maker, along with competitors like Anthropic and other big tech names, faces heightened scrutiny over safety protocols after a series of cyber incidents where autonomous agents escaped testing environments and hacked into outside systems.
Last week, OpenAI defended its decision to fire three safety researchers, alleging a "significant breach of trust," saying that the researchers "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."
Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni raised safety concerns in a letter to OpenAI's leadership, saying that communications around their exits "have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI."
—CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this article.

articles.title: Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds
articles.text:
Inflation will be in the crosshairs Wednesday as investors digest the latest Consumer Price Index. The reading may be one more sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.
It's a tricky situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to get it.
Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) are one option with "real" yields now at multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.
While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022 — a supply shock due to the Covid pandemic — it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. The headline Consumer Price Index is expected to hit 3.6% in September, partly due to rising energy costs stemming from the war with Iran. The Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, was at a 3% core rate in August.
Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.
TIPS deserve a second look
Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.
Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising interest rates — with the 10-year Treasury note recently hitting multi-year highs around 5.3%. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.
But rising yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS yield is currently at 2.87%, after closing at 2.951% on Oct. 5, levels not seen since November 2008, according to Tradeweb.
"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.
TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.
The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.
TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).
If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.
"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.
TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.
The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.
One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.
If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.
Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.
"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.
Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.
Stocks and other hedges
TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.
"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."
Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.
The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.
"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.
He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.
Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.
Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."
Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.
Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).
Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.
Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).
Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.
"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.
— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

articles.title: Judge says Musk engaged in intimidation of ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans, clears her name
articles.text:
A federal magistrate judge in Virginia ruled that Elon Musk engaged in "state sanctioned intimidation" of ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans when he posted falsehoods on X last year accusing her of "criminal action" and of "funneling $58 million to illegal migrant hotels in Manhattan."
Musk, the world's richest person, was working for the Trump administration as the head of DOGE when he shared those posts on Feb. 11, 2025. The Department of Homeland Security said the next day it was firing Comans and three colleagues, and labeled them "deep state activists."
In Tuesday's order, U.S. Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick cleared Comans' name.
Comans served as FEMA CFO from around January 2018 until February 2025, and was also FEMA's operating chief from 2020 to 2021.
Fitzpatrick wrote in the order that, "The facts establish that high-ranking government officials," including Musk, then a special government employee, had "engaged in a coordinated public relations campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans."
"Mr. Musk was the head of DOGE, he knew or should have known that any payments made to state or local governments through a FEMA grant in February 2025 were approved by his subordinates," the judge wrote.
He added that Musk posted a picture of Ms. Comans "to his millions of followers while falsely characterizing her government service as a 'criminal action,'" an act Fitzpatrick described as "little more than state sanctioned intimidation."
CNBC has reached out to Musk and White House attorneys involved in the case for comment.
Democracy Defenders Fund, which was involved in Comans' case, said in a statement that it was pleased with the decision.
"Mary Comans served in the federal government for 21 years," said Craig Becker, the group's head of affirmative litigation. "Career public servants are people, not pawns, and no one who has devoted their life to serving the American public should have their good name destroyed for partisan, political gain."

articles.title: Mastercard is up 8 days in a row. The charts indicate the run isn't over
articles.text: (See the video above for Jay's complete chart breakdown.) Mastercard shares have been on a tear. The stock is up eight days in a row and is just now ticking to an all-time high. articles.title: Bank of America fined $1.2 billion over money-laundering violations
articles.text:
Bank of America was hit with more than $1.2 billion in federal penalties Tuesday after regulators said the nation's second-largest bank failed for years to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions and fix longstanding anti-money-laundering problems.
More than $1 billion of the unreported activity involved national security and other high-priority risks, including Chinese money-laundering networks and activity tied to the southwest border, Treasury said in a press release.
The action also lands less than a day before the bank reports quarterly earnings Wednesday morning.
Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, which enforces anti-money-laundering rules, said the $1.2 billion penalty is the third-largest in Treasury history. Treasury separately announced an $11.6 million settlement over sanctions violations.
As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money-laundering program, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, according to Treasury.
"Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the press release.
Bank of America said in a statement to CNBC that the bank has invested billions in compliance and is "far along" in remediation efforts.
The bank said the penalties will result in a $1.2 billion non-tax-deductible charge in its third-quarter results, reducing net income by about 17 cents per share. It said remediation costs are already reflected in its current expense base.
"Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," spokesperson Christa Robinson said.
The bank's stock was down about 2% in after-hours trading on the news.
The new penalties will put renewed focus on the record of longtime CEO Brian Moynihan, who took over in 2010 and spent the early years of his tenure resolving tens of billions of dollars in mortgage-related legal and regulatory matters tied largely to decisions made before he became CEO.
For much of the past decade, Moynihan has emphasized what he calls "responsible growth," as Bank of America sought to distance itself from the risk-taking and legal problems that followed the 2008 financial crisis.
Moynihan is scheduled to appear on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" at 10:20 a.m. ET Wednesday following the bank's earnings report.
Treasury says BofA "prioritized its revenues"
Treasury said the bank "prioritized its revenues" while minimizing the impact on compliance resources. The agency said the bank relied so heavily on law-enforcement inquiries and referrals from other financial institutions that regulators said it effectively outsourced part of its responsibility for detecting suspicious activity.
The penalty from Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network came in coordination with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, or OCC, an independent bureau within the department, which announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America.
That sum, which is credited as part of the $1.21 billion total, is the largest penalty OCC has ever levied, the office said.
The office accused the bank of serious violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money laundering rules, and of failing to fix its deficiencies in accordance with a cease-and-desist order it signed in 2024.
"Despite its obligation to the American people as a national-chartered, global systemically important bank, the bank's BSA/AML compliance program continues to reflect widespread breakdowns in internal controls, which threatens U.S. national and economic security," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said in the OCC press release.
"The bank's poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable. The second largest bank's egregious and continued BSA violations warrant the OCC imposing its largest [civil money penalty] ever assessed against a bank," Gould said. "The OCC expects all banks to have an effective BSA/AML compliance program. Those that do not can expect swift and significant action from the OCC."
The 2024 order had identified a "breakdown" in Bank of America's systems for detecting and reporting suspicious activity, including a "systemic failure" to set appropriate thresholds for triggering investigations. It also said the bank had failed to make "acceptable substantial progress" correcting an earlier customer due diligence problem.
Treasury said the failures included red flags involving possible narcotics-trafficking proceeds, fraud and potential trade-based money laundering that were not addressed in a timely way.
Bank of America will also be required to conduct a third-party review for suspicious transactions that went undetected and undergo independent reviews of its transaction-monitoring and customer due-diligence programs, Treasury said.
– CNBC's Hugh Son contributed to this report.

articles.title: We're upgrading our rating on Wells Fargo as the stock's pullback offers a nice entry point
articles.text: Wells Fargo shares dipped 2% Tuesday after the bank reported mixed third-quarter results. However, we think better days are ahead as management's efforts to improve returns take hold, and we're upgrading the stock as a result. Total revenue at the bank increased 2% year over year to $21.9 billion in the third quarter, missing the LSEG-compiled consensus estimate of $22.3 billion. Earnings per share (EPS) for the three months ending Sept. 30 rose 13% to $1.87, beating the $1.85 consensus estimate. Bottom line We're not surprised to see a bit of weakness on Tuesday due to misses on key operating lines. Revenue missed expectations by $430 million, with shortfalls from both net interest income (NII) and non-interest income, a collection of Wells' fee-based businesses. Non-interest expenses came in below expectations, which is encouraging, but the $112 million beat versus the FactSet consensus didn't make up for all of the top-line softness. Given the bank's sensitivity to interest rates, we should start to see NII trend higher in this higher-rate environment. Net interest margin (NIM) — a key measure of a profitability, measuring the spread between what a bank earns on loans and pays out on deposits — stabilized quarter over quarter at 2.43%. This is in keeping with what CFO Michael Santomassimo said at a Barclays conference last month . The stabilization was a big deal because it ended four straight quarters of sequential declines, and the trend is expected to continue into the fourth quarter. It also beat expectations of 2.41%, which is notable because the bank entered today with misses in nine of the past 10 quarters. The bank said the better-than-expected performance was driven by slightly higher cash and securities balances, slightly lower funding costs, and additional efficiency in the deployment of its markets balance sheet. For Wells, a lot of attention is placed on NII and how the bank's NIM performs relative to the yield curve. However, we do not think investors should ignore the progress being made in building out a competitive investment bank — a big priority for CEO Charlie Scharf. Within investment banking, Wells Fargo's dedication to strengthening its client coverage is paying off through improved equity capital market share — up 84 basis points to 3.9% — and an improvement in the announced U.S. M & A volume ranking, going to No. 6 from No. 9 one year ago. Markets revenue within investment banking fell 1% year over year, mostly due to a decline in fixed income, currencies, and commodities, or FICC. Goldman Sachs also experienced a year over year decline in FICC revenue, although its decline was less pronounced than Wells Fargo's. We upgraded Goldman earlier Tuesday. More broadly in fees, non-interest income declined about 1% year over year despite growth across investment advisory, deposit-related fees, investment banking, and card fees. Lower net gains in trading activities, lower lease income after the sale of its railcar-leasing business , and lower gains from equity securities weighed on the result. Finally, the company isn't seeing any issues on the consumer credit side. The bank's charge-off ratio fell from the second quarter and year-ago period, while early-stage delinquencies are at historically low levels. Corporate credit is also strong with only 18 basis points of losses in the third quarter. All in, we're not surprised to see Wells Fargo shares move lower after a revenue miss. But Tuesday's decline — combined with the stock's 6% pullback since the start of September — could present a buying opportunity as the bank begins to see the benefits of stabilizing net interest margins and higher net interest income from elevated interest rates. This will flow through to its return on tangible common equity, another key metric for evaluating bank performance. An improved ROTCE over time will help the stock re-rate to a higher multiple on tangible book value per share. We are upgrading our rating on Wells Fargo to buy-equivalent 1 from 2, while keeping our $95 price target. Quarterly commentary Wells Fargo's Efficiency Ratio was a little worse than expected, falling 200 basis points year over year to 63%. The consensus estimate was 62.1%, according to FactSet. Remember, this is one of those key metrics where lower is better because it's a measure of how much non-interest expense goes into each dollar of revenue generated. Return on Tangible Common Equity (ROTCE) increased nicely year over year to 16.3% from 15.2% in the year ago period. It also exceeded expectations of about 16%. The year-over-year improvement moved the bank closer to management's stated target of 17% to 18%. The bank's ROTCE last quarter fell within that range. Tangible Book Value Per Share (TBVPS) increased slightly to $44.46, missing what the Street was expecting. Common Equity Tier 1 Ratio (CET1), which measures capital versus risk-weighted assets, came in a tick below expectations, but still well above bank's 8.5% regulatory minimum. As a result, the bank remains well-positioned with the capital needed to invest in the business while returning cash to shareholders. On that note, Wells Fargo repurchased $2.5 billion of stock in the quarter. That is down from the $3 billion repurchased in the second quarter, and it may have been disappointing to some looking for a larger buyback. Segment commentary Consumer Banking and Lending revenue increased 5% year over year. Consumer, Small and Business Banking (CSBB) revenue increased 7% year over year due to higher deposit balances, wider deposit spreads, higher deposit related fees, investment advisory fees, and higher volume on debit card fees. Credit card revenue growth was 3% on higher NII on higher loan balances and card fees. Home lending fell 15% due to lower mortgage services income and lower NII on lower loan balances. Commercial Banking saw revenue advance 6% year over year. Net interest income grew 9% on higher deposit and loan balances. Corporate and Investment Banking revenue increased 3% year over year. Banking revenue, which includes lending, treasury management and payments, and investment banking, was up 8% year over year. All three lines of business grew revenue year over year. Commercial real estate revenue dipped 1% year over year due to lower capital markets activity. Non-interest expense grew faster than revenues at 4% year over year due to higher personnel expense and professional and outside services expense. Wealth and Investment Management revenue increased 12% year over year with a balanced mix of Net Interest Income growth and Non-Interest Income growth. Non-Interest expense increased 9% year over year on higher revenue related compensation expense. 2026 guidance Wells Fargo kept its NII outlook for the year unchanged at plus or minus $50 billion. For the fourth quarter, the bank expects NII to be about $13 billion, which is better than the consensus estimate of $12.86 billion, according to FactSet. Fourth-quarter NIM is also expected to remain stable from the third quarter, implying 2.43% versus Street expectations of 2.41%. Non-interest expenses in 2026 were also reiterated to be about $55.7 billion, which is in line with the consensus estimate, according to FactSet. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long WFC, GS.
